comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose eliminating the grace period of up to 60 days. DHS has not shown that the administrative work saved would justify the disruption created.

The 1.9 million filings cited in Section IV.C measure potentially relevant cases, not hours saved. Footnote 29 says DHS cannot estimate the extra review time. Removing the grace period would not necessarily remove the need to check employment end dates or maintenance of status. It could also move work into enforcement, immigration courts, and departure and reentry processing. The 37 FY 2025 notices involving H-1B beneficiaries who exceeded the grace period describe what happened with that protection in place. They do not predict what happens when it disappears. I request a comparison of work avoided and added across agencies, using reasonable estimates where needed. Fees may pay for processing, but the work still has to be done.

The estimate of affected people also needs explanation. DHS describes 3,795 workers annually as an upper bound, although footnote 49 identifies missing employer notifications and visa categories with no notification requirement. Some records may include workers who never needed the grace period, while others omit people who did. I ask DHS to explain why possible overcounts support an upper bound despite the omissions. Dependents cannot be reliably counted either. These limits do not prove a large impact, but they also cannot establish a small one.

I am particularly concerned about businesses losing employees they still need. Consider a working dependent spouse whose authorization depends on the principal worker's status. One dismissal could force that spouse to stop working at another company. Where the spouse remains authorized during the grace period, that employer has a chance to retain the employee while the family finds another lawful option, or at least prepare for a handover. A prospective employer also loses time to interview and hire the principal worker. Hiring from abroad may remain possible, but travel and visa delays can make a planned hire impractical. DHS recognized these hiring benefits in 2016 (81 FR 82437-82439). A limited transition between qualifying jobs can serve an employment-based system. It does not itself authorize work, is available once per authorized validity period, ends sooner if that validity expires, and remains subject to DHS's discretion. Congress not requiring 60 days does not, by itself, explain why eliminating that transition is justified.

A worker dismissed after reporting misconduct may need time to collect evidence and seek help. In 2016, DHS declined a separate 30-day retaliation provision because the broader 60-day period addressed that need (81 FR 82454). I ask DHS to explain how the remaining remedies replace that practical opportunity, including whether workers and dependents can maintain status while seeking help. The proposed change to 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i) also removes the grace-period filing window for eligible compelling-circumstances applicants. Calling the amendment technical does not address that loss of access.

For families, a job loss could become an immediate international move. Section IV.D says affected workers and dependents would fail to maintain status the next day unless otherwise authorized to remain. Federal layoff-notice rules do not cover every dismissal. A person cannot always arrange flights, resolve medical travel restrictions, or obtain a child's travel documents that quickly. Willingness to comply does not make departure possible. Footnote 13 recognizes possible consequences for future immigration benefits, although a status violation does not automatically bar return. The rule could therefore create violations for people trying to leave responsibly. It could also separate family members, interrupt treatment and schooling, and force lease penalties or rushed sales. Employer-paid return transportation for certain dismissed H-1B and O-1 workers does not solve those problems. Section V.F should assess the difference between the same job loss with time to respond and without it. Some families could avoid departure by finding another lawful option.

I recognize DHS's authority to change policy. But families can reasonably make plans around an established regulation without assuming its protection is guaranteed. I request consideration of those commitments and transition protections under DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1 (2020). I also ask DHS to revisit clearer evidence requirements, which Section IV.E acknowledges could reduce work. The fact that some review would remain is not enough to justify removing the protection. A reasoned decision must connect the facts to the action chosen (State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)). I request withdrawal of this proposal and narrower administrative improvements that preserve the existing grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Opposition to the Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period and Request for Reasonable Exemptions
As a long-term legal non-immigrant worker, homeowner, and taxpaying resident of the United States for the past 14 years, I am writing to express deep concern regarding the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period. While I understand the agency's regulatory objectives, an immediate, same-day departure requirement upon job separation creates an unfeasible, highly disruptive burden on long-term visa holders, their families, and the broader financial and housing markets.
Specifically, this rule introduces critical challenges in the following areas:
1. Disruption to U.S. Citizen Children’s Education: Immediate departure forces minor children—who are U.S. citizens—to abruptly pull out of school without a logical transition. This sudden uprooting causes severe educational interruptions and psychological stress, forcing them to transition to an unfamiliar educational system overnight.
2. Severe Financial & Real Estate Vulnerability: Long-term residents establish deep roots, including property ownership tied to mortgages. Requiring immediate departure makes it virtually impossible to responsibly sell real estate, vacate properties, or manage existing mortgages. This not only places an overwhelming financial burden on the family through potential foreclosures or forced distressed sales, but it also introduces unnecessary risk to mortgage lenders and the housing market.
3. Logistical Impossibility: Packing an entire household, securing international travel arrangements for a family on a moment's notice, and winding up 14 years of settled life within hours is logistically impossible.
Proposed Constructive Alternatives:
Rather than completely eliminating the grace period without recourse, USCIS should consider incorporating sensible exemptions or a buffered transition window (e.g., 60 to 180 days) under specific circumstances:
Education Protection Window: Grant a buffered transition period for families with school-aged U.S. citizen children to allow them to finish the current school year or achieve a logical, structured transfer to a new school.
Tenure-Based Consideration: Provide a reasonable transition period for non-immigrant workers who have maintained legal status and worked in the U.S. for a significant duration (e.g., 5+ years), recognizing their long-term contributions and anchored assets.
Property & Mortgage Protection: Implement provisions or transition timelines for homeowners with active housing loans to prevent forced defaults and foreclosures, protecting both the borrower's credit/financial standing and the lenders from unnecessary risk.
I respectfully request that USCIS re-evaluate this proposed rule and introduce balanced, feasible safeguards that prevent extreme financial hardship, protect U.S. citizen children from educational disruption, and safeguard the stability of the housing market.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against eliminating the grace period, citing severe disruptions to families, children, and finances.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To USCIS and the Department of Homeland Security:

I respectfully urge you to preserve the existing up-to-60-day grace period for H-1B workers. Please consider what losing this protection would mean for workers and families who have spent years building their lives in the United States.

As an H-1B worker with an approved I-140, I have worked hard, paid taxes, followed immigration rules, and patiently continued through the immigration process. My career and my family’s future are rooted here. It is frightening to think that an unexpected job loss could put everything we have worked toward at risk.

This issue is deeply personal to me. My son is a NICU baby, and that experience has made me especially aware of how vulnerable a family can be when their child needs medical care. When your baby needs the support of a neonatal intensive care unit, your attention is on your child’s health and the hope of bringing your baby home safely.

Please consider a parent who loses their job while their baby is still in the NICU. That parent would already be facing fear, exhaustion, and financial uncertainty. Without the grace period, they would also have to urgently navigate their immigration situation while trying to remain beside their hospitalized child.

A family in that situation cannot simply pack up and move to another country. A baby in an incubator cannot be treated as though international travel is an ordinary relocation decision. Parents must rely on their child’s medical team to determine when travel is safe and how any necessary care can continue. They may need time to arrange medical records, find appropriate specialists, and coordinate care in another country. These decisions must center on the baby’s health.

Even the existing 60 days may be a very short time for a family facing a medical crisis. Removing that protection would make an already overwhelming situation much harder. No parent should have to sit beside their baby in the NICU wondering how an unexpected layoff will affect their ability to stay close and maintain continuity of care.

My concern also extends to the many other H-1B families who could face serious disruption after a job loss. A layoff can happen without warning because of restructuring, budget cuts, or a canceled project. A worker can perform well and follow every rule and still lose their job through no fault of their own.

Finding another qualifying employer takes time. Applications, interviews, background checks, hiring approvals, and immigration petition preparation involve steps outside the worker’s control. Even when an employer wants to hire someone immediately, the required process cannot always happen immediately. The grace period gives both the worker and the employer a reasonable opportunity to complete those steps.

Families also have responsibilities that cannot be resolved overnight: housing, medical treatment, school, car payments, and other financial commitments. If leaving the country becomes necessary, they need time to make responsible arrangements, especially when a child has medical needs.

As a parent, I want my son to have a stable childhood, an excellent education, and the opportunity to grow up alongside people from different cultures and backgrounds. I want him to feel secure and have the chance to pursue his dreams. It is painful to think that a sudden job loss could disrupt his care, his education, and the future we are working to provide for him. Many H-1B parents share these hopes and fears.

For those of us with approved I-140 petitions, the uncertainty is especially difficult. We have already invested years in the employment-based immigration process, but our ability to remain here still depends on our employment while we wait.

I respectfully ask DHS to retain, at minimum, the existing up-to-60-day grace period and give serious consideration to families facing hospitalization or other medical emergencies. Preserving this time also helps U.S. employers hire experienced workers who can continue contributing their skills, paying taxes, and supporting their communities.

Please consider the parent sitting beside a baby’s incubator when evaluating this proposal. Behind every immigration petition is a person, and often a family, trying to build a secure life while following the rules. An unexpected job loss is difficult enough. Please preserve the time we need to respond responsibly and care for the people who depend on us.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter urges USCIS to preserve the existing 60-day grace period to protect families facing sudden job loss.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Hi Sir/Madam,
I am a non-immigrant worker living and working in Texas. I would like to express my concern and strongly oppose any proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers following the termination of their employment.

In Texas, employment can be terminated with very little notice, sometimes even on the same day. If the 60-day grace period is removed, H-1B workers and their families could face an extremely difficult situation, potentially being forced to leave the United States immediately. This would create serious challenges in several areas:

1. Sudden Job Termination and Immigration Challenges

In Texas, an employer may terminate an employee with little or no advance notice. Requiring H-1B workers to leave the country immediately after termination would create an unfair and extremely stressful situation. Workers need reasonable time to explore new employment opportunities and manage their immigration status.

2. Children’s Education and Emotional Well-Being

Children’s education is one of the most important concerns for immigrant families. Imagine children who have attended the same American school for 5–10 years being forced to leave without preparation. Such a sudden disruption can cause significant emotional distress, psychological difficulties, and educational setbacks.

3. Serious Financial Hardships

Many H-1B families have invested their life savings in homes, vehicles, and other essential assets in the United States. Selling a house, managing a mortgage, and settling financial obligations cannot happen overnight. Forced immediate departure could result in substantial financial losses and unnecessary hardship.

4. Disruption to Children’s Academic Progress

Children who have spent many years in the American education system cannot easily transition to schools in their home countries without preparation. Finding suitable schools, obtaining academic records, completing admission procedures, and adjusting to a different curriculum all require time.

5. Loss of Personal and Household Assets

Families own cars, furniture, televisions, appliances, and other valuable household belongings. These assets cannot realistically be sold or transferred within a single day. Immediate departure would force families to abandon their belongings or sell them at significantly reduced prices.

6. A Reasonable Grace Period Benefits Everyone

The 60-day grace period provides H-1B workers with a reasonable opportunity to find another employer, transfer their H-1B status where eligible, and continue contributing their skills and experience to the American workforce.

This benefits not only employees and their families but also American businesses, which can retain experienced and skilled professionals rather than lose valuable talent unnecessarily.

My Request
I respectfully request that policymakers retain the existing 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and their families.

Losing a job should not mean losing the opportunity to protect one’s children’s education, financial stability, and family well-being overnight.

A reasonable transition period is not a special privilege; it is a humane and practical policy that recognizes the realities of family life, employment, and financial responsibilities.

Giving H-1B workers reasonable time to transition is a WIN-WIN situation for employees, American employers, and the United States economy.

Thank you for considering the challenges faced by thousands of hardworking immigrant families.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes eliminating the grace period, citing sudden job termination, family hardship, and education disruption.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Arun R
comments.commentText:
Subject: A Call to Preserve and Expand the H-1B 60-Day Grace Period – Protecting Families, Children, and American Communities

I strongly urge policymakers to maintain and consider expanding the existing 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders following involuntary employment termination.

Losing a job is already one of life’s most stressful experiences. For H-1B professionals, however, an unexpected layoff can have consequences that extend far beyond unemployment. It can place an entire family’s immigration status, housing, financial security, and children’s education at risk.

A reasonable grace period is not a special privilege. It is a necessary safeguard that recognizes the human realities behind employment-based immigration.

H-1B Families Are Part of America’s Communities

Thousands of H-1B professionals have spent years building their lives in the United States. They contribute to the economy, pay federal, state, and local taxes, purchase homes, support local businesses, and actively participate in their communities.

Many have mortgages, car loans, financial commitments, and children growing up in American schools. Their lives are deeply interconnected with the communities they call home.

When an unexpected layoff occurs, requiring families to make life-changing decisions within an extremely limited timeframe creates tremendous uncertainty and hardship.

The 60-day grace period provides an essential opportunity to find another employer, explore lawful immigration alternatives, manage financial responsibilities, and make relocation arrangements if necessary. An expanded grace period would offer an even more realistic opportunity to navigate these circumstances without forcing families into rushed and potentially devastating decisions.

U.S.-Born Children Should Not Bear the Consequences of Their Parents’ Job Loss

Perhaps the most important consideration is the impact on children, especially U.S.-born children who are American citizens.

These children attend American schools, build friendships, participate in extracurricular activities, and develop their identities within their communities. Their education and childhood stability should not be abruptly disrupted because of an employment decision beyond their parents’ control.

Relocating an entire family internationally is not an overnight exercise. Parents need time to coordinate with schools, secure academic records, arrange housing and transportation, manage household belongings, and prepare children emotionally for a potentially life-changing transition.

An insufficient transition period can result in children being pulled out of school unexpectedly, interrupted academic progress, and significant emotional distress.

Providing parents with adequate time is not simply an immigration accommodation; it is a meaningful way to protect children’s educational continuity, emotional well-being, and family stability.

While immigration status and employment regulations must be respected, the policies governing these transitions should also recognize the welfare of children and the practical realities faced by American families.

A Reasonable Policy With Meaningful Human Impact

The purpose of the grace period should be to provide a meaningful opportunity for transition—not merely a short administrative window that leaves families struggling to make impossible decisions.

Preserving the existing 60-day provision is essential, but policymakers should also consider expanding the period to 90 or 180 days, particularly in circumstances involving involuntary layoffs and families with school-aged children.

Such a change would provide greater flexibility without diminishing the importance of immigration compliance. It would recognize the contributions of skilled immigrants while demonstrating compassion toward families facing circumstances they did not choose.

America benefits from attracting global talent, but its commitment should extend beyond employment. It should also recognize the families, children, and communities that grow alongside that talent.

I strongly support maintaining and expanding the H-1B grace period to ensure that legal immigrant professionals and their families are treated with fairness, dignity, and humanity during difficult transitions.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly urges policymakers to maintain or expand the existing 60-day grace period.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose DHS's proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364; RIN 1615-AD22).

I am a resident of Mountain View, California, in the heart of Silicon Valley, where many of my neighbors, colleagues, and friends work lawfully in E, H-1B, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, and TN status. Since 2017, workers, their families, and their employers have structured their lives around this grace period — leases and mortgages, children's schooling, and the time needed to find a new sponsoring employer. These are exactly the reliance interests DHS asked commenters to address, and they are substantial.

Ending a worker's status the day after employment ends — often because of a layoff or project cancellation entirely outside the worker's control — would force abrupt departures, separate families, and uproot U.S.-citizen children. It would also make H-1B portability practically unusable, because no new petition can realistically be prepared and filed overnight, and it would harm U.S. employers and competitiveness by driving skilled workers out of the country over a short, involuntary gap in employment.

The existing grace period is already modest: it is discretionary, capped at 60 days, and never extends beyond the worker's authorized validity period. DHS has not shown abuse proportionate to eliminating it entirely. Less drastic alternatives — retaining the grace period, or at most narrowing it — would address any stated concern without these harms.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully request that the Department of Homeland Security reconsider and withdraw its proposal to remove 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), which provides a grace period for certain employment-based visa holders following job loss.

This provision gives workers and their families reasonable time to find new employment or make arrangements to maintain their immigration status, particularly when job loss is beyond their control. The NPRM's own data show that the grace period serves a substantial population, while the potential consequences of removing it have not been adequately measured.

USCIS guidance provides a straightforward start date: the day after the last day for which wages are paid. The NPRM's 1.9 million figure includes filings where the grace period "could have potentially applied," not necessarily cases where it was used. DHS also admits it cannot estimate the additional administrative time involved (footnote 29).

Meanwhile, DHS acknowledges that removal could increase Notices to Appear (NTAs), EOIR referrals and ICE workload. FY2025 had only 37 such NTAs. Practitioners also anticipate more I-539 change-of-status filings and consular processing abroad, potentially shifting rather than reducing the administrative burden. If documentation is the concern, a standard evidentiary requirement, such as a final pay stub or termination letter, would be a practical alternative. DHS considered this option but rejected it based on its alignment rationale.

The proposal does not establish that the existing grace period is unlawful. INA 214(a) provides DHS authority that it previously exercised when establishing this provision in 2016.

Congress recognized employment mobility through H-1B portability under INA 214(n) and AC21, allowing eligible workers to begin employment with a new employer upon filing the required petition. F-1 visa holders also receive a 60-day grace period, while J-1 holders generally receive 30 days.

A worker unexpectedly laid off, particularly without notice, has not necessarily violated any immigration requirement. Immediate loss of status would effectively penalize workers for an employer's business decision. A reasonable transition period supports the objectives of employment-based immigration programs.

In DHS v. Regents (2020), the Supreme Court emphasized that agencies reversing long-standing policies must consider reliance interests.

For nearly ten years, workers and families have made significant commitments based on this provision, including purchasing homes, enrolling children in schools and signing leases. H-4, L-2 and E dependent spouses authorized to work may also lose status when the principal visa holder loses employment, leaving entire families with little time to make alternative arrangements.

Describing family impact as "negligible" is difficult to support when DHS acknowledges it lacks sufficient family-level data to estimate the number affected.

Removing the grace period could prevent employers from retaining already-vetted talent without waiting for consular processing abroad. It also shifts return-transportation costs onto employers who lay off H-1B and O-1 employees.

Reduced employment mobility may increase worker dependence on existing employers, potentially affecting wage negotiations and employment conditions, with broader implications for U.S. colleagues as well.

Recommendations

I respectfully request that the Administration:

Withdraw the proposed rule and retain the existing grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

Alternatively, retain the grace period and establish a clear evidentiary standard, such as a final pay stub or termination letter, to determine its start date.

At minimum, preserve the grace period for involuntary job losses and affected dependents.

The grace period provides a reasonable transition for workers who have complied with immigration requirements. It supports employment mobility, family stability and employers' ability to retain experienced professionals.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and preserve this important protection.

Thank you for considering these comments.
comments.reason: The commenter asks DHS to withdraw the proposal and keep the grace period for visa holders.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear USCIS Leadership,

I am writing to formally oppose the proposed removal of the discretionary 60-day grace period. Having worked lawfully in the United States on an H-1B visa for more than 16 years, I currently hold a senior position at one of the leading organizations in my industry sector. Over the past decade and a half, I have strictly adhered to every U.S. immigration requirement while contributing to American economic growth and tax revenues.

Rescinding the 60-day transition window undermines settled administrative law principles, weakens statutory protections enacted by Congress, and directly harms U.S. businesses:

• Disregard for Settled Reliance Interests Under the Administrative Procedure Act. Under controlling Supreme Court precedent, a federal agency reversing a longstanding regulation must weigh the serious reliance interests built around the prior rule. Since the 2016 AC21 regulations took effect, my family and hundreds of thousands of others—alongside our U.S. employers—structured major financial, housing, and multi-year green card sponsorship commitments around the predictability of a 60-day transition buffer. Abruptly eliminating this safeguard without accounting for those deeply rooted commitments is arbitrary and unfair.

• Erosion of Statutory H-1B Portability Under AC21. When Congress passed the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act (AC21), it created job portability so skilled professionals could move between U.S. employers upon the filing of a new petition without halting critical projects. Because a change of employer requires maintaining valid underlying status, removing the 60-day window makes AC21 portability practically unworkable after a sudden layoff—forcing workers out of status before a prospective employer can even obtain a Labor Condition Application and file a transfer.

• Hiring Uncertainty, Loss of Competitiveness, and Incentivized Employment Discrimination. Imposing severe transition risks and administrative burdens on companies will create profound uncertainty in the minds of U.S. employers regarding the hiring of visa-based talent in the future. By making foreign professionals vulnerable to overnight departure, the rule directly inhibits American firms from recruiting top global talent needed to stay competitive, while creating perverse incentives for employers to discriminate against qualified candidates based on citizenship or visa status—directly undermining federal anti-discrimination protections under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. § 1324b) and Title VII.

• Direct Harm to U.S. Businesses, Startups, and Economic Growth. In my senior role at a top industry company, I hold specialized expertise that competing U.S.-based firms actively seek to leverage to grow their revenues and profitability. Eliminating the 60-day bridge leaves zero time for another American employer—particularly emerging startups and mid-sized innovators that rely on recruiting seasoned talent during corporate restructurings—to file a transfer petition.

• Counterproductive Administrative and Consular Bottlenecks. Rather than reducing agency workload, a zero-day cutoff will trigger a wave of emergency filings, expedited requests, and complex status-violation adjudications that slow down regular petition processing across all industries. Simultaneously, forcing displaced workers abroad for visa stamping simply exports the backlog to the Department of State, lengthening embassy wait times for all travelers.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the 60-day discretionary grace period so that statutory portability, settled reliance interests, fair hiring practices, and U.S. business competitiveness remain protected.

Thank you
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed removal of the grace period and argues it harms workers and businesses.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As a current H-1B visa holder, I am deeply concerned about the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period. This change would introduce unnecessary uncertainty into the lives of professionals who have followed the legal immigration process and built their careers in the United States.

Losing a job is difficult enough without the immediate threat of losing one's immigration status. Employment termination is not always a reflection of an individual's performance or abilities. Layoffs, restructuring, and economic downturns are often beyond an employee's control. Yet, under this proposal, even highly qualified professionals could face immediate consequences for circumstances they had no role in creating.

Securing a new position is not an overnight process. For H-1B workers, it involves finding an employer willing to sponsor them, completing interviews, navigating legal requirements, and preparing immigration filings. Eliminating the grace period would make this transition unnecessarily difficult.

More concerning is the power imbalance this could create in the workplace. When an employee's ability to remain in the country depends entirely on uninterrupted employment, the freedom to report unfair treatment, negotiate working conditions, or change employers becomes severely constrained.

The 60-day grace period provides a reasonable safeguard against these circumstances. It does not guarantee employment or indefinite permission to remain in the country. It simply allows individuals a limited opportunity to navigate an unexpected career disruption responsibly.

I strongly urge DHS to retain this provision. A lawful worker should not face the possibility of having to uproot their entire life immediately because of a single employment decision beyond their control.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period creates unfair hardship and advocates for keeping it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Comment Opposing the Proposed Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

1. I am exactly the worker whose settled reliance this rule would upend.

I write as a worker in H-1B status in the U.S. technology sector, with an employment-based immigrant petition currently pending with USCIS. Like many affected workers, I hold a long-term housing lease and my children are enrolled in local schools. Every one of these commitments — the lease, the children's schooling, the pending green-card case — was made under a regulatory framework that has included the 60-day grace period since 2016. A decade of workers, employers, landlords, and schools have built plans on it. Eliminating it outright, rather than adjusting it, is a reversal of longstanding policy, and the reliance it disrupts is not abstract: it is leases signed, children enrolled, and immigrant petitions pending.

2. DHS's own analysis concedes the harm and proceeds anyway.

The proposal acknowledges that eliminating the grace period could impose real financial and logistical hardship on affected workers — airfare and transportation costs, lease-termination fees, time spent arranging a sudden departure, and lost income — and DHS's own estimate puts roughly 3,795 workers at risk of lost income from a forced, immediate departure. An agency that identifies concrete, foreseeable harm to thousands of law-abiding workers and then finalizes the rule unchanged will have to explain to a reviewing court why that record supports its decision rather than undermines it.

3. The stated justification does not survive its own terms.

DHS says the rule would "restore a direct relationship" between status and the underlying employment and reduce administrative burden. But the burden does not disappear — it moves. Workers who lose their jobs will not vanish; they will file emergency change-of-status applications, seek the discretionary relief USCIS still retains the authority to grant, or depart and trigger consular reprocessing. Each of those paths consumes more agency resources than the grace period ever did, while adding litigation risk on top. A rule that increases the very burden it claims to reduce is not reasoned decisionmaking.

4. "Depart immediately" is not a workable instruction for families.

Under the proposal, a worker — and the worker's spouse and children in dependent status — would fail to maintain status the day after employment ends, and would be expected to leave the country immediately. There is no realistic way for a family with a lease, school enrollment, and a pending immigrant petition to wind down a life in 24 hours. The practical result is not orderly departure; it is families forced to choose between an impossible timeline and accruing unlawful presence, with its 3- and 10-year bars — a penalty wildly disproportionate to losing a job through no fault of one's own.

5. The rule damages the U.S. employers and industries it claims to protect.

H-1B, L-1, O-1, and TN workers are, by definition, already vetted, employed, and contributing — many in the data-infrastructure and AI teams American companies depend on. Forcing experienced engineers out of the country mid-project the day after a layoff does not protect American workers; it strands their teams, their managers, and their projects. The grace period exists precisely so that a job loss becomes a job search rather than a deportation. Removing it converts ordinary labor-market churn into forced departures of the workers the U.S. immigration system has already selected.

6. Request.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule. At a minimum, DHS should (a) retain a grace period rather than eliminating it outright — even a shortened one preserves the rule's function; (b) exempt workers with pending immigrant petitions, for whom a forced departure destroys years of lawful process; and (c) provide a meaningful transition period so workers and employers who relied on the decade-old regulation can adjust.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly urges DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and keep the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Runhan Li
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

Finding a new job in the United States is already extremely difficult, especially in the current challenging job market. Even highly skilled and experienced professionals can face unexpected layoffs, company restructuring, hiring freezes, and lengthy recruitment processes. Losing a job is already a stressful and financially difficult experience. Removing the 60-day grace period would add an unnecessary layer of uncertainty and hardship to people who have spent years building their careers and lives in the United States.

The 60-day grace period is not an unreasonable privilege. It provides a very limited and necessary transition window for individuals to find another qualifying employer, explore alternative immigration options, settle their financial and personal affairs, or prepare to return to their home countries if they cannot secure another opportunity.

For many of us, the United States is not simply a place where we came to work temporarily. We have spent many years here, contributed our professional skills to American companies, paid taxes, purchased homes, supported local communities, and raised families. Our children may attend American schools, and our spouses may have careers and lives established here. Losing a job should not mean that an entire family must suddenly uproot its life with virtually no time to prepare.

Eliminating the grace period would create a particularly difficult situation for workers who are already facing circumstances beyond their control. Finding a new employer willing to sponsor a work visa is not something that can happen overnight. Interviews, hiring approvals, immigration attorney consultations, petition preparation, and USCIS processing all take time. Even when a new employer is willing to hire someone, completing the necessary immigration procedures can take weeks or longer.

I also want to highlight that DHS itself acknowledges in the proposed rule that individuals and their dependents may have made significant personal and financial commitments in reliance on the existing grace period, including purchasing homes, paying taxes, and investing in local communities. These are real reliance interests that deserve meaningful consideration.

Furthermore, the original 2016 AC21 rule introduced the grace period partly to help highly skilled workers respond to unexpected employment termination and allow U.S. employers to retain and recruit experienced talent more easily. Eliminating this protection could make the United States a less attractive and less predictable place for international professionals to build long-term careers.

I respectfully urge USCIS to reconsider this proposal and retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period.

At a minimum, individuals who unexpectedly lose their employment should be given a reasonable transition period to find another qualifying opportunity or make an orderly departure from the United States. Sixty days is already a very short period when someone must navigate a job search, immigration requirements, housing arrangements, family responsibilities, and potentially an international relocation all at once.

Please remember that behind every immigration petition is a real person, a family, and years of contributions to this country. Giving people 60 days to get their lives in order is not an unreasonable burden on the immigration system. It is a reasonable measure of fairness, stability, and humanity.

I strongly encourage DHS to preserve the 60-day discretionary grace period rather than eliminate it entirely.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to respectfully express my concern about the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers who lose their jobs.

I understand that immigration laws need to be enforced and that the government has a responsibility to prevent misuse of visa programs and protect American workers. I support those goals. However, I believe removing the 60-day grace period would create more problems than it solves.

Losing a job is not always a choice. Companies lay off employees for many reasons, including restructuring, budget cuts, and economic uncertainty. These decisions are often completely outside an employee’s control. Someone who has followed every immigration rule, worked legally, and paid taxes for years should not suddenly face the possibility of having to leave the country simply because their employer eliminated their position.

Finding a new job takes time, even for highly qualified professionals. There are interviews, background checks, internal approvals, and immigration paperwork. Even when another employer is ready to hire someone, the process cannot always be completed immediately. The 60-day grace period provides a reasonable window to navigate these steps. In fact, even 60 days can be challenging in today’s job market.

There is also a human side to this issue that should not be overlooked.

Many H-1B workers have spent a significant portion of their adult lives in the United States. They have built careers, bought homes, started families, and become part of their local communities. Their children may attend American schools, and their spouses may have careers of their own. Asking these families to uproot their lives immediately after an unexpected job loss seems unnecessarily harsh.

I also worry about the unintended consequences for American businesses. If a company wants to hire an experienced professional who is already living and working in the United States, why make that process more difficult? Removing the grace period could mean losing qualified workers who would otherwise continue contributing to American companies and the economy.

Another concern is the increased dependence on employers. H-1B workers already face limitations when changing jobs. Without a reasonable transition period, employees may feel pressured to remain in unhealthy or unfair working environments because losing their job could immediately affect their immigration status. I do not believe that is a healthy outcome for any labor market.

I recognize that the government may have concerns about individuals using the grace period improperly. Those concerns deserve attention. But if misuse exists, I would encourage DHS to address it through targeted enforcement rather than removing the grace period for everyone.

There should be a reasonable middle ground between enforcing immigration laws and treating an unexpected job loss as an immigration emergency.

The 60-day grace period is not a pathway to permanent residency, nor does it guarantee anyone a job. It simply gives people a limited amount of time to find another lawful opportunity, change their immigration status, or make arrangements to leave the country.

I respectfully ask DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period and carefully consider the consequences of eliminating it for workers, families, and American employers.

Immigration policy should be fair, practical, and enforceable. I believe those goals can coexist.

Thank you for taking the time to consider my comment.

Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 / RIN 1615-AD22

Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace PeriodI am a proud U.S. citizen writing in strong support of the proposed rule to remove the discretionary 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).These nonimmigrant classifications exist because an employer claimed a specific need for a particular alien’s services. Continuing to treat the alien as maintaining status for up to two additional months severs the direct relationship Congress established between the visa and the underlying employment or activity. If the talent or services were truly necessary, the employer would not have terminated the relationship. A grace period that exists only after the employment basis disappears primarily serves the convenience of the alien and the next employer who may want to pick them up, not the integrity of the classification or the interests of American workers.The previous policy of tying status tightly to the authorized employment was sound. U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents do not receive a government-sponsored 60-day runway after job loss; neither should temporary nonimmigrants whose status was granted solely because of a specific job.I urge the Department to finalize the rule as proposed and return the regulations to their proper statutory foundation.

I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule and respectfully ask DHS to withdraw it.

Job losses are usually sudden and unanticipated, often with little or no warning. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and USCIS,

I am writing as a current H-1B visa holder, a legally employed professional, and a contributing member of the American workforce to express my strong opposition to the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

While I fully support protecting American workers, preventing immigration fraud, and maintaining the integrity of the H-1B program, I believe this proposal would have serious unintended consequences for both the United States and the thousands of lawful professionals who have built their careers and lives here.

1. Unfair consequences for legally employed H-1B professionals

H-1B workers are already subject to significant immigration restrictions. Our ability to remain in the United States depends heavily on continued employer sponsorship, and changing employers requires additional immigration filings and compliance procedures.

Job losses can occur unexpectedly because of layoffs, restructuring, economic downturns, or circumstances entirely outside an employee's control.

Removing the 60-day grace period would effectively punish individuals who have complied with immigration laws, maintained lawful employment, and contributed to the American economy.

Finding another qualified employer, completing interviews, obtaining sponsorship, and preparing an H-1B transfer petition cannot realistically happen overnight.

2. Negative consequences for the U.S. economy and American employers

The United States benefits from highly skilled professionals working in engineering, technology, healthcare, manufacturing, energy, and other specialized industries.

Many H-1B workers contribute to projects that support American businesses, create economic value, and strengthen domestic technological capabilities.

Forcing experienced professionals to leave the country immediately after an unexpected job loss could result in the loss of valuable expertise, delays to ongoing projects, additional recruitment expenses, and increased operational disruptions for American employers.

It could also discourage international professionals from building long-term careers in the United States, potentially benefiting competing economies that offer greater employment stability.

3. Increased employer dependency and reduced worker protections

H-1B workers already face substantial dependence on their sponsoring employers.

Eliminating the grace period would increase this imbalance by making the consequences of losing employment even more severe.

Workers may become reluctant to report workplace violations, challenge unfair treatment, or seek better employment opportunities because losing their jobs could immediately threaten their ability to remain in the country.

A policy intended to protect American workers should not inadvertently create conditions where another category of lawful workers becomes more vulnerable to exploitation.

4. Disruption to individuals pursuing lawful permanent residency

Many H-1B professionals have spent years working legally in the United States while their employers pursue permanent residency sponsorship through the PERM labor certification and I-140 processes.

These processes involve significant waiting periods, employer investments, legal expenses, and strict compliance requirements.

An unexpected job loss can already jeopardize an individual's long-term immigration plans. Eliminating the grace period would compound this uncertainty, potentially forcing individuals to leave the United States before having a reasonable opportunity to secure another sponsoring employer.

Such a change could undermine the confidence of skilled professionals who have followed the lawful immigration process for years.

5. Severe financial and emotional consequences for families

Many H-1B professionals have established meaningful ties to their communities. They pay federal and state taxes, contribute to Social Security and Medicare, rent or purchase homes, support local businesses, and raise families.

An unexpected termination should not immediately place an entire household at risk of having to abandon its home, employment arrangements, and financial commitments.

The existing grace period provides a limited opportunity to make responsible decisions while maintaining compliance with immigration requirements.

6. The existing 60-day period is already limited and reasonable

The current grace period is not an indefinite right to remain in the United States. It is discretionary, limited to a maximum of 60 days or the remaining authorized validity period, whichever is shorter, and does not independently authorize employment.

It provides a reasonable transition period for affected workers to pursue lawful alternatives or prepare for departure.

Eliminating this protection would create disproportionate hardship without necessarily addressing the underlying concerns about H-1B program misuse.

comments.commentText:
Dear USCIS Leadership,

I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposal to eliminate the 60-day discretionary grace period. As a family that has lived and worked lawfully in the United States on H-1B status for over 16 years, we have built our life, home, and financial future in this country in full compliance with federal law.

Removing this 60-day window creates impossible compliance demands and inflicts severe, avoidable harm on U.S. citizen children and law-abiding households:

• Severe Educational Disruption for U.S. Citizen Children. My wife and I are raising two U.S.-born citizen children—one currently in elementary school and the other having just completed elementary school. Because corporate layoffs frequently occur with little or no advance notice, forcing a family to depart the United States the very next day would pull our U.S. citizen children out of their American schools mid-term during critical transitional years. Relocating abroad overnight carries no guarantee of immediate school enrollment, differing academic calendars could force them to repeat grade levels, and this sudden instability would harm their long-term educational and career prospects.

• Prolonged Separation from Their Home Country. Due to severe visa appointment backlogs at U.S. embassies and consulates abroad, departing immediately after a sudden job loss could prevent our family—and by extension our U.S. citizen children—from returning to the United States in the near term, even when a new U.S. employer is ready to sponsor a transfer.

• Severe Financial, Investment, and Estate Harm. Relying on the stability of the existing 60-day window, we committed to purchasing a U.S. home with a mortgage, investing a substantial down payment and building significant home equity through years of regular payments. My wife and I also hold substantial dollar deposits in U.S. banks and U.S. stock investments that support American capital markets, while consistently paying federal, state, property, and payroll taxes. Being forced to leave overnight without a reasonable window to manage real estate, banking, and investment accounts would cause severe financial losses and directly erode the assets and generational inheritance intended for our two U.S. citizen children.

• Manufacture of Technical Status Violations. Rather than improving compliance, a zero-day rule manufactures unavoidable infractions. When an employee is terminated late on a Friday afternoon, liquidating a household, settling tax and utility accounts, and securing international flights for a family of four before Saturday morning is physically impossible. Because the existing 60-day period is already discretionary, USCIS retains full authority to deny it in cases of fraud without turning compliant families into technical overstays overnight.

For more than sixteen years, our family has respected every rule of the U.S. immigration system. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the 60-day discretionary grace period so families with U.S. citizen children have a fair, orderly transition window.

comments.commentText:
Dear U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services,

I am writing to respectfully oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). While I understand the agency’s intent to maintain orderly immigration enforcement, removing this grace period entirely creates severe, impractical, and humanitarian hardships for lawful nonimmigrant workers, their families, and the U.S. economy.

In the modern economy, layoffs and corporate restructurings often happen without advance notice. Expecting a law-abiding worker to lose their job one day and depart the United States the very next day is logistically impossible. The current 60-day grace period is not a loophole; it is an essential, practical window that allows families who have followed every rule to either secure new authorized employment or wind down their lives in the United States responsibly and lawfully.

Eliminating this period creates immediate, unmanageable crises across multiple areas:

- Impact on Children, Including U.S. Citizen Children: Many H-1B and employment-based visa holders raise families here, including U.S. citizen children and school-aged dependents. Forcing an overnight departure disrupts children’s education mid-semester without time to obtain school records, arrange transfers, or prepare them emotionally. Families with U.S. citizen children also require time to secure passports and travel documentation before international travel is even legally possible.

- Housing, Vehicle Leases, and Personal Property: Lawful workers are deeply integrated into local communities through binding contracts. You cannot terminate a residential apartment lease, sell a home, close utility accounts, or return or sell a leased vehicle in 24 hours.

- Harm to U.S. Banks, Loan Providers, and Credit Institutions: Lawful workers contribute significantly to the U.S. financial system through mortgages, auto loans, personal loans, and credit card accounts. Forcing an abrupt 24-hour departure gives borrowers zero time to sell assets, liquidate accounts, or settle balances before leaving the country. This will inevitably cause unintended loan defaults and unpaid credit balances, passing direct financial losses onto American banks, credit unions, auto lenders, and landlords.

- Harm to U.S. Employers and Talent Retention: Skilled workers who are laid off are often quickly rehired by other American companies facing critical talent shortages. Removing the 60-day window forces experienced, vetted professionals out of the country immediately, depriving U.S. businesses of ready-to-work talent and forcing employers to incur higher costs and delays to recruit and sponsor replacements from abroad.

- Practical Barriers to Immediate Travel: International flights for an entire family on short notice are often unavailable or prohibitively expensive. Packing a household and arranging international logistics take weeks, not hours.

I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the 60-day discretionary grace period so that lawful workers, their families, U.S. employers, and American financial institutions are protected from sudden, avoidable disruption.

Thank you for your time and consideration of these concerns.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers.

I came to the United States to pursue my Master's degree in Computer Science and have since built my professional career here. Like many international professionals, I have invested years of my life in this country, developed my skills, worked for American companies, paid taxes, and contributed to the technology industry.

Losing a job is stressful for anyone. But for someone on an H-1B visa, an unexpected layoff can put their entire life in the United States at risk. Layoffs happen because of restructuring, budget cuts, and changing business conditions. They are not necessarily a reflection of an employee's performance, and employees often have no control over these decisions.

Finding another job within 60 days is not always realistic. The process involves applications, multiple interview rounds, negotiations, finding an employer willing to sponsor a visa, and completing immigration paperwork. Even when someone has the skills and experience another American company needs, hiring and sponsorship can take longer than 60 days.

There is also the uncertainty of visa appointments. For people who need to travel internationally and obtain a new visa stamp, appointment availability at U.S. consulates can be extremely limited. Processing delays make it difficult to predict when someone can return. A new employer may not be willing to wait indefinitely. As a result, the country could lose qualified professionals even when they have found another job.

The impact on families deserves consideration too. Many of us have spent years building lives here. We have purchased homes, taken out long-term mortgages, paid property taxes, enrolled our children in schools, and become part of our communities. These commitments cannot simply be reversed overnight.

Imagine a family with young children suddenly having to worry about mortgage payments, selling their home, disrupting their children's education, and relocating to another country because one parent was laid off. This creates enormous financial and emotional stress for an entire family, including children who have no control over the situation.

I also believe this proposal could work against America's own interests. The United States educates thousands of international students in fields such as computer science, engineering, and science. Many of us earn our degrees here and go on to build careers, develop technology, and contribute to the American economy. It makes little sense to attract and educate global talent, benefit from their contributions for years, and then make it so difficult for them to remain after an unexpected job loss.

The existing 60-day grace period is already limited and discretionary. It does not authorize unauthorized employment or guarantee indefinite stay. It simply provides reasonable time to find another employer, explore lawful immigration options, or make arrangements to leave responsibly. DHS already has discretion to shorten or eliminate the period when circumstances justify it.

I understand the importance of immigration rules and compliance. I simply hope the policy will also consider the realities of employment, family responsibilities, and immigration processing delays.

I respectfully ask DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period. People who have studied here, worked here, paid taxes, purchased homes, and raised families here deserve a reasonable opportunity to deal with an unexpected job loss.

A job loss should not mean that an entire family must put its life on hold or leave the country almost immediately. I sincerely hope DHS will reconsider this proposal and preserve this modest but meaningful protection.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that eliminating the 60-day grace period is unfair because finding a new job takes longer.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an H-1B worker, and I oppose this rule. From the perspective of someone who actually has to live under H-1B rules, the current 60-day grace period is not a luxury. It is barely enough time to comply with the law after a layoff. Eliminating it would make compliance practically impossible for blameless workers.

1. Hiring an H-1B worker is not like hiring anyone else. A new employer cannot simply offer me a job and have me start. The employer must agree to sponsor me, complete internal legal and budget approvals, file a Labor Condition Application, wait through the required posting period, prepare and file Form I-129, and decide whether to pay for premium processing. Many employers will not even consider a candidate who needs sponsorship on a 60-day timeline. Even when an employer is willing, its lawyers and HR do not move at the speed the rule assumes. A 60-day window can be consumed before a petition is even filed.

2. The job search itself takes far longer than 60 days. Specialty occupations in my field involve multiple interview rounds, reference checks, background checks, and internal approvals. Layoffs often happen in waves, so many H-1B workers are competing for the same roles at the same time. If a layoff happens around the holidays or during a slow hiring period, the 60 calendar days include weekends and holidays and leave even fewer actual business days. The rule treats 60 days as if it were 60 working days of uninterrupted job-search time. It is not.

3. H-1B portability does not solve the problem. It is true that an H-1B worker may begin new employment upon the filing of a new petition in some circumstances. But that only helps if a willing employer has already been found and has already prepared and filed the petition. The hard part is getting to that filing. Many employers will not let a worker start until the petition is approved, and premium processing is expensive and not guaranteed. The grace period is what gives workers the chance to reach the filing stage at all.

4. The 60 days are not just for job hunting. They are for arranging an orderly departure if no job is found. In 60 days, a family must decide whether to leave the country, book flights, ship belongings, withdraw children from school, break a lease or sell a home, close accounts, and arrange the transition of dependents whose status is tied to mine. H-4 spouses with work authorization may face confusion about when they must stop working. These are not abstract costs. They are the ordinary logistics of uprooting a family, and 60 days is already a very short time to do them.

5. The rule would punish workers for employer decisions. I do not control whether my employer has a reduction in force. If I am laid off on a Friday, the proposed rule would require me to depart “immediately” after my status ends. That is not a realistic standard. It turns my employer’s business decision into an immediate removal risk for me and my family.

I am not asking for indefinite status. I am asking for enough time to comply with the law. The current 60-day period is already a minimum, not a generous benefit. DHS should withdraw this rule and retain the 60-day grace period. If anything, DHS should consider whether 60 days is sufficient—not eliminate the only transition period H-1B workers have.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that the grace period is essential for compliance and job searching after a layoff.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposal and advocate keeping the 60 day period because it treats leaving the United States as something a family can do as soon as a job ends. Has DHS considered the legal risks when departure is impossible, the financial losses from urgency, and the costs to U.S. employers and agencies?

Section IV.D says affected workers and dependents would fail to maintain status the day after employment ends unless otherwise authorized to remain. Federal layoff-notice protections do not cover every dismissal. Knowing a job might end someday is not notice that it will end today.

Even someone willing to leave may be unable to arrange it immediately. A child may need travel documents, a family member may be medically unable to fly, or flights may not allow everyone to travel together. Removing the grace period could leave families choosing between separation, interrupted care, and remaining after losing status. I ask DHS to explain how people in these circumstances can realistically comply.

Footnote 13 acknowledges that failure to maintain status can affect future immigration benefits. A status violation does not automatically mean unlawful presence or a bar to returning. Still, DHS should examine whether removing the time to comply could itself create violations with later consequences. Section V.A.3.a says employers may bring workers back after a new petition is approved if the worker is admissible. That does not address people unable to leave before falling out of status.

The financial comparison in Section V.A.3.a also concerns me. It treats some departure expenses as costs workers would eventually face anyway. But moving today is financially different from having time to arrange a move. Selling a car over several weeks may bring a reasonable price; selling it immediately may mean a substantial loss. Families may need emergency storage, expensive shipping, last-minute tickets, or paid help handling belongings after departure. Ending a lease abruptly can add penalties.

Employers must cover reasonable return transportation for certain dismissed H-1B and O-1 workers. That does not resolve the cost of moving a household, arrangements for dependents, or medical and travel-document barriers. Some costs also fall on U.S. employers. Paying for departure does not remove the disruption.

I ask DHS to compare the same job loss with the grace period and without it. For someone who ultimately leaves, preparation time can reduce avoidable losses. For someone who finds another qualifying job or lawful option, it can prevent departure altogether. Neither outcome is guaranteed. But DHS should distinguish costs that would arise anyway from costs increased or created by removing the period.

These consequences also matter to the United States. Another U.S. employer may need the worker's skills. Departure can add travel, visa processing, and delays before a new qualifying job can begin. A planned hire may fall through, leaving the employer to recruit again or redistribute unfinished work. These are domestic business costs, not only losses to a departing family.

There may also be added public work if people who would have used the grace period to arrange departure instead fall out of status and face enforcement or removal proceedings. These costs may not exceed the savings, but I ask whether DHS has adequately compared them.

I recognize DHS's authority to change policy. Its explanation should address these consequences. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983), requires a reasoned connection between the relevant facts and the decision. Section V.F's family assessment should also address the added effects of removing preparation time, including disrupted care and possible separation.

I respectfully request that DHS retain the grace period of up to 60 days. Before removing it, DHS should explain how people can realistically comply and why the added financial losses, legal risks, and burdens on U.S. employers and public agencies are justified.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposal and advocates keeping the 60-day grace period.

Eliminating the grace period would hurt more than foreign workers. It would also make it more difficult for U.S. businesses to hire skilled people who are already living and working in the country. Based on DHS's five-year averages in its own Table 3, roughly 3,795 workers per year had new Form I-129 petitions filed on their behalf by new employers during the grace period.
Without the grace period, some of these workers would need to leave the United States and go through further immigration processing abroad before starting with a new employer. Employers would lose strong candidates, see important projects delayed, take on extra immigration expenses, and suffer lost productivity. Small businesses could be hit especially hard, since they often don't have the resources to handle unexpected overseas processing and drawn-out hiring delays.
DHS assumes that affected employers can simply hire other qualified workers, but that overlooks the specialized skills, experience, training, and institutional knowledge each employee brings to their role. U.S. employers should not lose access to qualified workers just because those workers experienced a layoff at their current firm. Eliminating the grace period goes directly against the very purpose of the H1B program which is to access a global talent pool for roles that require highly specialized knowledge. The national interest would be served better by extending the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Eliminating the 60-day grace period for H1B workers could have far reaching consequences, not just for individual employees but for entire families who have built their lives in the United States.

Thousands of immigrants have come to the U.S. through legal employment-based visa programs, built their careers, contributed to the economy, paid taxes, purchased homes, and established stable lives for their families. Their children are growing up here, attending schools, and building their futures. Abruptly removing the grace period would put all of this at risk.

Losing a job is already an emotionally and financially stressful experience. Imagine being told that you must leave the country almost immediately, without reasonable time to find another employer or make essential arrangements for your family.

Sixty days is not an unreasonable luxury. It is a necessary transition period. Families need time to:

- Search for another qualifying job and explore available immigration options.
- Arrange lease termination, housing, and relocation.
- Close bank accounts and manage financial obligations.
- Withdraw children from school and collect their academic and personal records.
- Sell vehicles and other assets that cannot easily be transferred or retained.
- Organize travel, documents, and other essential family arrangements.

These are not tasks that can realistically be completed overnight or within a matter of hours.

H-1B workers have gone through extensive eligibility checks, employer sponsorship, documentation, and legal authorization to work in the United States. While employment authorization is tied to the sponsoring employer, workers should still have a reasonable opportunity to transition to another qualifying employer or explore other lawful immigration options.

This issue goes beyond one employee or one family. It affects spouses, children, employers, schools, communities, and the future stability of thousands of immigrant families.

I urge policymakers to consider the human impact of this proposal and the legitimate reliance interests of families who have built their lives around the existing immigration framework.

**If we put ourselves in the shoes of these families, we can understand that this is not simply an immigration policy change. It is a decision that could disrupt careers, children’s education, financial stability, and years of hard work.**

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear USCIS and Department of Homeland Security,

Thank you for providing the opportunity to share public comments on this proposed rule.

I am currently working in the United States as a software engineer under H-1B status. I understand and respect the importance of maintaining a well-managed immigration system, and I appreciate the work that USCIS does to administer these programs.

I would like to respectfully express my concerns about the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period and share how this change could affect people in situations like mine.

1. Finding a new job and completing immigration paperwork takes time, even when everyone is acting responsibly.

As a machine learning engineer, finding a new position typically involves multiple rounds of technical interviews, coordination with hiring managers, background checks, and internal approvals. Even when an employer is interested in moving forward, these steps can take several weeks.

For H-1B workers, accepting a new job also involves additional immigration procedures, including preparation and certification of the Labor Condition Application (LCA) and filing an H-1B petition.

These processes are largely outside the employee's control. My concern is that without a grace period, someone could receive a job offer from a willing employer but still face difficulties maintaining lawful status while the required paperwork is being completed.

I hope USCIS will consider that the 60-day grace period provides a reasonable opportunity for both employees and employers to complete these steps properly.

2. Unexpected job loss also creates practical challenges in everyday life.

Like many people who have spent years working in the United States, I have built a life here. I have housing commitments, monthly bills, personal belongings, and financial responsibilities that cannot be resolved immediately.

If I were unexpectedly laid off, I would need time to determine whether I could find another employer or whether I should prepare to leave the country.

Arranging international travel, ending an apartment lease, moving personal belongings, and settling financial obligations can be complicated and expensive, especially during a period without income.

The existing grace period gives workers time to make these arrangements thoughtfully and responsibly. Even if someone ultimately needs to leave the United States, having a reasonable transition period can make a significant difference.

3. Many H-1B workers have limited control over unexpected layoffs.

I understand that employment-based immigration status is connected to maintaining qualifying employment, and I fully respect that requirement.

At the same time, layoffs can happen for reasons unrelated to an employee's performance, such as business restructuring, budget changes, or economic conditions.

For someone on H-1B status, losing a job is already a stressful experience because it affects both employment and immigration status.

My concern is that removing the grace period would leave very little room to respond to circumstances that are often beyond an individual's control.

I believe the current 60-day period offers a fair balance. It does not guarantee that someone can remain in the country indefinitely or continue working without authorization. It simply allows a limited amount of time to explore lawful options or prepare for departure.

4. I respectfully hope USCIS will consider preserving this important transition period.

I recognize that DHS may have valid concerns regarding administrative efficiency and the consistent application of immigration rules.

However, I hope those goals can be achieved without removing a provision that provides meaningful stability to workers and their families.

If additional documentation or clearer procedures would help address those concerns, I would welcome such improvements.

My request is simply to preserve the existing 60-day grace period so that individuals who have complied with immigration requirements have a reasonable opportunity to manage an unexpected employment transition.

I am grateful for the professional opportunities I have had in the United States, and I want to continue contributing through my work while respecting the country's immigration laws.

Thank you very much for taking the time to consider my perspective and the practical impact this proposed change could have on people like me.

Sincerely,

An H-1B Worker in the United States
