comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my concern and opposition to the proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and other affected employment-based visa holders.

I have been living and working legally in the United States on an H-1B visa since 2018. Over the past eight years, this country has become my home. I have built my career here, purchased a house, financed a vehicle, made long-term financial commitments, and built a life with my family. Throughout this time, I have followed immigration laws, complied with applicable regulations, paid my taxes, and contributed to the economy and the community in which I live.

I understand that H-1B status is tied to employment, and I respect the requirements that come with maintaining that status. However, losing a job should not mean losing the opportunity to remain in the country long enough to responsibly manage the consequences of that job loss.

Eliminating the 60-day grace period could create significant and unnecessary hardship for individuals and their families.

For someone who has legally lived in the United States for eight, ten, or fifteen years, an unexpected layoff is already a difficult experience. Being required to leave the country immediately would add another layer of uncertainty and stress at a time when the individual and their family are already trying to navigate a major life change.

Many of us have established substantial financial and personal ties to the United States. We have purchased homes and taken on long-term mortgage obligations. We have vehicles with outstanding loans, investments, retirement savings, and other financial commitments accumulated over years of working and saving. Having to leave the country on extremely short notice would make it very difficult to manage these responsibilities properly.

It could also affect the careers and employment of our spouses. In many families, both partners work and have independently established professional lives in the United States. An unexpected departure could disrupt not just one person's career but the livelihood and plans of an entire household.

Finding a new employer willing to sponsor an H-1B transfer takes time. It involves interviewing, receiving an offer, negotiating terms, coordinating with immigration attorneys, preparing documentation, and filing the necessary paperwork. Even when someone is highly qualified and actively pursuing employment, these processes cannot realistically be completed overnight.

The 60-day grace period provides a critical window to navigate this process. It gives workers a reasonable opportunity to find new employment, allows employers to complete the necessary immigration paperwork, and provides families with time to make informed decisions about their future. It also allows individuals who cannot secure new employment to organize their departure responsibly.

I believe eliminating this grace period would undermine the stability and predictability that skilled foreign workers rely on when making long-term commitments in the United States. Many of us have invested years of our lives here, purchased homes, contributed to retirement accounts, paid federal, state, and local taxes, and become part of our communities.

We have made a genuine effort to follow the rules, contribute to society, support ourselves and our families, and build stable lives here. We are not asking for special treatment or an exemption from immigration requirements. We are simply asking for a reasonable amount of time to respond to circumstances that are often completely outside our control.

A layoff is already a stressful and financially difficult experience. It would be particularly challenging if it also meant that a family had to make immediate decisions about leaving their home, managing financial obligations, and potentially giving up established careers, all without sufficient time to plan.

It is also important to recognize that the existing grace period is limited and does not provide an unlimited right to remain or work in the United States. It provides a short, defined period to find another lawful immigration pathway or make arrangements to depart. Retaining this provision offers a reasonable balance between enforcing immigration requirements and recognizing the practical realities of people's lives.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing personal hardship.

I am writing to express deep concern about the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60‑day grace period for individuals who lose their employment while on a work‑authorized visa. While I understand the intent to maintain immigration compliance, removing this grace period ignores the basic realities of human life.

Losing a job is already destabilizing. Expecting a person—especially one with children in school, a lease or mortgage, and community ties—to leave the country immediately is not just unrealistic, it is inhumane. It prevents panic, homelessness, rushed school withdrawals, and sudden financial collapse. It also protects employers by allowing skilled workers to remain available for re‑employment rather than being forced out of the country overnight.

Eliminating this grace period would disproportionately harm families, especially those with young children, special‑needs dependents, or medical obligations. It would also undermine the United States’ reputation as a country that values stability, fairness, and human dignity.

I urge lawmakers to consider the real‑world consequences of this proposal. Immigration policy should be firm, but it should also be humane. Retaining the 60‑day grace period is essential to ensuring that families can navigate job loss without being pushed into crisis.

Please preserve the grace period. It is not only practical—it is the compassionate and responsible choice.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant visa holders.

Losing a job due to layoffs, corporate restructuring, economic downturns, or business decisions is often beyond an employee’s control. Such circumstances should not immediately turn into an immigration crisis for skilled professionals who have lawfully lived, worked, paid taxes, and contributed to the United States for years.

The existing 60-day grace period is a reasonable and limited safeguard that gives affected workers time to find another qualifying employer, pursue an eligible change of immigration status, or make an orderly departure. It does not provide unrestricted employment authorization, nor does it prevent USCIS from exercising its existing discretion.

Eliminating this protection would disproportionately hurt skilled workers and their families. Spouses and children should not face sudden disruption to their education, housing, healthcare, and established lives simply because the primary visa holder experiences an involuntary job loss.

Furthermore, the United States benefits enormously from attracting and retaining international talent. These professionals contribute specialized expertise, innovation, tax revenue, economic growth, and competitiveness across critical industries. Introducing additional immigration uncertainty could discourage experienced talent from choosing the United States and make it harder for American employers to retain skilled workers.

Administrative efficiency should never come at the expense of basic fairness and reasonable protections. If there are administrative challenges with the existing provision, DHS should improve its implementation rather than eliminate it altogether.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

A fair and competitive immigration system should recognize that an involuntary job loss is not misconduct, immigration abuse, or a reason to force individuals and their families into immediate uncertainty. The United States should continue to attract global talent while treating the people who contribute to its economy with fairness, dignity, and reasonable consideration.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that eliminating the grace period harms skilled workers and their families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose DHS's proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

The existing 60-day grace period provides an essential transition period for highly skilled foreign professionals who unexpectedly lose employment. Eliminating this protection would create significant immigration uncertainty, financial hardship and unnecessary disruption for workers, their families and U.S. employers.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider and withdraw this proposal for the following reasons:
1. Employment termination is often beyond an employee's control.
Employees lose jobs because of corporate restructuring, mass layoffs, outsourcing, project cancellations, economic downturns and business closures. These circumstances are not necessarily related to an employee's performance or actions. Individuals who have legally worked and contributed to the United States for many years should not face immediate immigration uncertainty because of an employer's business decisions.
2. Finding new employment requires reasonable time.
Securing a new position involves applications, multiple interview rounds, technical assessments, background checks, offer negotiations, Labor Condition Application processing and immigration petition preparation. These procedures cannot always be completed immediately. Eliminating the grace period could force qualified professionals to leave the country before they have a reasonable opportunity to secure another qualifying employer.

3. Significant consequences for families and dependents.

This proposal affects not only primary visa holders but also their dependent spouses and children. Unexpected employment termination could interrupt children's education, affect spouses' employment opportunities, disrupt established family lives and force families into unplanned international relocation. Immigration policies should consider the well-being and stability of entire families.

4. Negative impact on U.S. employers and the economy.

American businesses depend on experienced international professionals in technology, healthcare, engineering, financial services and other specialized industries. Eliminating the grace period could increase employee turnover, disrupt critical projects, increase recruitment costs and reduce workforce flexibility. It could also discourage highly skilled professionals from pursuing long-term careers in the United States.

5. Disregard for long-term contributions and immigration investments.

Many foreign professionals have legally worked in the United States for 5, 10 or more years. They have paid federal and state taxes, contributed to Social Security and Medicare, purchased homes, supported businesses and established families. Some have also invested years in employment-based permanent residency processes, including PERM labor certification and I-140 petitions. An unexpected layoff should not unnecessarily jeopardize years of legitimate immigration efforts.

6. Disproportionate hardship during economic downturns.
During widespread layoffs, finding another qualifying employer becomes increasingly difficult because multiple companies may reduce hiring simultaneously. Eliminating the grace period during these circumstances would disproportionately penalize workers who are already experiencing financial hardship through no fault of their own.

7. Administrative convenience should not outweigh significant human and economic consequences.
The existing regulation provides DHS discretion to shorten or eliminate the grace period when appropriate circumstances warrant it. Completely removing this flexibility could harm individuals who genuinely need reasonable transition time. DHS should carefully evaluate whether the administrative benefits justify the substantial consequences for workers, families and employers.
I respectfully recommend that DHS:
1. Retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period.
2. Consider extending it to 90 days in exceptional circumstances.
3. Provide additional flexibility for involuntary layoffs and mass workforce reductions.
4. Protect individuals with qualifying change-of-employer or change-of-status petitions pending.
5. Consider safeguards for individuals with ongoing employment-based permanent residency processes.
6. Maintain appropriate protections for dependent family members.
Conclusion:
Employment termination should not automatically become an immigration crisis. Losing a job because of an unexpected corporate decision should not deprive a qualified professional of a reasonable opportunity to find another employer, pursue available immigration options or make an orderly departure with their family.
The 60-day grace period is not unlimited permission to remain or work in the United States. It is a reasonable transition mechanism that benefits workers, families and American employers.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the grace period, citing hardship and transition needs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Opposition to Proposed Rule USCIS-2026-0364 – Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period
Dear Department of Homeland Security and USCIS,
I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule, USCIS-2026-0364, which seeks to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B and other employment-based nonimmigrant workers.
I strongly urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
1. Job loss is often beyond an employee’s control
Layoffs, corporate restructuring, budget reductions, and project cancellations can affect even highly skilled, experienced, and consistently performing employees.
Eliminating the grace period would impose severe immigration consequences on workers who have complied with immigration laws and lost their employment through no fault of their own.
2. The 60-day period supports lawful immigration compliance
The existing grace period provides a reasonable opportunity to secure new employment, arrange an employer-sponsored visa transfer, change immigration status, or prepare for departure.
Removing this protection could create unnecessary immigration uncertainty and hardship for individuals who are actively attempting to maintain lawful status.
3. American employers would also be negatively affected
U.S. employers depend on experienced professionals in technology, healthcare, engineering, research, and other specialized industries.
Recruitment, interviews, background checks, immigration petition preparation, and internal approvals often require several weeks.
Eliminating the grace period would make it significantly harder for American companies to recruit skilled workers already residing legally in the United States. This could result in lost talent, higher recruitment costs, and disruptions to business operations.
4. Families would face disproportionate hardship
Many H-1B professionals have established their lives in the United States over several years. They maintain homes, pay taxes, support local communities, and have spouses and children who depend on their immigration status.
Sudden employment termination should not immediately place an entire family’s ability to remain in the country at risk.
Families need reasonable time to manage housing, financial obligations, children’s education, healthcare, and other essential responsibilities.
5. Long-term immigration applicants have significant reliance interests
Many employment-based workers have spent years complying with immigration requirements and pursuing permanent residency through employer-sponsored processes.
Workers with approved immigrant petitions may still face lengthy green card backlogs. Eliminating the grace period would create additional uncertainty for individuals who have invested years in following the legal immigration process.
DHS should carefully consider these established reliance interests and the consequences of abruptly removing an existing regulatory protection.
6. The proposed administrative benefits do not justify the hardship
DHS identifies administrative efficiency and immigration program integrity as reasons for eliminating the grace period.
However, eliminating this protection could increase the need for urgent immigration filings, international travel, consular processing, and employer recruitment activities.
DHS should provide clear evidence demonstrating that eliminating the grace period would produce benefits sufficient to outweigh these economic and humanitarian costs.
My recommendation
I respectfully request that DHS:
Withdraw the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period.
Retain the existing protections under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
Consider the economic impact on U.S. employers and the reliance interests of affected workers and families.
Explore administrative improvements that preserve a reasonable transition period rather than eliminating it.
The existing 60-day grace period is a reasonable and important safeguard. It supports American employers, promotes orderly immigration compliance, and provides essential stability to law-abiding workers and their families.
I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to reconsider this proposal and retain the existing 60-day grace period.
Thank you for considering my comment.
Sincerely,
A Concerned Employment-Based Nonimmigrant Worker
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and urges DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period.

comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period and ask DHS to retain it.

I am a long-term H-1B holder, and I am grateful for the education and career opportunities this country has given me. I pay taxes, follow the law, and have built a life here with my family.

Job loss for H-1B workers often has nothing to do with performance. Layoffs, restructurings, funding changes and business decisions can affect even highly skilled employees. Today, the grace period gives affected workers and their dependents a reasonable window to find a new sponsor, change status, or arrange an orderly departure. Even 60 days is a short time to secure a new offer, have a new employer file a petition, and handle practical matters like ending a lease, settling finances, or managing a child’s school year. Without any grace period, families could be required to leave almost immediately. Employers, too, rarely have a new petition ready on the day a worker is let go.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jianing Xu
comments.commentText:
Dear USCIS and DHS Officials,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

As a software engineer who has built a career in the United States, I believe this proposal would impose substantial economic and human costs while undermining American competitiveness, workforce mobility, and the stability of the legal immigration system.

1. The grace period promotes lawful compliance rather than undermining it.

The existing 60-day grace period is not unrestricted work authorization. It is a limited, discretionary transition period that allows eligible workers to seek new sponsorship, apply for a change of status, or prepare for an orderly departure.

Eliminating this protection would mean that workers who unexpectedly lose employment could fall out of status almost immediately, despite years of lawful employment and compliance with immigration requirements.

A system that penalizes lawful workers for circumstances beyond their control does not necessarily improve immigration integrity.

2. Eliminating the grace period would harm American employers and economic competitiveness.

Recruiting skilled professionals involves interviews, background checks, legal preparation, and immigration filings. These processes cannot reasonably be completed overnight.

The proposed rule would make it significantly harder for American companies to recruit qualified professionals already living in the United States.

It would also increase workers’ dependence on individual employers, reduce labor mobility, and potentially discourage employees from leaving exploitative or unhealthy working environments.

A competitive American economy benefits when skilled professionals can move efficiently between employers rather than being forced to leave the country during temporary employment disruptions.

3. The proposed rule does not adequately establish that its benefits outweigh its costs.

DHS estimates approximately 3,795 annual cases involving new employer petitions filed within the existing grace period. However, DHS also acknowledges limitations in estimating affected dependents and the number of workers who would depart the United States because of the proposed change.

The proposal also acknowledges potential lost compensation, employer productivity losses, and additional immigration enforcement proceedings.

Before eliminating an established protection, DHS should provide a more comprehensive assessment of these economic and administrative consequences.

Reducing one category of adjudicative work does not necessarily reduce the overall cost to the government, employers, or society.

4. The proposal would create disproportionate hardship for families.

Many employment-based visa holders have established homes, signed leases, paid taxes, and raised families in American communities.

An unexpected layoff should not force a family to immediately disrupt housing, education, and employment arrangements.

The existing grace period provides a reasonable and limited opportunity to manage such transitions while respecting immigration requirements.

5. Less disruptive alternatives are available.

I respectfully urge DHS to retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period.

If the agency seeks to reduce administrative burdens, it should consider clearer documentation requirements, standardized employment-termination reporting, and more efficient adjudication procedures.

Existing discretion to shorten or eliminate the grace period in appropriate individual cases should be preserved rather than replacing a targeted safeguard with a blanket removal.

Conclusion

The United States should maintain an immigration system that protects national interests, encourages legal compliance, supports American businesses, and treats workers fairly.

Eliminating the 60-day grace period would create unnecessary instability without a sufficiently demonstrated corresponding public benefit.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the discretionary 60-day grace period.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly expresses strong opposition to the proposed rule eliminating the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to formally express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for certain high-skilled nonimmigrant workers and their dependents (8 CFR 214.1(l)(2)). Removing this vital buffer harms U.S. economic competitiveness, creates unworkable logistical realities, destabilizes families, and undermines basic workplace fairness.

Supporting Facts and Arguments to Include:

• Unrealistic Expectation of Immediate Departure or Re-Sponsorship:
• The proposal assumes a nonimmigrant worker can find a new corporate sponsor, file a new petition, or completely wind up years of life and leave the United States overnight the moment employment ceases.
• In reality, corporate hiring cycles, background checks, legal reviews, and USCIS administrative processing times take weeks or months. Eliminating the 60-day window effectively turns a sudden layoff into an immediate forced deportation or unlawful status violation through no fault of the individual.
• Severe Disruptions to Dependent Families:
• DHS’s own estimates acknowledge that roughly 208,000 dependent family members (spouses and children on H-4, L-2, and E-dependent visas) are affected annually.
• Eliminating the grace period means spouses and children—including school-aged children—fall out of status simultaneously with the primary worker, disrupting schooling, health insurance coverage, and household stability overnight.
• Increased Vulnerability to Workplace Exploitation:
• The 60-day grace period provides a critical measure of mobility and safety. Without it, workers facing toxic work environments, wage violations, or unsafe conditions cannot safely report or leave abusive employment without the terror of becoming "illegal within minutes" of job separation. This imbalance hands immense coercive power to bad-actor employers.
• Damage to U.S. Innovation and Business Competitiveness:
• U.S. employers hiring specialized talent in STEM, tech, medical, and executive fields (H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN) need a reasonable transition window to evaluate, interview, and onboard skilled candidates who have been laid off through no fault of their own (such as broader tech or industry-wide downsizing).
• Forcing top global talent to flee the country immediately rather than transition to a new U.S. employer actively drives innovation and human capital to competing economies like Canada, the UK, or the EU.
• Administrative Burden vs. Human Cost:
• DHS justifies the rule by citing a reduction in administrative burden, yet the downstream social, familial, and economic costs of uprooting hundreds of thousands of legal tax-paying residents far outweigh any marginal administrative convenience.
For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Priyank GAJERA
comments.commentText:
I oppose DHS’s proposal to eliminate the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I urge DHS to retain the existing regulation or adopt safeguards rather than eliminate this transition period.

The grace period is not an automatic 60-day guarantee and does not authorize work. It gives workers and dependents limited time to pursue lawful next steps after employment ends. A layoff may result from restructuring, budget cuts, project cancellation, mergers, or business closure—not employee misconduct or lack of skill.

The effects extend well beyond the individual worker. H-1B households contribute to the U.S. economy through rent or mortgage payments, property taxes, income and payroll taxes, vehicle purchases, insurance, groceries, restaurants, retail, healthcare, childcare, home improvement, transportation, and other local spending. If families must relocate abruptly, local businesses and service providers lose customers. Homeowners may be pressured to sell property quickly, potentially at a discount; families may also need to sell vehicles quickly. These outcomes can affect real-estate professionals, lenders, insurers, auto dealers, repair shops, and local tax bases. These effects deserve analysis.

Employers can also lose experienced workers who could otherwise move to a new sponsoring employer. Abrupt departure can delay projects, disrupt customer commitments, increase recruiting and onboarding costs, and eliminate institutional knowledge. A prospective employer may be willing to hire the worker, but international departure and subsequent processing can make the transition slower, more expensive, or impractical. The United States may lose skilled professionals in science, technology, research, healthcare, and other specialized fields to countries competing for the same talent. This can weaken innovation, research continuity, product development, and future entrepreneurship.

The family consequences are especially serious. Some affected households include U.S.-citizen children born in this country. A parent’s sudden job loss could force an American child to leave school, friends, established healthcare providers, and community in the middle of an academic year. Other families may face separation if the worker departs while a spouse or children remain. Spouses who are employed or contribute to the local economy may also have their work and lives disrupted. DHS should consider these effects in its family assessment.

DHS’s own analysis estimates approximately 3,795 beneficiaries across the affected classifications had a new Form I-129 petition filed by a new petitioner during the grace period annually, of whom approximately 3,765 (99.2%) were H-1B beneficiaries. DHS identifies a median annual wage of $131,000 for the relevant H-1B group and estimates a potential upper-bound lost-income amount of $21,877 for a two-month delay. These figures show that the grace period supports real employment transitions. The analysis should also evaluate household spending and taxes, home and vehicle dispositions, employer project delays, replacement costs, local business effects, educational disruption, and the loss of talent to other countries. DHS itself acknowledges that employers, families, and communities may be affected and that people may have purchased homes, paid taxes, and invested in local communities in reliance on the existing policy.

A 60-day transition period is already limited. Finding a suitable job, securing an employer willing to file a petition, preparing documentation, and coordinating a lawful status change can take time. Eliminating the period may turn a temporary layoff into a forced international relocation, even where a U.S. employer still needs the worker’s skills. Retaining the discretionary period does not guarantee a new status or permit unauthorized work; it preserves time to pursue lawful options while DHS retains discretion to shorten or eliminate the period where justified.

I urge DHS to:

Withdraw the proposal and retain 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

If safeguards are needed, clarify documentation and reporting requirements rather than eliminate the grace period.

Preserve discretion to shorten or eliminate the period in specifically justified cases.

Assess direct and indirect effects on U.S. employers, small businesses, household spending, tax revenue, housing, vehicles, schools, U.S.-citizen children, and local communities.

Publish the data, assumptions, and methodology used to evaluate these broader impacts and consider transition protections for families and employers who relied on the current framework.

The grace period is a measured transition mechanism, not a guarantee of continued immigration status or employment authorization. Eliminating it risks harming American employers, communities, families, and the country’s ability to retain skilled talent. I respectfully ask DHS not to finalize this proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Rajesh Kumar
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (RIN 1615-AD22)

I am writing to respectfully oppose the proposed rule that would eliminate the 60-day grace period for workers in H-1B and other employment-based statuses. I ask the Department to withdraw this proposal and retain the grace period.

Any project can end with little warning, but it can change quickly a family's stability can turn on a single business decision that the worker did not make. For many of my colleagues, a layoff means the job itself ends — and under this proposal, their lawful status would end the very next day.

The 60-day period is what makes H-1B portability real. A new employer cannot complete a hire in a day: interviews, an offer, a certified Labor Condition Application, and a prepared petition take weeks. Without the grace period, a laid-off worker would fall out of status before any new employer could file a petition on their behalf, even though Congress created portability precisely so that skilled workers could change employers. Removing the grace period would not just shorten a benefit; it would make portability illusory for anyone who loses a job.

The harm would fall hardest on families. H-4 spouses, many of whom work lawfully on employment authorization, and school-age children would lose their status overnight along with the worker. A layoff would become an order to uproot an entire family with no time to finish a school term, wind down a lease, or arrange medical care. That is a severe consequence for families who have followed every rule, paid taxes, and built their lives here in good faith.

The Department's own estimate that about 3,795 people could lose income understates the impact, because it does not account for spouses who would lose their jobs or children pulled out of school. Nor does the remaining 10-day provision help: it runs from the end of a petition's validity, not from the day a job is lost, so it offers nothing to a worker laid off mid-petition.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the 60-day grace period. It is a modest, humane bridge that protects law-abiding workers and their families, supports American employers who need experienced talent, and keeps the H-1B program working as Congress intended.

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose DHS’s proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers. I urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw the proposal and preserve this practical protection for workers, families, and American employers.

THE GRACE PERIOD DOES NOT AUTHORIZE AN INDEFINITE STAY

The grace period is not permission to remain in the United States indefinitely or work without authorization. It gives eligible workers limited time to find another sponsoring employer, pursue another lawful immigration option, address emergencies, or arrange an orderly departure. Providing a reasonable opportunity to comply with immigration requirements serves both the government and affected families.

ELIMINATING THE GRACE PERIOD COULD HARM AMERICAN EMPLOYERS

Layoffs often result from restructuring, budget reductions, or project cancellations. Another American employer may need the affected worker’s skills and be prepared to offer a position, but preparing and filing the required petition takes time.

Eliminating this transition period could cause U.S. businesses to lose experienced professionals they want to hire, disrupt recruitment, and delay important work. A worker’s employment ending at one company does not mean that the worker’s skills are no longer needed elsewhere in the American economy. Retaining the grace period gives employers a practical opportunity to retain that talent.

SAFE AND ORDERLY DEPARTURES REQUIRE TIME

For families who must leave, international departure involves much more than buying a ticket. They may need travel documents, available flights, school transfers, medical records, and arrangements for housing, mortgages, leases, vehicles, and belongings.

Last-minute flights may be costly or unavailable, especially for an entire family. Children and medically vulnerable relatives may require additional preparation. A limited transition period helps people organize a responsible departure and meet their obligations.

CHILDREN AND FAMILY UNITY DESERVE CONSIDERATION

Many H-1B professionals have lived in the United States for 10–20 years, paying taxes, buying homes, and contributing to their communities. Their children may have been born and raised here, attending local schools and knowing no other country as home.

An unexpected layoff is already a serious financial and emotional shock. Eliminating the grace period could force families to make life-changing decisions with almost no time. Children could be removed from school midsemester, separated from friends, and uprooted from their communities.

Some children are U.S. citizens. Their families may face the painful choice of relocating together or separating. A parent’s job loss should not leave a child facing that choice without a reasonable opportunity for the family to plan.

MEDICAL EMERGENCIES REQUIRE HUMANITARIAN FLEXIBILITY

Employment can end while a worker or family member is hospitalized, undergoing tests or treatment, or recovering from surgery. A doctor may advise that the patient cannot safely fly. Obtaining records, arranging continued treatment, and coordinating safe travel can take weeks.

No family should have to choose between necessary medical care and an abrupt departure deadline. DHS should preserve the grace period and consider additional flexibility for hospitalization, medical incapacity, recovery, and other circumstances that prevent safe travel.

LONG GREEN CARD BACKLOGS COMPOUND THE HARDSHIP

Many workers, particularly those born in India, have waited years or decades for employment-based permanent residency. Some have approved I-140 petitions but cannot proceed because immigrant visa numbers are unavailable. These delays are outside their control.

After years of lawful employment and contribution, an unexpected layoff should not leave these families with almost no time to protect their homes, arrange their affairs, or pursue another lawful option.

THE EXISTING REGULATION ALREADY HAS LIMITS

The current rule provides up to 60 days or until the end of the authorized validity period, whichever is shorter. It does not itself authorize employment, and DHS retains discretion to shorten or eliminate the period in individual cases. Concerns about misuse should be addressed through case-specific review.

I respectfully request that DHS retain the discretionary 60-day grace period and consider additional humanitarian flexibility for exceptional medical and family emergencies. The Department should assess the consequences for American employers, orderly departures, children, healthcare, family unity, and long-term residents.

Behind every H-1B petition is a person and often an entire family. Immigration compliance, economic stability, and humanitarian consideration can coexist. Please withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing grace period.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period and argues it harms workers and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Mahesh S
comments.commentText:
Subject: Opposition to the Proposed Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period for H-1B Workers

I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposal to eliminate the existing 60-day discretionary grace period for H-1B workers and other affected employment-based nonimmigrant visa holders.

The 60-day grace period is an essential protection that provides highly skilled foreign professionals with a reasonable opportunity to find new employment, secure another qualifying employer, complete the H-1B transfer process, or make appropriate arrangements regarding their immigration status.

Job loss can happen unexpectedly due to layoffs, company restructuring, project cancellations, budget constraints, or business closures. These circumstances are often beyond an employee’s control. Eliminating the grace period would place an unreasonable burden on workers who have otherwise complied with U.S. immigration laws and contributed to the American workforce.

1. Unreasonable pressure on workers during unexpected job loss

Finding a new employer is not an immediate process. It involves applications, interviews, technical assessments, offer negotiations, immigration documentation, and petition filing. Employers also need sufficient time to review candidates and complete the necessary immigration procedures. Removing the grace period would create unnecessary pressure and uncertainty during an already difficult situation.

2. Negative impact on highly skilled professionals and the U.S. economy

H-1B professionals contribute significantly to the technology, healthcare, engineering, research, financial services, and other critical industries. Eliminating this protection could force experienced professionals to leave the United States simply because they cannot secure another qualifying employment opportunity immediately.

This would result in the loss of valuable skills, experience, productivity, and investments that American employers have already made in these professionals.

3. Significant hardship for families and H-4 dependents

The consequences extend beyond the primary H-1B worker. Spouses and children may also be affected by the sudden loss of immigration status. Families may face disruption to their children’s education, housing arrangements, healthcare, financial obligations, and established lives in the United States.

4. The current grace period provides a reasonable and balanced safeguard

The existing 60-day grace period does not automatically authorize employment. It provides a limited period for individuals to pursue lawful immigration options and make necessary arrangements. DHS already retains discretion to shorten or eliminate the grace period in appropriate circumstances.

Removing this protection entirely is disproportionate when the existing regulation already provides flexibility and safeguards.

5. Request for reconsideration

I respectfully urge USCIS and DHS to withdraw the proposed elimination of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period.

If the agency has concerns about administrative burden, those concerns should be addressed through improved processing procedures rather than eliminating an important safeguard for workers and their families.

The United States benefits from attracting and retaining talented professionals from around the world. Immigration policies should provide reasonable stability, fairness, and predictability to individuals who have followed the rules and contributed to the country’s economy.

I strongly urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day grace period.

Thank you for considering my comments.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Chengze Wang
comments.commentText:
To U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:

I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I urge DHS to retain this protection for H-1B workers and other covered nonimmigrants and their dependents.

As an H-1B worker, I believe that lawful immigrants who contribute their skills, labor, and taxes to this country deserve a reasonable opportunity to navigate an unexpected employment transition. We help build America’s technology, businesses, research capacity, and infrastructure. Our contributions do not disappear the moment an employer announces a layoff.

1. The grace period supports American employers and economic competitiveness.

Losing a job does not necessarily mean a worker’s skills are no longer needed in the United States. Layoffs can result from restructuring, financing decisions, mergers, or the cancellation of a particular project. Another American employer may still need that worker’s expertise.

Recruitment, interviews, immigration review, and petition preparation take time. Requiring an otherwise eligible worker to leave the country immediately can interrupt that process, delay hiring, and make valuable talent less accessible to U.S. businesses. DHS’s own economic analysis acknowledges potential lost compensation, departure costs, and temporary productivity losses. These are costs to workers, employers, and communities, not merely administrative inconveniences.

2. The existing protection is limited and does not authorize unrestricted unemployment or work.

The current rule provides up to 60 days, or until the end of the authorized validity period, whichever is shorter. It is discretionary, generally available once during each authorized validity period, and does not itself provide unrestricted employment authorization.

Workers must still qualify for any subsequent immigration benefit. DHS also retains discretion to shorten or eliminate the period in individual cases. Preserving this narrowly defined transition mechanism is compatible with enforcing immigration requirements; it is not equivalent to allowing indefinite residence without qualifying employment.

3. Administrative efficiency does not justify eliminating a substantial protection without stronger evidence.

Section IV.C emphasizes the burden of determining whether the grace period applies. However, footnote 29 acknowledges that DHS cannot estimate the additional adjudication time required. The number of filings potentially requiring review does not, by itself, establish the actual burden attributable to this protection or demonstrate that elimination is the most proportionate solution.

DHS should evaluate clearer filing instructions, standardized employment-cessation documentation, and streamlined adjudication procedures before removing the protection entirely. Administrative complexity should be addressed through better administration wherever reasonably possible.

4. A reasonable transition period promotes fair treatment in the workplace.

Making immigration stability depend even more tightly on uninterrupted employment with a particular employer can discourage workers from leaving abusive conditions or raising legitimate workplace concerns. A limited transition period reduces that vulnerability.

Protecting workers’ ability to seek another lawful employer supports fair competition and labor standards. DHS should evaluate these effects on both immigrant workers and the American workers alongside whom they work.

5. The proposal would impose disproportionate disruption on families.

Section IV.D recognizes that affected workers and dependents may have purchased homes, paid taxes, and invested in their communities. Families may also need to address leases, medical care, school arrangements, and international travel after an unexpected termination.

Acknowledging these reliance interests is not the same as adequately addressing them. A sudden employment interruption should not require a family to dismantle its life without a realistic transition period.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposal and retain the discretionary 60-day grace period. Any legitimate concerns about documentation, fraud, or administrative burden should be addressed through targeted measures rather than blanket elimination.

H-1B workers are contributors to America’s success, not disposable inputs. Preserving a reasonable transition period would support lawful compliance, protect families, and help American employers retain the talent they need to build and compete.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:

I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). While administrative efficiency and immigration compliance are important, DHS has not adequately demonstrated that eliminating this provision is necessary or that its benefits outweigh the economic and human consequences.

1. Insufficient Justification and Evidence

The 60-day grace period was established in 2016 to support job portability and employment stability. DHS has not sufficiently explained why these original policy objectives are no longer valid.

DHS cites over 1.9 million petitions and applications that potentially required grace period assessments, but this figure does not establish how many individuals actually used the provision or how much additional processing time it required.

Furthermore, eliminating the grace period would not eliminate the need to review employment termination dates and immigration status. It may simply shift administrative burdens to other immigration processes and agencies.

2. Failure to Adequately Consider Reliance Interests

For nearly a decade, U.S. employers, foreign professionals, and their families have made employment and life decisions under the existing regulatory framework.

The discretionary nature of the grace period does not eliminate DHS's responsibility to consider these reliance interests when changing established policy.

Employers rely on reasonable transition periods for recruitment and workforce planning. Workers and their families rely on them when making significant commitments, including housing, education, and relocation.

3. Unreasonable Human Consequences

It is unrealistic to expect someone who is unexpectedly laid off to pack up their entire life and leave the United States on extremely short notice.

These individuals are not just employees. They have spouses, children, pets, homes, cars, financial obligations, and communities. These responsibilities cannot simply be abandoned overnight.

Losing a job is already a significant hardship. Removing a reasonable transition period would make an already difficult situation unnecessarily harsh, particularly for individuals who have complied with immigration requirements.

4. Damage to America's Ability to Attract Global Talent

Highly skilled professionals have choices about where to build their careers. A policy that makes their ability to remain in the United States so vulnerable to an unexpected layoff could discourage talented individuals from coming here.

Potential H-1B workers may instead choose countries offering greater stability and more reasonable employment-transition protections. This could undermine the competitiveness of U.S. businesses and America's ability to attract and retain global talent.

5. Less Disruptive Alternatives

DHS should consider clearer eligibility standards, standardized documentation, or streamlined adjudication procedures rather than eliminating the grace period entirely.

At a minimum, a meaningful transition period should be preserved for involuntary terminations and layoffs. Any final rule should also protect individuals already relying on the existing regulation.

Conclusion

The 60-day grace period is not an unreasonable privilege. It is a practical safeguard that recognizes employment uncertainty and the reality that people's lives extend beyond their jobs.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and retain the existing 60-day grace period. Administrative efficiency should not come at the expense of basic fairness, economic competitiveness, and America's ability to attract and retain global talent.

Thank you for considering this comment.

The rule treats them as having failed to maintain status “the day after” a layoff. After more than 15 years here, my family’s life is rooted in this country: our children are in school, we own a home, we have paid taxes for over a decade, and we are part of our community. A child in the middle of a school year, a family with a home, and a spouse with a career cannot responsibly leave the country in one day. The rule offers no transition for people who have built their entire lives here in full compliance with the law.

3. A layoff could destroy years of lawful progress.

DHS acknowledges in footnote 13 that failing to maintain status can bring unlawful presence consequences, bars to adjustment of status under INA 245(c)(2), and negative discretionary factors. For someone who has waited more than a decade for permanent residence, one layoff outside their control could jeopardize the entire process. The grace period exists to prevent exactly this. Layoffs are common and unpredictable, and workers should not lose their path to permanent residence for an event they did not choose.

4. The reliance interests analysis is inadequate.

The grace period has been codified in regulation for nearly ten years, since 2017. DHS dismisses reliance by calling the grace period “discretionary.” But DHS itself says many cases result in a grant, and workers, employers and families have structured their lives around it: buying homes, signing leases, enrolling children, accepting job offers. A decade of regulatory text is not a mere enforcement expectation. The Administrative Procedure Act requires DHS to weigh serious reliance interests, not dismiss them in one paragraph.

5. The cost analysis understates the harm and overstates the benefit.

DHS estimates about 3,795 people per year would be directly affected and says it cannot quantify costs for dependents. It does not monetize any costs or benefits in its accounting statement. Its own footnote 54 estimates up to $21,877 in lost income per worker from a two-month delay, and that does not count relocation, lease termination, forced home sales, children’s schooling, or lost spousal income. Meanwhile, DHS’s cited benefit is reduced adjudication burden, even though it reports only 37 NTAs issued for H-1B holders in FY 2025 for failure to maintain status beyond the grace period. The rule does not show that administrative savings justify displacing tens of thousands of families.

6. Departing and returning is not a realistic option.

DHS says affected workers can leave and return after finding a new job. In practice that means consular appointments, visa stamping delays, and travel uncertainty, with no guarantee of readmission. Families would be separated or forced to relocate abroad during a job search, which is far harder than searching from within the community where the worker’s skills and network are.

7. Less harmful alternatives exist.

DHS rejected shortening the period or limiting it to certain classes, but did not consider narrower measures. I urge DHS to consider: (a) retaining the grace period for anyone with an approved I-140, a pending I-485, or a priority date in a backlogged category; (b) making the 60 days non-discretionary and predictable, which would also cut the adjudication burden DHS cites; (c) streamlining proof of the employment end date through a simple employer attestation; and (d) a transition period so that people already in the United States can adjust.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule or, at minimum, to preserve the grace period for those who have waited years in a backlogged green card category.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Shaishav Shah
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed elimination of the 60-day discretionary grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers. While the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) outlines specific goals regarding status integrity, administrative efficiency, and policy re-evaluation, the proposed solution of immediate status termination upon job separation is counterproductive. It creates undue hardship for high-skilled workers and worsens the exact operational challenges the agency seeks to resolve.
Below, I offer a counter-analysis of the proposed justifications alongside constructive, alternative solutions that balance regulatory oversight with economic competitiveness.

1. Restoring Status Integrity vs. Implementing a Digital Intent Tracker

• The Counter-Argument: Eliminating the grace period does not preserve status integrity; instead, it forces highly skilled professionals into instant, involuntary unlawful status due to employer-driven business decisions or market layoffs. Stripping workers of a reasonable window to orderly depart, change status, or find a new sponsor penalizes individuals for circumstances beyond their control.
• Alternative Solution: Rather than a punitive elimination of the grace period, USCIS should implement a digital Status Notification & Intent Tracker. Upon a job separation, employers would register the termination date, and workers would be required to log into a secure USCIS portal within 10 days to declare their intent (e.g., actively job hunting, preparing for departure, or filing a change of status). This maintains strict real-time transparency and continuous oversight without forcing immediate unlawful presence.

2. Reducing Administrative Burdens vs. Automated Visa Transfer Portals

• The Counter-Argument: Proponents argue this rule eases the agency's tracking workload, but eliminating the grace period will actually increase administrative backlogs. Without a clear 60-day window to secure a standard visa transfer, thousands of displaced workers will simultaneously flood USCIS with emergency Change of Status (Form I-539) applications to avoid falling out of status. This will create a massive influx of manual paperwork and compound existing processing queues.
• Alternative Solution: USCIS should establish an Automated Employer-Sponsored Visa Transfer Portal. When a new employer seeks to hire a recently displaced nonimmigrant worker, the transfer petition could be fast-tracked through a simplified, automated electronic verification system. Streamlining and automating the transfer process for workers within their 60-day window reduces the manual administrative burden on USCIS officers far more effectively than managing thousands of sudden status violations and emergency applications.

3. Re-evaluating Past Policy vs. Creating a Conditional Talent Pool Status

• The Counter-Argument: The 2017 grace period was established to prevent a severe talent drain, recognizing that the United States competes globally for top tech, medical, and engineering talent. Forcing a specialist to leave the country the exact day a contract or position ends severely damages U.S. economic competitiveness, deters global talent from choosing the U.S., and deprives American companies of a readily available local pool of skilled labor.
• Alternative Solution: Rather than severing the connection between status and utility, USCIS should create a conditional "Talent Pool Status" tied to a job-matching database. The 60-day grace period could be maintained on the condition that the displaced worker registers in a verified, government-vetted database. This database would be accessible exclusively to U.S. employers looking to fill critical skill shortages, keeping the worker’s status directly aligned with the ultimate goal of domestic economic contribution.

Conclusion

Eliminating the 60-day grace period introduces systemic instability for both American employers and international professionals. I urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw this proposal and instead consider modernized, digital solutions that protect high-skilled workers while giving the agency the oversight and efficiency it requires.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Nikhil Agrawal

Subject: Strong Opposition to Eliminating the 60-Day Grace Period — DHS Docket USCIS-2026-0364

Dear USCIS and Department of Homeland Security,

I strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other employment-based visa holders.

As a skilled professional working in the United States, I believe removing this protection would unfairly punish lawful immigrants who have followed immigration regulations, contributed to the American economy, paid taxes, and built their lives here.

1. Job loss is often beyond an employee's control.

Layoffs, corporate restructuring, and economic downturns can affect even highly skilled and hardworking employees. Losing a job should not immediately put someone's immigration status and family's stability at risk. The existing 60-day grace period provides a reasonable opportunity to find another employer and maintain lawful status.

2. The hiring and immigration process takes time.

Finding a new job involves multiple interviews, background checks, employer approvals, and immigration paperwork. For H-1B workers, employers may also need to obtain a Labor Condition Application and prepare a transfer petition. These processes cannot realistically be completed immediately after an unexpected layoff.

3. American families and communities will suffer.

Many visa holders have lived in the United States for years, purchased homes, established families, and raised children here, including U.S. citizen children. Requiring families to abruptly leave the country after a job loss could disrupt children's education, healthcare, housing, and financial stability.

4. Eliminating the grace period will hurt American businesses and the economy.

Skilled foreign professionals contribute through innovation, tax payments, consumer spending, and specialized expertise. American businesses also benefit from retaining access to experienced workers. Forcing qualified professionals to leave the country instead of transferring to another employer would create unnecessary disruptions and costs.

5. The grace period supports legal immigration rather than undermining it.

The existing grace period is not an authorization to work without permission, nor does it provide indefinite immigration status. It is a limited, temporary mechanism that allows workers to comply with immigration requirements during an unexpected employment transition.

6. Administrative efficiency should not come at the expense of human hardship.

I understand USCIS's interest in reducing administrative burdens. However, eliminating a reasonable protection could increase the need for international travel, consular processing, and additional immigration filings. USCIS should consider simplifying the administration of the grace period rather than eliminating it.

My request:

I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw this proposed rule and retain the existing 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

The United States should continue to attract and retain talented professionals while maintaining a fair, predictable, and humane immigration system. A temporary period of unemployment should not erase years of lawful contributions or unnecessarily uproot families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Shruti G
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose removing the discretionary grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.

1. It will increase, not reduce, administrative burden. The grace period requires no application. It applies automatically and is only reviewed when a later petition is filed. Without it, a worker falls out of status the day employment ends. Many will file Form I-539 to change to B-2 or another status, to avoid unlawful presence while they find work or wind down their affairs. That creates thousands of new filings, biometrics and adjudications that do not exist today, plus more status-violation RFEs on change-of-employer petitions. DHS should quantify these offsetting costs before claiming a net burden reduction.

2. It undercuts H-1B portability that Congress created. INA 214(n) lets an H-1B worker begin work for a new employer upon filing, but only if the petition is filed during a period of authorized stay. The grace period is what makes portability usable after a layoff. Without it, portability would in practice exist only for voluntary job changes. Workers laid off without notice, through no fault of their own, would lose it, contrary to AC21's purpose of job mobility.

3. DHS has not adequately addressed reliance interests. DHS adopted the grace period through notice and comment in 2016 (81 FR 82398). It found then that the grace period would promote stability and flexibility and help U.S. employers retain talent. For nearly a decade, workers, families and employers have planned around it: leases, mortgages, children's schooling, hiring timelines. Under DHS v. Regents (2020) and Encino Motorcars v. Navarro (2016), an agency changing course must weigh such reliance and explain why the change justifies it. A general appeal to administrative convenience does not meet that standard.

4. It harms U.S. employers and the economy. Employers routinely hire skilled professionals already in the U.S. whose prior job ended. These workers are vetted, local and immediately available. Forcing them to depart first adds months of consular delays and cost. It also pushes talent to competitor countries, taking tax revenue, spending and skills with it.

5. It increases worker vulnerability, which also hurts U.S. workers. If losing a job means instant loss of status, employers gain outsized leverage over visa holders. Those workers become less able to report abuse, refuse unpaid overtime or negotiate pay, which depresses wages and conditions for the U.S. workers alongside them. The grace period is a modest protection consistent with safeguarding U.S. labor standards.

6. The current rule is already narrow. It is capped at 60 days or the end of the validity period, whichever is shorter. It is available once per validity period, and DHS may already shorten or deny it. DHS has ample tools to address misuse case by case. Abolishing the grace period penalizes the majority who use it as intended.

7. Humanitarian impact. Layoffs often arrive without warning. Without a grace period, families, including U.S.-citizen children, could be forced to leave immediately, abandoning homes, schools and medical care. Sixty days to find a job, change status or depart in an orderly way is reasonable and humane.

A better alternative: If the discretionary standard is confusing, DHS can fix that without removing the benefit. It could make the 60 days a bright-line automatic period that needs no adjudicator judgment, or issue clearer guidance. Either would reduce burden while preserving stability.

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and retain 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 | RIN 1615-AD22

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period".

The current 60-day grace period provides critical stability for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers who face sudden layoffs through no fault of their own. Eliminating this grace period entirely is unnecessarily punitive. An unexpected termination is already a devastating emotional and economic shock; stripping away the remaining buffer period exacerbates this distress exponentially, leaving individuals entirely unable to manage their transition in an orderly fashion.
A mandatory, immediate exit upon termination fails to account for the real-world legal and financial obligations that individuals incur while residing lawfully in the United States. DHS must consider the severe logistical, operational, and humanitarian hardships that an immediate departure timeline would mandate:
1. Residential Lease Liabilities: Standard American residential leases universally require a 30- to 60-day written notice of intent to vacate. Forcing an employee to depart immediately creates an undue financial encumbrance via broken lease penalties. Concurrently, property management offices face unrecoverable economic losses and administrative burdens when forced to clear, store, or dispose of abandoned personal property on zero notice.
2. Liquidation of Personal Assets: Highly skilled workers establish long-term roots in the U.S., accumulating significant physical and financial assets, including automobiles and real property. Liquidating a vehicle title, settling a home sale, or managing the cross-border relocation of household goods cannot legally or logistically be executed in 24 hours.
3. Severe Educational Disruption for Children: The dependents of H-1B, L-1, O-1, E, and TN workers—many of whom are birthright U.S. citizens—would face the abrupt cessation of their primary or secondary education mid-term. Uprooting children instantly from their schools without an opportunity to close out a grading period introduces profound developmental and psychological harm.
4. Interruption of Essential Medical Continuity: Families undergoing active medical treatments, specialized therapies, or prenatal care within the U.S. healthcare system would have their care dangerously interrupted. Forcing vulnerable dependents to immediately cease medical regimens without a window to safely transition records or secure safe travel clearances presents a severe humanitarian concern.
Rather than reducing administrative complexity, this rule will increase the burden on immigration systems as individuals are forced into emergency filings. I strongly urge DHS to recognize the necessity of an orderly wind-down period, withdraw this proposal, and maintain the existing 60-day grace period framework.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

The 60-day grace period is the only thing standing between a layoff and an immediate loss of status. In recent years I have watched skilled colleagues lose their jobs overnight in industry-wide layoffs, through no fault of their own. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed removal of the up to 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

I have lived and worked in the United States for nearly 11 years on an employment-based visa. In that time I have paid my taxes every year, obeyed the law, and given my time and effort to my employer, its customers, and my community. I built a life here from the foundation up. I paid off loans, made every payment on time, and spent my income at local small businesses. I earned my place by competing against the best talent in the world. Under this proposal, a single layoff decision outside my control could require me to leave the country the next day. I would have to leave behind my car loan and my mortgage, obligations I have honored for years, with no time to sell, refinance, or arrange anything responsibly. I would walk away with no plan for the next day and nothing to show for a decade of work. That is not an orderly departure. It is a collapse, and it would harm my lenders and community as much as me.

The reliance interests are real and serious (Section IV.D). DHS says reliance on the grace period is “misplaced” because it is discretionary. But for nearly a decade, workers, families, and employers have planned around this rule. Workers sign leases, buy homes, carry car loans and mortgages, and enroll children in school. With zero days to depart, a laid-off worker would have to break leases, sell property at a loss, risk defaulting on obligations, and pull children out of school mid-year, all because of an event the worker did not cause. Lenders, landlords, and local businesses would be harmed too.
The cost analysis understates the harm (Section V.A). DHS estimates about 65,752 workers per year lose or change jobs and counts about 208,187 dependents of workers in these classifications per year. Yet it lists annualized monetized costs as “Not Estimated” and says its data cannot estimate the impact on dependents. A rule affecting this many people should not be finalized without a real estimate of relocation costs, lost wages, broken leases, forced home sales, and disruption to children’s education. DHS’s own upper-bound estimate of lost income, about $21,877 per worker, leaves all of these out.
The grace period is not being abused. DHS reports only 37 Notices to Appear in FY 2025 for H-1B workers who failed to maintain status beyond the grace period. Workers use this window as intended, to find new sponsorship or change status lawfully. Removing it would likely increase status violations and NTAs, which DHS admits would add work for USCIS, ICE, and the immigration courts.
The family assessment is not credible (Section V.F). DHS concludes the rule would not harm family well-being. Forcing a spouse, including a working H-4 or L-2 spouse, and children to leave the country immediately after the principal’s job ends plainly harms family stability, household income, and children’s schooling.
Employers and small businesses would be harmed. DHS identifies 1,852 small entities among the 2,886 employers that hired workers during a grace period in FY 2025. Losing access to skilled workers already in the U.S. means longer vacancies, lost productivity, and new return-transportation costs for H-1B and O-1 employers.
Less drastic alternatives exist (Section IV.E). If administrative burden is the concern, DHS could adopt clear evidentiary standards for the employment end date, an option it considered itself, or require petitioners to state when they rely on the grace period. Either fixes the burden without forcing people out overnight. At minimum, DHS should keep the grace period for long-term workers, such as those with approved immigrant petitions, and for workers laid off through no fault of their own.

Congress created these classifications to attract and retain skilled workers who strengthen the U.S. economy. People like me have spent years paying taxes, repaying debts, and contributing to our communities. We ask only for a short, fair window to find our next role when a job ends. Please withdraw this proposal and keep the 60-day grace period.

Without any grace period, I would have to leave almost immediately. For my high schooler, that could mean being pulled out of school during the years that matter most for college and their future. My family and I want to keep contributing, working, paying taxes, spending, and investing in this country. I'm grateful for the opportunity to be here, and I respectfully ask that you keep the 60-day grace period in place for families like mine.

I strongly oppose ending the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers who lose their jobs.

Most people who are affected by layoffs are experienced professionals who have spent years building their careers in the United States. Many have been here for a decade or even longer. They have established their lives, purchased homes, raised families, paid taxes, and become part of the communities they live in.

Losing a job is difficult enough. But taking away the 60-day grace period makes an already stressful situation much worse. It is important to understand that this decision does not just affect one individual. In most cases, it affects an entire family of three or four people.

Think about a family that has lived in the U.S. for 10–15 years. They have a home, children in school, friendships, community connections, financial commitments, and an entire life built here. Can we realistically expect them to pack up everything and leave the country at such short notice?

The situation is even more difficult when children are involved. Many of these children are U.S. citizens. America is the only home they may have ever known. Their education, friendships, and future are all connected to this country. What is their fault in a parent's unexpected job loss? Why should their lives and future be put into uncertainty because of something beyond their control?

These children are also the future of this country. In 10–15 years, they will be contributing to the same nation in which they are growing up today. Disrupting their education and family stability today could have consequences that go far beyond the immediate situation.

We should also recognize the economic contribution these families are already making. They are not simply living in the country; they are actively contributing to its economy. They pay taxes, own homes, spend money in local businesses, support their communities, and are part of the economic ecosystem.

Many of these professionals have valuable skills and years of experience. A layoff does not erase their knowledge, experience, or ability to contribute. Given a reasonable amount of time, many can find another employer and continue contributing to the American workforce.

The existing 60-day grace period is not an unreasonable privilege. It provides a basic window of time for people to recover from an unexpected job loss, find another opportunity, and make responsible decisions for their families.

Ending this grace period would be a lose-lose situation for everyone involved. It would hurt experienced professionals, disrupt families, put children in difficult circumstances, and potentially cause the country to lose people who have already invested years of their lives and careers in America.

A person's unexpected job loss should not erase decades of hard work, contribution, and a life built in this country.

I sincerely hope policymakers will consider the human side of this decision and retain the 60-day grace period. Immigration policies should not lose sight of the families and children whose lives are directly affected by them.
