comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services,

I am a software engineer, homeowner, and parent living in Texas on H-1B status. I oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), docket USCIS-2026-0364. I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw the proposal and retain the existing grace period of up to 60 days for eligible workers and their dependents.

A layoff can happen with little or no notice. Even when a worker quickly finds an employer willing to sponsor them, that employer needs time to complete interviews, obtain internal approvals, and prepare and file a petition. Much of that timeline is outside the worker’s control. The current grace period gives workers a limited opportunity to pursue a lawful transition and gives U.S. employers time to complete the required hiring and filing steps.

Losing a job cuts off income, but mortgage and car loan payments still come due. As a homeowner with mortgages in Texas, I would have to decide whether to sell or rent a property, coordinate with lenders, and figure out how to manage those obligations from abroad if my family had to leave. A home can take months to sell. A financed vehicle may need to be sold while there is still a loan balance, and rushing to sell a home, a car, or other assets can mean accepting a lower price. Even a short transition period gives families time to contact lenders, compare their options, and make arrangements to keep payments current.

As a parent of a young child, I would have to make those financial decisions while arranging housing, medical care, and international travel for my family. I ask DHS to account for these combined costs in its analysis of family well-being, including the possibility of missed payments and losses from rushed sales of household assets.

The current rule already limits the transition period and gives DHS discretion to shorten or eliminate it in individual cases. If DHS believes administering that discretion creates an undue burden, I ask the agency to quantify that burden and consider clearer adjudication guidance before eliminating the grace period. I also ask DHS to weigh the costs to U.S. employers when they find a qualified candidate but cannot complete the filing before that person must leave.

Please retain the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days so workers and their families have a practical opportunity to comply with immigration requirements and manage their financial obligations after an unexpected job loss.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states opposition to the elimination of the grace period and asks DHS to withdraw it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period. I believe this change will create more problems than it solves and could have unintended consequences for skilled workers, legitimate employers, and the U.S. economy.

Many H-1B professionals contribute significantly to American businesses and innovation. Losing a job due to layoffs, restructuring, or budget cuts does not make their skills or contributions any less valuable.

Finding another employer willing to sponsor an H-1B transfer is not as simple as accepting a job offer. Interviews, background checks, negotiations, immigration attorneys, petition preparation, and USCIS processing all take time. Sixty days is already a relatively short window to navigate this process.

My bigger concern is that eliminating this protection could actually strengthen the position of exploitative staffing agencies and consulting companies that are already a problem in the H-1B ecosystem.

Some of these companies keep workers on the bench with minimal pay, sometimes without an actual client contract or a project to work on. Workers can become financially and professionally dependent on these employers because their immigration status is tied to sponsorship. Removing the grace period would make it even harder for them to leave unfavorable employment arrangements.

Consider a highly skilled professional earning $150,000–$200,000 who loses a job at a legitimate American company. Instead of having a reasonable opportunity to find another direct employer, that person may feel pressured to accept a significantly lower-paying consultancy position with questionable employment practices simply to maintain immigration status.

The United States risks losing highly skilled, highly compensated talent while unintentionally strengthening businesses that profit from workers having fewer employment options.

This proposal does not address the underlying problems of H-1B fraud or employer exploitation. It could instead discourage workers from reporting unfair treatment, make them more dependent on sponsoring employers, and create conditions that encourage abusive workplace practices.

If DHS is concerned about individuals misusing the grace period to remain in the country through repeated or improper changes to other immigration statuses, such as F-1 or B-1/B-2, it should address those specific practices through appropriate eligibility checks and enforcement. Legitimate changes of status should not be treated as abuse, and legitimate workers who lose their jobs should not be penalized for it.

The existing 60-day grace period is already discretionary. USCIS has the authority to evaluate individual circumstances and shorten or eliminate the period when appropriate. There is no reason to remove this flexibility for everyone because of concerns involving certain individuals or employers.

DHS should instead focus on stronger enforcement against fraudulent employers, transparency in employment arrangements, accountability for abusive bench practices, and protections that allow workers to leave exploitative employment without facing an immediate immigration crisis.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the elimination of the 60-day grace period, arguing it harms workers and the economy.

I strongly oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers. This grace period is a modest but essential safeguard for people facing unexpected layoffs, corporate restructuring, or other job losses beyond their control.

comments.commentText:
RE: Comments in Opposition to Proposed Rule: Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364)
I am writing to express strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Removing this buffer creates extreme human hardship, disrupts U.S. business hiring, and fails to serve any legitimate administrative goal.
* Severe Humanitarian and Financial Harm
Eliminating the grace period forces legal workers into immediate out-of-status conditions the moment a contract or employment ends. It leaves zero time for individuals and their families to wrap up leases, manage personal assets, maintain continuous health insurance, or transition children out of schools. Forcing legal residents into overnight non-compliance is inhumane and chaotic.
* Increased Risk of Worker Exploitation
The 60-day window is a critical safety valve. Without it, employees lose the ability to leave toxic workplaces, report wage theft, or object to unfair labor conditions out of immediate fear of deportation. Eliminating this period grants employers disproportionate leverage over foreign talent and invites workplace abuse.
* Disruption to U.S. Business Hiring
It is practically impossible for a U.S. employer to complete a Labor Condition Application (LCA), internal HR approvals, and file a new H-1B petition on the exact day an employee is separated. Stripping this grace period prevents American companies from hiring experienced, vetted professionals who are already in the country.
* Increased Agency Workload
Rather than reducing paperwork for USCIS, removing the grace period will trigger an influx of emergency petitions, requests to excuse late filings under Nunc Pro Tunc claims, and unnecessary litigation—shifting administrative costs rather than reducing them.
DHS must retain the 60-day discretionary grace period to protect legal workers, maintain workforce portability, and uphold basic human dignity.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Introduction

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers. Eliminating this transition period could create significant socioeconomic consequences for workers, their families, American businesses, and the broader economy.

1. Insufficient Time to Find Alternative Employment

Finding another H-1B sponsoring employer involves applications, interviews, sponsorship decisions, attorney coordination, and immigration filings. This cannot happen overnight. Eliminating the grace period would leave workers with virtually no reasonable opportunity to secure alternative employment following unexpected layoffs, potentially forcing experienced professionals to leave the country despite having opportunities to continue working in the United States.

2. Disruption to Families and Children’s Education

Sudden employment termination could force entire families to relocate internationally without adequate preparation. Children may have to discontinue schooling in the middle of an academic year, disrupting their education and social development. Dependent college students could also face interruptions to their academic programs, education loan repayment difficulties, delayed degree completion, and potentially jeopardized graduation.

3. Auto Loans and Vehicle Repossessions

Many H-1B workers have financed vehicles based on their long-term employment and income. Immediate departure following job termination may leave insufficient time to sell vehicles or settle outstanding loans. This could result in payment defaults, vehicle repossessions, outstanding loan liabilities, and substantial financial losses for borrowers and American lending institutions, despite years of responsible repayments.

4. Housing Loans, Mortgages and Other Financial Obligations

Many workers also have mortgages, housing loans, rental agreements, personal loans, and credit card debts. These commitments cannot be resolved overnight. Abrupt departure could leave families unable to sell properties, settle mortgages, or responsibly close financial obligations. The resulting defaults, foreclosures, damaged credit histories, and unpaid debts could devastate families financially while creating avoidable losses for American banks, mortgage providers, and landlords.

5. Disruption to Medical Care

Employment termination can result in the loss of employer-sponsored health insurance. Eliminating the grace period could further disrupt ongoing treatments, specialist consultations, scheduled appointments, prescription medications, and follow-up care. Families with infants, children, pregnant women, or individuals requiring continued medical attention could face serious healthcare disruptions without adequate time to arrange alternatives.

6. Loss of Highly Skilled Talent and Economic Contributions

H-1B professionals bring specialized expertise to American industries, including healthcare, technology, engineering, research, and finance. Unexpected job loss does not diminish their skills or the demand for their expertise. Other American businesses may need precisely the same talent. However, insufficient transition time could prevent these professionals from joining new employers, resulting in lost talent, reduced productivity, project disruptions, and additional recruitment and training costs. The United States could lose experienced professionals who are willing and qualified to continue contributing to its economy.

Conclusion

The 60-day grace period provides a reasonable opportunity to pursue lawful employment alternatives and responsibly manage family, financial, educational, and healthcare commitments. I respectfully request that DHS reconsider its proposed elimination and retain this transition provision, balancing immigration compliance objectives with the practical realities faced by workers, families, American businesses, and communities.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that eliminating the grace period harms workers, families, and businesses, and asks DHS to reconsider.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sunil R
comments.commentText:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day discretionary grace period for nonimmigrant workers. We travel across the globe with the hope of building a life and contributing our skills to the United States through employer-sponsored nonimmigrant visas like the H-1B. Removing this critical 60-day safety net is devastating, unnecessarily punitive, and fundamentally disconnected from the realities of living and working in America.1. The Logistical Impossibility of an "Overnight" Departure
Highly skilled nonimmigrant workers are not transient day laborers who fly in, work for a few weeks, and fly out. We are legal professionals who spend years building established lives in the United States. We sign long-term leases, obtain mortgages, purchase vehicles, and enroll our children in local schools. If a worker is suddenly laid off, expecting a family to sell a house, break a lease, pull children out of school, and leave the country within 24 hours is not just an administrative oversight—it is practically and humanly impossible.2. Severe Economic Chilling Effect
If this rule takes effect, it will force a drastic shift in how nonimmigrant workers interact with the U.S. economy. Under the constant, looming threat of overnight deportation, high-skilled professionals will be forced to stop making tangible investments in their local communities. If we cannot guarantee we have even 60 days to wind down our affairs safely, we will stop buying homes, purchasing cars, and investing in local goods. Spending will be strictly limited to the bare essentials of food and temporary shelter, and all remaining income will be sent out of the country as a safety net. Industry estimates project that removing this grace period could cost the U.S. economy nearly $1.85 billion over the next decade. 3. Creating a Hostile Environment for Global Talent
The 60 days currently provided is the only relief that allows us to sustain our American Dream during sudden corporate downsizing. Removing it essentially downgrades the H-1B program from a pathway for highly specialized career professionals to a precarious, month-to-month contract. Furthermore, the constant instability will force many workers to leave their families behind in their home countries rather than risk trapping their spouses and children in a sudden overnight eviction scenario. No skilled professional desires a life permanently separated from their family. This hostile environment will ultimately drive the world's best talent to competing nations with more stable immigration systems, severely harming the U.S. companies that sponsor and rely on us.The current 60-day grace period is barely enough time to secure a new employer, file a complex change-of-employer petition, or safely wind down years of an established life. Eliminating it entirely punishes legal, tax-paying professionals and harms local U.S. economies. I strongly urge DHS and USCIS to abandon this proposal and maintain the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose any proposal to eliminate the existing 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders and other eligible employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

The United States has welcomed skilled professionals who have contributed to its economy, innovation, technology, healthcare, financial services, and other critical industries. Many of these individuals have lived and worked legally in this country for years, paid substantial taxes, purchased homes, and raised families while waiting patiently for permanent residency.

It is deeply concerning that an individual who has followed every immigration law, maintained lawful status, and contributed to the American economy for decades could suddenly face severe immigration consequences simply because an employer decides to eliminate a position.

Corporate layoffs are business decisions, not immigration violations committed by employees. Workers should not be penalized for circumstances they cannot control.

The current 60-day grace period is already extremely limited. Recruiting processes often require several rounds of interviews, background checks, internal approvals, immigration assessments, and government filings. Even a highly experienced professional may need more than 60 days to secure a new position. Eliminating this protection would make an already challenging situation unnecessarily devastating.

This proposal is especially troubling for individuals with approved I-140 petitions who remain trapped in employment-based green card backlogs. These workers have already demonstrated eligibility for an employment-based immigrant classification, yet their ability to remain in the United States can still depend on continued temporary employment. Removing the grace period would create additional instability for families who have invested years of their lives in this country.

There are broader economic consequences as well. American businesses benefit from being able to recruit experienced professionals already living in the United States. Eliminating the grace period could reduce access to skilled workers, increase hiring difficulties, and encourage valuable talent to relocate to competing economies.

It could also create an unhealthy imbalance between employers and employees by increasing workers’ dependence on their current employers and making them more vulnerable during layoffs or workplace disputes.

Immigration enforcement and reasonable worker protections are not mutually exclusive. The grace period does not authorize unrestricted employment. It simply provides a limited opportunity to arrange a lawful transition following an unexpected job loss.

I respectfully urge DHS to preserve the existing 60-day grace period and consider extending it to 90 days for involuntarily terminated workers, especially those with approved I-140 petitions and lengthy green card backlogs.

A fair immigration system should distinguish between individuals who violate immigration laws and hardworking professionals who unexpectedly lose their jobs.

A corporate layoff should not become an immigration emergency that forces an entire family to abandon the life they have legally built in the United States.

Please retain the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to you not as a policy lobbyist or a corporate executive, but as a U.S. citizen, a wife, and a mother of two young boys whose family life has been torn apart by the current crisis in the American technology job market. I am begging you to finalize this rule and eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and 8 CFR 204.5(p)(1)(i) immediately.
My husband did everything this country tells young Americans to do. He worked tirelessly to earn his Bachelor's and Master's degrees in Computer Science. For years, he poured his heart into building enterprise software, often working late into the night so our family could have a safe, stable future. When we finally saved enough to buy our family home, we cried tears of joy. We painted our sons' bedrooms, planted a small garden in the backyard, and believed that hard work and education meant we could pay our mortgage and raise our children in peace.
Then the tech layoffs hit our home. When my husband lost his software engineering job, we thought it would only take a few weeks for someone with his degrees and years of experience to find another position. Instead, I have watched the man I love slowly break down over months of endless rejection.
Every single morning, my husband wakes up at 6:00 AM and sits at his computer until midnight. He has submitted hundreds upon hundreds of applications. He studies for coding tests, passes multiple rounds of technical interviews with glowing feedback, and then gets told the position went to someone else at a fraction of the salary. Why? Because third-party staffing agencies are flooding every single job opening with laid-off temporary visa holders who are inside the 60-day grace period. Because those workers are desperate to get a new visa transfer filed before their 60 days run out, staffing vendors undercut American engineers by 25% to 30%. An American father trying to pay a mortgage and feed two kids cannot compete against a system that traps him in a race to the bottom.
Two months ago, our savings finally ran out. We could no longer make our mortgage payments. Having to sit our two little boys down and explain that we had to sell our house—that they had to pack up their toys and leave their bedrooms and their friends because Daddy still couldn't find a job—was the most heartbreaking moment of my life. On the day we handed over the keys to the home we worked so hard to buy, my husband sat in our car and wept because he felt he had failed us.
He did not fail us. Our government's regulations failed us.
When a temporary visa holder's job ends, the reason they were brought into the United States has ended. Yet DHS's own numbers show that keeping the 60-day grace period leaves thousands of unemployed foreign workers—and over 200,000 dependents with work permits each year—competing directly against laid-off Americans during the worst tech downturn in decades, with over 830,000 tech jobs lost since 2022.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Yuan Li
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. DHS's own data show the grace period works as intended. According to Table 3 of the NPRM, between FY 2021 and FY 2025, workers who lost or left jobs used the grace period to file 18,975 change-of-employer petitions (Form I-129), 1,924 adjustment-of-status applications (Form I-485), and 5,596 change/extension-of-status applications (Form I-539). These are lawful, fee-paying filings of exactly the kind Congress contemplated when it enacted job portability in AC21. Portability presupposes a bridge between jobs. The NPRM identifies no pattern of fraud or abuse attributable to the grace period itself.

2. Elimination creates a status cliff, not compliance. Under the proposal, a worker whose employment ends on a Friday falls out of status immediately — unable to complete a pending transfer, wind up a household, or depart in an orderly fashion. A layoff is an employer's decision, not worker misconduct, and it is often purely cyclical. Yet the consequences fall entirely on the worker and family: spouses lose work authorization overnight, children are pulled out of school mid-year, leases and mortgages are abandoned, and workers risk accruing unlawful presence with three- and ten-year inadmissibility consequences. Before 2017, this is precisely the chaos that led DHS itself to adopt the grace period in the 2016 AC21 retention rule.

3. Reliance interests are substantial and are not seriously analyzed. For nearly a decade, employers, universities, hospitals, and workers have structured hiring timelines, onboarding, relocations, and family decisions around 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Under Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Assn. v. State Farm and Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, an agency reversing course must give a reasoned assessment of serious reliance interests. The NPRM's assertion that those interests are "outweighed" is a conclusion, not the required analysis.

4. The administrative-burden rationale fails on DHS's own numbers. The filings the NPRM counts amount to roughly 26,000 over five years — a rounding error in USCIS's annual workload — and they represent the system operating as designed, not a defect. Eliminating the grace period will generate more work, not less: emergency status filings, motions to reopen, a surge in consular visa applications abroad, duplicative employer petitions, and litigation over status determinations.

5. The rule harms U.S. employers and competitiveness. The grace period lets a laid-off engineer, physician, or researcher join another U.S. employer — frequently in an underserved area — rather than taking U.S.-acquired training to Canada or another competitor country. Rural hospitals and universities that rely on H-1B physicians and faculty cannot replace them overnight.

6. A less drastic alternative was acknowledged but not analyzed. DHS states it considered shortening the grace period but chose total elimination. If adjudication burden is the concern, a shorter period or clearer evidentiary standards would address it. Selecting the most extreme option requires a fuller explanation than the NPRM offers.

The 60-day grace period is narrow, discretionary, and has operated for nine years without demonstrated abuse. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the rule and urges DHS to withdraw it, arguing the grace period is essential.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders following an involuntary job termination.

I have resided in the United States on an H-1B visa for the past 13 years. Throughout this time, I have maintained a spotless record, strictly complied with all immigration and legal regulations, contributed significantly to the local economy, and raised a family. My US born children attend American schools, and my spouse and I are homeowners who have deeply rooted our lives in our community.

The existing 60-day grace period provides a essential, humane buffer that allows lawful visa holders to handle sudden, unforeseen employment disruptions. Decision-making for long-term investments—most notably purchasing a home—relies on the modest stability this safety net provides. Eliminating this grace period creates extreme uncertainty and subjects law-abiding families to severe hardship:

Disruption to Families and Children: Requiring immediate departure upon job loss leaves no time to wind down household affairs, sell real estate, or transition children out of their schools smoothly. For children who know no other home, an abrupt exit is deeply destabilizing.

Property and Financial Strain: Homeownership involves complex legal and financial obligations. Liquidation or management of real estate assets cannot realistically occur overnight. Removing the 60-day period forces sudden financial distress on property owners and local real estate markets.

Loss of Qualified Talent: A complete lack of transition time discourages high-skilled, law-abiding foreign national professionals from investing long-term in the U.S. workforce and local communities.

The 60-day grace period strikes a balance between regulatory compliance and basic fairness for legal residents who contribute to the nation’s growth and pay taxes. Removing this period subjects families to immediate distress without providing any clear regulatory benefit.

I urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider this proposal and maintain the 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant visa holders.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the existing discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B and other affected employment-based visa holders and their dependents under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the protection.

Sixty days is already extremely short to find new employment. Securing an H-1B-sponsored position involves applications, multiple interviews, background checks, offer negotiations, and immigration processing. Corporate hiring can take weeks or months. Layoffs, restructuring, mergers, and budget cuts are often beyond an employee’s control. Eliminating the grace period would leave workers virtually no reasonable opportunity to find another employer or explore lawful alternatives.

Impact on children and families: I have lived in the United States since 2011, spending approximately 15 years building my career and raising my family. I have two daughters, aged 10 and 14. My younger daughter is a U.S. citizen, while my older daughter is not. Both are growing up and pursuing their education here.

An unexpected job loss could force our family to leave the country, disrupting both children’s lives, including a U.S. citizen child who has the right to live in her own country. They could leave school mid-year, abandon academic programs and extracurricular activities, lose educational continuity, or potentially lose an entire school year adjusting to another education system. They would also leave friends, teachers, and support networks. Parents should not have to choose between family unity and allowing their U.S. citizen children to remain in their own country.

Financial hardship: Families have long-term commitments including mortgages, car loans, credit cards, school fees, insurance, and property taxes. These obligations do not disappear when employment ends. Sudden relocation could cause mortgage defaults, vehicle repossessions, damaged credit, forced property sales, and losses in savings and investments. H-4 spouses may also have employment authorization, careers, and financial responsibilities that would be disrupted.

Impact on American businesses and the economy: H-1B professionals contribute specialized skills, institutional knowledge, and experience. Employers invest significantly in recruiting and training them. Unexpected departures could disrupt projects, delay customer commitments, reduce productivity, and increase recruitment costs. The U.S. economy could lose skilled talent, tax revenue, consumer spending, homeowners, innovation, and professionals who mentor the domestic workforce. Such uncertainty could also discourage global talent and complicate workforce planning.

Relocation and human consequences: International relocation requires arranging employment, housing, school admissions, educational records, travel, banking, insurance, and managing or selling property. These arrangements cannot reasonably be completed within days. Children and families would face significant educational, cultural, social, and emotional disruption. The uncertainty of losing employment and the ability to remain in the country creates enormous stress.

Long-term contributions and reliance interests: Many H-1B professionals have spent years or decades paying taxes, purchasing homes, raising families, and contributing to American businesses and communities. Workers and employers have made substantial commitments under the existing regulatory framework. DHS should consider these reliance interests before removing an established protection.

The existing 60-day grace period is discretionary and limited. It does not guarantee another job, an H-1B transfer, or permanent immigration status. It simply provides eligible individuals an opportunity to explore lawful alternatives and make responsible arrangements after unexpected employment termination. Retaining it does not prevent DHS from enforcing immigration requirements.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing 60-day grace period. DHS should consider the consequences for U.S. citizen children, dependent families, long-term residents, American employers, and the broader economy.

This is not merely an immigration regulation. It affects children’s education and future, family unity, financial security, business continuity, and America’s ability to retain skilled professionals.

I have spent approximately 15 years building my life in the United States. The possibility that an unexpected job loss could force my family to abandon that life, potentially disrupting my U.S. citizen daughter’s future, is deeply concerning.

Please do not eliminate this essential protection. Preserving the 60-day grace period is vital to protecting families, supporting American businesses, and maintaining U.S. competitiveness in attracting and retaining skilled global talent.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
(Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364) - Withdraw

I as a parent of US Citizen* and on behalf of **All special** need kid’s voice - am writing to express my strong and unequivocal opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day post-employment grace period for employment-based nonimmigrants (8 CFR 214.1(l)(2)).
While DHS asserts that this change reduces administrative burdens and ensures program integrity, the operational and humanitarian reality of a zero-day grace period is profoundly destructive. It introduces severe systemic friction and inflicts immediate, disproportionate trauma on the most vulnerable members of nonimmigrant families: special needs children.
1. Irreparable Disruptions to Special Needs Children
The absolute elimination of the 60-day window is a humanitarian crisis for families with special needs children. These children—many of whom are U.S. citizens or have lived here their entire formative lives—rely on highly localized school districts, established Individualized Education Programs (IEPs), specialized therapies, and trusted medical teams.
Endangering Health and Development: Medical and developmental progress for neurodivergent or medically fragile children requires strict continuity. Forcing families into an immediate departure or instant loss of status abruptly severs these vital healthcare and therapeutic lifelines overnight.

Mid-Semester Educational Trauma: Uprooting a special needs child instantly mid-semester causes catastrophic psychological and academic regression. These children cannot simply adapt to a sudden foreign environment or a new healthcare system without a transition window.

2. Failure of DHS Rationale: Increased Administrative and Judicial Burdens
DHS claims that removing the grace period reduces administrative burdens and aligns with statutory intent. In practice, it achieves the exact opposite:
Flooding USCIS and the Courts: Stripped of a clear, standard 60-day window to transfer visas, thousands of suddenly terminated workers will be forced to simultaneously file complex, auxiliary bridging applications (such as B-2 change-of-status or humanitarian requests). This surge will severely exacerbate existing USCIS processing backlogs.

Judicial Backlogs: The sudden, severe impact on families will inevitably trigger an influx of federal immigration litigation and court appeals, shifting an immense financial and operational burden onto the U.S. judicial system.

3. Economic Penalties for U.S. Employers and Lost Filing Fees
The rule harms the very ecosystem it claims to protect by creating steep liabilities for American businesses:
Wasted Employer Investments: U.S. companies invest tens of thousands of dollars in initial H-1B registrations, legal fees, and premium processing. If a highly skilled worker is laid off during a market fluctuation and forced to leave the country immediately, the employer’s financial investment is completely permanently lost.
Brain Drain: Rather than remaining in the U.S. to find alternative employment and continue paying taxes, top-tier international talent will permanently resettle in their home countries or move to competing nations with predictable immigration frameworks, like Canada or the UK.

Employer Friction: U.S. companies face intense operational strain to coordinate immediate, same-day terminations, while losing access to a vital local pool of vetted, immediately employable nonimmigrant talent.

4. Assumptions on Program Integrity and U.S. Workers
The 60-day grace period does not compromise program integrity; it actively protects it by providing a structured, legal, and traceable transition window. Furthermore, DHS provides no empirical evidence that a zero-day grace period improves opportunities for domestic workers. High-skilled nonimmigrant professionals with approved Form I-140 petitions have already been vetted and determined to fulfill critical U.S. labor shortages.
If the goal is to support domestic workers, and the solution is not to penalize legal, high-skilled taxpaying families. Instead, DHS and U.S. corporations should focus on Hiring more positive workforce for DHS and development by expanding internships, mentorships, and entry-level career pathways specifically targeted at domestic U.S. students and graduates.

Conclusion - Withdraw
Eliminating the 60-day grace period replaces an orderly, compassionate, and economically stable system with administrative chaos and humanitarian cruelty. It punishes innocent children—particularly those with special needs & US Citizens—for temporary corporate market adjustments. I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain the current 60-day grace period framework. Thank you. Appreciate it!

I strongly oppose the proposed rule in Docket USCIS-2026-0364 (RIN 1615-AD22) and urge DHS to withdraw it.

Under the proposal, an H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN or E worker who is laid off would fail to maintain status the day after the job ends and would be expected to depart immediately, along with their spouse and children. That expectation does not hold up. A worker told of a layoff in the morning cannot, in any reasonable sense, leave the country within a day. A home has to be sold or a lease broken, children have to be withdrawn from school mid-year, a spouse’s life has to be uprooted, and belongings and finances have to be dealt with. In practice, the rule would force law-abiding families out of the country on almost no notice, because of an employer’s decision they had no part in.

DHS’s own analysis undercuts the rule. It finds that the rule “would not negatively affect family well-being,” while the same rule ends the status of every dependent on the same day as the worker. It acknowledges that workers have homes, careers, taxes and community ties, then dismisses those reliance interests without estimating their cost. DHS’s own data shows the grace period is working and is rarely misused: only 37 Notices to Appear went to H-1B workers who stayed beyond it in FY 2025, while thousands of workers a year use it to find a new employer lawfully. Meanwhile, roughly 65,000 workers and 200,000 dependents lose or change jobs each year.

Eliminating the grace period is unlikely to reduce administrative burden. Workers who are forced to leave and seek readmission, or who scramble to file before their last day, will generate more filings, not fewer. DHS also rejected a shorter grace period without serious analysis.

A rule that gives families zero days to respond to a layoff is arbitrary and unjustified. DHS should withdraw it. At a minimum, it should keep the grace period and fully account for the harm to workers, families and U.S. employers.

comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period," 91 Fed. Reg. 57807.

I oppose removing the 60-day grace period at 8 C.F.R. § 214.1(l)(2) and ask DHS to withdraw the proposal. My full comment is attached. I am an energy professional in H-1B status with a Ph.D. from a U.S. university, so this rule applies directly to me.

If I were laid off without a grace period, I would have to leave the next day. I would face a $1,500 lease penalty plus rent and landlord charges for abandoned belongings; a car worth at least $10,000, with a loan only halfway paid off, that I could not sell in time; a last-minute flight to Delhi costing roughly $700 to $1,000 or more; immediate loss of health insurance; 401(k) penalties; bank and brokerage accounts I could not sort out; and an approved EB-2 NIW petition that becomes, in practice, a sunk cost because of the India backlog. I also know families with U.S.-citizen children whose schooling and specialized medical care depended on having time to plan.

1. It guts the job mobility Congress created (INA §§ 214(n), 204(j)). A new employer needs a certified Labor Condition Application, which can take up to 7 working days, before it can file. Without a grace period, a worker laid off without notice cannot use these protections.
2. It will not reduce DHS's workload. DHS would still have to determine when employment ended, the same reason it gave for rejecting another option. USCIS already used a simple last-day-paid rule. DHS lists the rule's benefits as "Not Estimated."
3. Workers, families, and employers have relied on it since 2017. DHS dismisses that reliance without weighing it.
4. DHS's cost estimate leaves out most real costs and undercounts those affected. Its own data show 65,752 workers a year losing or changing jobs and 208,187 dependent approvals a year.
5. It harms families, including U.S.-citizen children, and removes the window to apply for compelling-circumstances work permits.
6. It makes reporting employer abuse riskier and creates confusion about when a job "ends."
I ask DHS to withdraw the rule. If it wants less paperwork, it can make the grace period automatic using the last day paid. At a minimum, it should keep the grace period for involuntary layoffs, apply any change only going forward, and collect real data first.

Respectfully submitted,
A concerned H1B beneficiary

My name is Joy Fan, and I am a Senior FP&A Analyst at Rivian, an American electric vehicle manufacturer. I currently work in the United States under H-1B status, and I work alongside many talented international professionals, including colleagues who also rely on H-1B visas.

In industries such as electric vehicles, technology, and advanced manufacturing, competition for global talent is intense. These professionals contribute not only technical expertise but also financial planning, operational efficiency, strategic decision-making, and innovation that help American businesses grow.

Eliminating the H-1B grace period would not make the United States stronger. It could instead push valuable talent toward America's global competitors.

Consider the electric vehicle industry. American companies such as Rivian compete in a global market against international manufacturers, including China's BYD. If working in the United States means facing immediate immigration uncertainty following an unexpected layoff, talented individuals may increasingly choose to build their careers in countries offering greater stability.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear DHS and USCIS:

I respectfully oppose eliminating the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days for H-1B and other affected nonimmigrant workers and their dependents. Please retain this protection and address specific compliance concerns through targeted measures.

1. DHS previously recognized why this protection is necessary.

In its 2016 final rule, effective January 17, 2017, DHS explained that the grace period helps workers facing an unexpected end to employment seek another job, request another immigration status, or prepare to depart. DHS also recognized benefits for U.S. employers seeking to hire these workers. Those practical needs remain relevant today.

2. Sudden job loss should not eliminate a realistic opportunity to comply.

A worker cannot control every layoff or business closure. Finding an employer, completing interviews, obtaining an offer and preparing an immigration filing require coordination. Removing the transition period could make compliance depend on advance notice that many workers do not receive.

3. The existing protection is limited.

The regulation provides up to 60 consecutive days, or the remaining authorized validity period, whichever is shorter, once during each authorized validity period. DHS retains discretion to shorten or eliminate it. The grace period itself does not authorize employment. This is a temporary transition mechanism, not unrestricted permission to remain or work.

4. Removing it could increase workers’ vulnerability to retaliation.

In the 2016 rule, DHS specifically recognized that workers facing employer retaliation could benefit from the grace period. Removing that protection could discourage workers from reporting wage or other employment violations because termination could immediately jeopardize their ability to remain in the country. That potential consequence deserves careful consideration.

5. DHS should fully evaluate costs to employers and families.

Please assess the consequences for employers recruiting workers already in the United States, dependent spouses and children, housing commitments, medical treatment and departure arrangements. Administrative convenience should be weighed against these foreseeable disruptions.

6. Less disruptive alternatives deserve consideration.

If verifying employment end dates creates administrative burdens, DHS could consider standardized documentation or clearer filing instructions. If misuse is the concern, DHS should identify supporting evidence and explain why existing discretion and targeted enforcement are insufficient.

I request that DHS retain the existing grace period, publish a thorough assessment of alternatives and explain how eliminating it would improve compliance rather than make timely compliance harder.

A limited transition period supports orderly immigration administration, responsible departures and fair treatment of workers who lose employment unexpectedly.

T.hank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period and asks to retain it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B and other nonimmigrant workers. I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing 60-day grace period.

Thousands of skilled foreign workers have legally lived and worked in the United States for many years. We contribute to the American economy, pay federal and state taxes, purchase homes, support local businesses, and build our families and futures here. Many of us have followed immigration laws carefully while waiting years for employment-based permanent residency.

The existing 60-day grace period is not an unnecessary benefit. It is an essential protection that allows legally employed individuals to manage unexpected job losses and transition to new employment without immediately facing immigration uncertainty.

1. Job Loss Is Often Beyond an Employee’s Control

Layoffs, company restructuring, budget reductions, and economic downturns can happen unexpectedly. Even highly skilled and dedicated employees can lose their jobs through no fault of their own. Removing the grace period would impose severe immigration consequences on workers who have complied with the law.

2. Finding a New Job Requires Reasonable Time

Securing new employment involves applications, multiple interviews, background checks, employer sponsorship, and immigration paperwork. These processes cannot realistically be completed immediately. The 60-day grace period already provides only a limited window for workers to secure another opportunity.

3. Significant Financial Hardship for Families

Many H-1B workers have purchased homes, taken mortgages, financed vehicles, and made long-term financial commitments in the United States. They pay property taxes, contribute to their communities, and support the local economy. Unexpected job loss is already financially stressful. Removing the grace period would add the possibility of having to leave the country on short notice, creating devastating consequences for families who have spent years building their lives here.

4. Impact on Spouses and Children

A worker’s immigration status often directly affects their spouse and children. Families may have children attending American schools, spouses pursuing careers, and ongoing medical or financial responsibilities. These families deserve a reasonable transition period when unexpected employment changes occur.

5. Negative Impact on the American Economy

Highly skilled foreign professionals contribute to technology, healthcare, engineering, research, and many other industries. Eliminating the grace period could result in the unnecessary loss of experienced talent from the American workforce. Maintaining a reasonable transition period benefits both employees and American employers.

6. Fairness for Legal Immigrants

Many employment-based immigrants have waited years, sometimes decades, for permanent residency because of immigration backlogs. During this time, they continue working legally, paying taxes, and following immigration regulations. It would be unfair for an unexpected layoff to place their established lives and families at immediate risk.

7. The Existing Grace Period Is Already Limited

The current 60-day grace period is discretionary and subject to existing immigration requirements. It does not provide unlimited permission to remain in the United States or guarantee employment authorization. It simply allows a reasonable period for workers to pursue lawful alternatives after employment ends.

Instead of eliminating this protection, DHS should preserve the existing framework, which balances immigration enforcement with the practical realities of employment transitions.

I respectfully request that DHS reconsider and withdraw this proposed change. Legal immigrants who have contributed to the United States for years should not face immediate disruption to their families, homes, and livelihoods because of circumstances beyond their control.

The United States should continue to recognize the contributions of skilled workers while maintaining a fair, practical, and humane immigration system.

Please retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period.

Thank you for considering this public comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Emma Addams

The proposed rule risks conflating several legally distinct immigration concepts.

These include:

- Maintenance of nonimmigrant status;
- A period of stay authorized by DHS;
- Employment authorization;
- Eligibility to request an extension of stay;
- Eligibility to request a change of status;
- Eligibility to adjust status;
- Statutory H-1B portability under INA § 214(n).

The existence of a grace period does not independently authorize employment.

Likewise, the termination of employment does not necessarily mean that every independently existing immigration benefit or authorization is automatically extinguished.

DHS must explain the precise legal consequences of rescission for each relevant category.

In particular, the Department should clarify how the proposed rule interacts with pending Forms I-129, I-539, I-485, and independently valid employment authorization documents.

The Department must not create uncertainty by treating the termination of one employment relationship as automatically invalidating unrelated statutory or regulatory rights.

DHS should provide explicit guidance distinguishing these legal concepts in its final rule.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sasikumar Rajagopal
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket USCIS-2026-0364 – Opposition to Eliminating the 60-Day Grace Period

I respectfully oppose DHS’s proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR § 214.1(l)(2). This provision is an essential safeguard for legally employed nonimmigrant professionals, American businesses, and families. It provides a reasonable, limited opportunity to transition to another employer, pursue lawful immigration options, or arrange departure following unexpected job loss.

1. Economic impact on the United States

DHS estimates that approximately 3,795 workers annually have new employer petitions filed during the grace period, including approximately 3,765 H-1B workers. DHS also identifies a median annual offered wage of approximately $131,000 for a subset of H-1B workers changing employers.

At $131,000 annually, one month of gross earnings equals approximately $10,917. If just 25% of the estimated 3,765 H-1B workers experience an additional month of delayed employment, approximately $10.3 million in gross earnings would be affected annually. At 50%, that exposure increases to $20.5 million.

These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts. They exclude potential employer recruitment costs, delayed projects, relocation expenses, and reductions in taxable earnings.

DHS should evaluate these potential economic consequences against the administrative savings expected from eliminating the grace period.

2. Impact on American businesses

U.S. employers depend on experienced professionals in technology, engineering, healthcare, and critical infrastructure. Recruiting and replacing specialized workers requires time, resources, and training.

The grace period allows qualified professionals already in the United States to transition to new employers without unnecessary disruption. Eliminating it could increase recruitment expenses, delay projects, and reduce access to experienced workers.

A 60-day transition period supports workforce continuity and U.S. business competitiveness without granting unrestricted employment authorization.

3. Family stability and financial obligations

H-1B professionals often have spouses, school-age children, housing commitments, and other financial obligations.

For a household with $4,000 in monthly fixed expenses, 60 days represents approximately $8,000 in financial commitments. This illustrative figure excludes international relocation, travel, and immigration expenses.

Immediate loss of the transition period could force families to make major decisions involving employment, children’s education, housing, and international relocation without adequate preparation.

The existing grace period is a reasonable humanitarian protection, not an indefinite immigration benefit.

4. Worker mobility and protection

H-1B portability provisions are intended to facilitate lawful employer changes. However, identifying a new employer, completing recruitment procedures, obtaining a Labor Condition Application, and filing an H-1B petition require time.

Eliminating the grace period could increase workers’ dependence on their existing employers and discourage reporting of workplace concerns.

Retaining the provision supports lawful workforce mobility and fair employment practices.

5. Impact on workers with approved I-140 petitions

Many H-1B professionals have completed lengthy immigration processes and obtained approved I-140 petitions but remain subject to employment-based immigrant visa backlogs.

An unexpected job loss should not unnecessarily disrupt their ability to pursue lawful immigration options. DHS should preserve the relevant compelling-circumstances employment authorization provisions for eligible workers.

6. Less disruptive alternatives

If DHS seeks administrative efficiency, it should consider requiring clearer documentation of employment termination dates, standardized reporting, or other streamlined verification procedures rather than eliminating the grace period.

DHS should also publish a comprehensive cost-benefit assessment addressing lost earnings, employer replacement expenses, tax implications, and family relocation costs.

Requested action

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period.

The current provision is limited, practical, and economically beneficial. It allows legally employed professionals to navigate unexpected job loss while supporting American employers, preserving workforce continuity, and reducing unnecessary disruption to families.

Administrative efficiency should not come at the expense of substantial economic consequences and avoidable hardship.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing negative economic impacts and loss of safeguards.

The existing grace period serves an important purpose: it provides highly skilled foreign professionals and their families with a reasonable transition period when employment unexpectedly ends. Eliminating this provision would create significant hardship for individuals, families, and US employers without adequately considering the practical realities of today's employment and immigration landscape.

**1. Employment transitions require reasonable time**

Losing employment does not mean an individual has lost their professional qualifications, economic value, or intention to contribute to the United States. Finding a new position, completing multiple interview rounds, negotiating an offer, obtaining employer sponsorship, and filing the necessary immigration paperwork can take considerably longer than a few days.

These professionals contribute through their expertise, productivity, taxes, consumer spending, and innovation. Eliminating the grace period could force experienced professionals to leave the country, resulting in a loss of institutional knowledge and talent that US employers have spent years developing.

Immigration decisions affect entire families, not just the primary visa holder. Many families have established their lives in the United States, with children attending local schools, participating in community activities, and building long-term relationships.

At a minimum, DHS should consider alternatives that preserve a reasonable transition period, including clarifying eligibility requirements and maintaining appropriate case-by-case discretion.

A policy that encourages skilled professionals to remain, transition between employers, and continue contributing to the US economy benefits both American businesses and the broader community.

Re: Opposition to the Proposed Rule Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364)

To U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

1. Eliminating the grace period would harm the competitiveness of the U.S. economy.

Highly skilled foreign workers contribute significantly to American innovation, economic growth, and technological leadership. Many have invested years building their careers and contributing to U.S. businesses. Layoffs are often caused by economic conditions, corporate restructuring, or business decisions beyond an employee's control. Requiring these workers to leave the United States immediately after losing their jobs would unnecessarily drive experienced talent out of the country.

2. The proposal would reduce labor mobility and increase workers' dependence on employers.

The 60-day grace period provides workers with a reasonable opportunity to find new employment and maintain lawful immigration status. Without this protection, workers would become even more dependent on their current employers. This imbalance could discourage employees from reporting workplace misconduct, negotiating fair compensation, or seeking better opportunities. A policy that makes employees vulnerable to sudden loss of immigration status risks undermining fair labor practices and healthy competition in the American labor market.

3. The proposal would impose disproportionate hardship on workers and their families.

Losing a job is already a significant financial and emotional burden. Eliminating the transition period would make an already difficult situation substantially worse. Affected workers may have spouses, children attending American schools, housing commitments, and other long-term obligations. It is unreasonable to expect families to uproot their lives immediately because of an unexpected layoff. The existing grace period provides a modest but essential opportunity to manage these transitions responsibly.

4. The proposed change could increase costs for American businesses.

Employers seeking to recruit experienced foreign professionals would face additional complications if qualified candidates were forced to leave the country shortly after losing employment. This could increase recruitment costs, create unnecessary immigration processing burdens, and delay hiring. Retaining the grace period helps American employers recruit qualified workers already residing in the United States.

5. The potential benefits do not justify the economic and human costs.

The current grace period is limited and discretionary. It provides a practical transition mechanism rather than indefinite authorization to remain in the United States. Eliminating it would create substantial uncertainty for workers and employers without clearly demonstrated benefits that outweigh these costs. I urge DHS to thoroughly evaluate the economic consequences, labor-market effects, and reliance interests before making such a consequential policy change.

In conclusion, I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period. I respectfully request that DHS retain the existing protections under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Maintaining a reasonable transition period serves the interests of American businesses, protects workers against unnecessary hardship, and supports the United States' ability to attract and retain skilled professionals.

Thank you for considering my comments.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**Re: USCIS-2026-0364 — Proposed Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period**

I oppose DHS's proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrants under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). A brief transition period after job loss is a practical safeguard that allows people to seek new sponsorship, change status where eligible, or arrange departure. Eliminating it would impose serious costs on workers, employers, and families without a persuasive showing that doing so solves DHS's stated administrative problems.

**First, DHS has not adequately quantified the benefit of repeal.** The proposal cites more than 1.9 million filings for which grace-period applicability might have been considered. That is not the number of people who used the grace period, nor does it establish how often officers conducted burdensome reviews or how much staff time those reviews required. DHS acknowledges that it cannot estimate the additional adjudication time attributable to the grace period. An unquantified administrative inconvenience is a weak basis for abolishing a widely relied-upon transition mechanism.

**Second, repeal would not eliminate the need to determine when employment ended.** USCIS would still need to establish the termination date to decide whether a person maintained status or qualified for another immigration benefit. The proposal may remove one calculation while leaving the difficult underlying factual determination intact. DHS should explain how much work would actually disappear, rather than assuming that removing the grace period resolves the problem.

**Third, the proposal does not meaningfully compare its claimed savings against the costs it creates.** A worker laid off without warning cannot necessarily find a new sponsor, coordinate an immigration filing, or arrange international relocation immediately. U.S. employers may lose access to qualified candidates already in the country. Workers may lose income, and families may face financial and emotional disruption. More people may inadvertently fail to maintain status; DHS may also incur additional enforcement and removal-related costs. These effects deserve a serious, evidence-based assessment.

**Fourth, DHS should consider a less disruptive alternative:** make the grace period an automatic, clearly defined transition period, subject to appropriate exceptions, rather than an individualized discretionary determination. That would reduce uncertainty and some officer review while preserving time for job transitions or orderly departure. DHS could also standardize documentation for establishing the cessation-of-employment date. The proposal does not adequately explain why such alternatives would fail.

**Finally, the fact that Congress did not mandate a 60-day grace period does not mean the INA prohibits one.** DHS has authority to prescribe conditions of nonimmigrant stay, and a short period after involuntary job loss is consistent with an employment-based system that recognizes real-world hiring and travel timelines. Saying immediate departure better aligns with DHS's preferred approach does not establish that immediate departure is necessary.

Administrative Procedure Act principles require reasoned explanation, attention to foreseeable consequences and reliance interests, and meaningful consideration of important alternatives. The September 14, 2026 district-court opinion concerning DHS's duration-of-status rule illustrates the importance of those obligations, although it does not control this separate proposal.

I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed repeal and retain the 60-day grace period, preferably in a simpler and more predictable form. It is a modest protection that supports orderly compliance, worker mobility, and U.S. employers without allowing indefinite unemployment in the United States.

I respectfully write to oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B and other high-skilled nonimmigrant workers.
As an H-1B professional living and working legally in the United States, I pay federal, state, and local taxes, support American businesses, and contribute daily to my workplace and local community. I respectfully ask DHS to consider the severe, real-world harm this proposed rule would inflict on compliant workers, their families, and U.S. employers.
Experiencing an unexpected job loss is fundamentally different from violating immigration rules. Skilled professionals frequently lose employment due to corporate restructuring, budget cuts, mergers, or broader economic shifts—circumstances entirely beyond their control and unrelated to their job performance or legal compliance.
The 60-day grace period is a practical necessity, not an unfair advantage. Securing a new qualifying role does not happen overnight. Even a highly qualified candidate needs several weeks to interview, clear background checks, wait for internal corporate approvals, complete the Labor Condition Application (LCA) process, and allow immigration counsel to prepare and file a transfer petition. Sixty days provides the bare minimum timeframe required to complete these mandatory steps lawfully.
Equally important is the human impact on families. Many H-1B workers are the primary providers for households that include H-4 spouses and children enrolled in U.S. schools. An abrupt termination without a transition period threatens every part of a family's stability—putting spousal work authorization at risk, disrupting children’s education mid-year, and forcing families to break housing leases, sell homes and vehicles, and arrange international travel within days. A family that has followed every rule should not face sudden upheaval simply because a company downsized.
This issue is particularly critical for long-term H-1B workers who have spent many years contributing to the United States while waiting in decades-long employment-based green card backlogs. Many of these individuals hold approved I-140 petitions, own homes, raise families, and have built deep roots here while still relying on H-1B status for legal continuity.
Preserving the 60-day grace period also directly benefits American businesses and the U.S. economy. When a displaced worker transitions smoothly to a new U.S. employer within 60 days, they continue paying taxes, supporting local businesses, and filling critical skill gaps without forcing companies to endure costly international recruitment delays. Forcing a worker to depart the country immediately—only for another U.S. employer to sponsor them back months later—creates needless financial and administrative burdens for everyone involved.
Importantly, the current regulation already grants USCIS full discretion. If DHS identifies specific cases of abuse, the agency already has the authority to shorten or deny the grace period on an individual basis rather than eliminating a vital safeguard for all law-abiding professionals.
The 60-day grace period does not grant permanent status or guarantee employment; it simply provides a brief, orderly bridge to transfer status or wind down affairs responsibly. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day discretionary grace period.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Emma C
comments.commentText:
Re: USCIS-2026-0364 — Proposed Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period

I oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for employment-based visa holders. I am in a relationship with someone who holds H-1B status, and I want DHS to consider the impact this rule would have not only on visa holders and their employers but also on the people who share their lives.

An unexpected layoff is difficult for anyone. For an H-1B worker, this proposal would add a sudden immigration-status crisis to the loss of a job. The worker could lose the ability to maintain status almost immediately after employment ends, without a meaningful transition period to find another employer, explore lawful options, or make arrangements to leave. Even a person who has followed every rule could face major disruption because of an employer's business decision.

For people in relationships, the effects extend further. Couples make plans about where to live, whether to take jobs, and how to build a future together. Dating partners are not necessarily recognized as immigration dependents, but their lives can still be deeply affected by an abrupt requirement to relocate or separate. We should not have to treat an unexpected layoff as a decision about whether our relationship can continue in the same country.

The existing grace period does not guarantee indefinite stay or permission to work without authorization. It provides a limited window—up to 60 days, or until the existing authorized validity period ends, whichever is shorter—to take lawful next steps. That window is already short given the time needed to interview, secure an offer, have an employer prepare a petition, or plan international travel. Eliminating it entirely is disproportionate.

I also question whether this proposal will accomplish DHS's stated goals. USCIS may still need to determine the exact date employment ended, even if the grace period disappears. And a rule that leaves people almost no time to comply could increase inadvertent status violations instead of improving compliance. DHS has not demonstrated that the administrative savings justify these consequences.

There is a more reasonable approach: retain the 60-day transition period and simplify its administration, for example through clearer documentation and an automatic rule with appropriately defined exceptions. That would help employers and workers follow the law without placing unnecessary strain on relationships and families.

I ask DHS to withdraw this proposal. A system can enforce employment-based visa requirements while still allowing a short, humane, predictable transition after job loss. The people affected are not just entries in an immigration database; they are coworkers, friends, partners, and members of communities who need a reasonable opportunity to make responsible decisions when circumstances change unexpectedly.

* Increased Agency and Court Backlogs: Far from reducing administrative burden, the rule will overwhelm U.S. consulates with abroad visa processing requests and clog the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) with avoidable Notices to Appear (NTAs) and removal proceedings for technical status lapses.
* Undermining Worker Protections: Tying lawful status strictly to unbroken employment without a transition period creates a coercive dynamic, leaving nonimmigrant workers unable to report wage theft or unsafe workplace conditions out of fear of immediate deportation.
* Punishing Lawful Immigrants in Backlogs: Revoking the link between the grace period and eligibility for compelling circumstances Employment Authorization Documents (EADs) under 8 CFR 204.5(p) unfairly deprives approved I-140 beneficiaries—trapped in multi-decade immigrant visa backlogs—of a vital safety net.
The 60-day grace period is a practical, essential component of an orderly and competitive immigration system. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this rulemaking in its entirety.
Respectfully Submitted
Thomas Jacob
California

comments.commentText:
Dear Officers and Reviewing Officials,

Thank you for the opportunity to submit public feedback on this proposed rulemaking. I write to express my respectful opposition to the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrants.

I approach this submission with deep appreciation for the U.S. immigration system, federal regulatory oversight, and the ongoing efforts of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to maintain system integrity. As a law-abiding nonimmigrant professional who has called the United States home for years, I fully respect the Department’s duty to ensure that nonimmigrant statuses remain aligned with authorized employment. However, preserving the existing up-to-60-day grace period is essential to achieving that goal fairly, while protecting the stability of local communities, U.S. infrastructure and engineering sectors, and dedicated foreign professionals.

1. Sustained Economic Contributions and Multi-Earner Family Stability
High-skilled nonimmigrant professionals make significant, daily contributions to the American economy. Across critical technical sectors-such as civil engineering and infrastructure development-we contribute directly to public projects, private-sector innovation, and regional growth, while paying substantial federal, state, and local taxes.

Furthermore, many nonimmigrant households operate as multi-earner families, with spouses supporting local businesses, healthcare systems, and other industry. Eliminating the grace period creates immediate, cascading economic disruption. Unanticipated job separations happen due to corporate restructurings, project funding shifts, or economic downturns that are entirely outside a worker's control. Without a modest buffer window, a single termination instantly strips status from the entire household overnight. This leaves families no practical runway to wrap up financial obligations responsibly-such as settling residential leases, managing mortgages, or concluding tax liabilities-resulting in unmonetized financial strain for local U.S. landlords, lenders, and community commerce.

2. Realistic Portability and Engineering Recruitment Timelines
The 60-day grace period was designed to afford high-skilled foreign workers realistic job portability and flexibility. In technical fields like civil engineering, recruitment and onboarding involve rigorous background verifications, professional license verifications, and compliance checks. Even when a qualified U.S. employer extends an offer immediately, preparing and filing a change-of-employer petition (including Labor Condition Applications) routinely takes several weeks.

Requiring an employer’s petition to be received by USCIS on or before the final day of employment eliminates practical portability. This places an unintended administrative bottleneck on U.S. engineering firms seeking to retain specialized talent already present in the domestic workforce. Retaining a flexible 60-day window allows compliant, qualified professionals to transition smoothly between employers without disrupting ongoing public or private infrastructure projects.

3. Protecting Law-Abiding Families and School-Aged Children
Nonimmigrant workers strictly follow complex visa regulations, maintain flawless compliance records, and actively invest in their local neighborhoods. For families with children enrolled in local schools and are US citizens, the sudden, immediate loss of status creates severe psychological and logistical hardship, and creating a difficult situation difficult to explain that why they cannot stay here being an US citizen. Dislocating children mid-school year and abruptly severing deep community ties undermines the stability of families who have consistently acted in good faith under existing immigration framework policies. A predictable grace period upholds basic fairness for law-abiding residents.

Conclusion
The 60-day grace period serves as a vital bridge that preserves economic value, rewards lawful compliance, and supports U.S. industry flexibility. Rather than eliminating this provision entirely, I respectfully encourage DHS to maintain the 60-day discretionary grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) to ensure a stable, fair, and competitive environment for workers and employers alike.

Thank you for your time, consideration, and dedication to public service.

Respectfully submitted,

An Anonymous Law-Abiding Nonimmigrant Professional & Resident
