To: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22, “Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period”
Date: November 10, 2026
I oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period and respectfully ask DHS to withdraw it.
I am an H-1B worker who has lived in the United States for more than 10 years. I work as a Technical Project Manager in Maryland and have an approved I-140 immigrant petition. My wife is a Physical Therapist with her own H-1B status. We have a toddler son who was born in the United States, and we own a home with a mortgage.
For my family, the grace period represents a limited but important opportunity to respond responsibly to an unexpected job loss. Eliminating it would create significant uncertainty for our careers, financial obligations, and ability to keep our family together.
Finding another sponsor takes time
My greatest concern is finding another employer willing and able to sponsor an H-1B worker. In the difficult job market I am navigating, securing a suitable position is already challenging. Sponsorship adds another requirement that narrows my options.
Finding a new job requires identifying suitable openings, completing interviews, obtaining an offer, and coordinating the necessary immigration filing. I cannot control employers’ hiring schedules, internal approvals, or sponsorship decisions. These steps cannot realistically be completed immediately after an unexpected termination.
The 60-day grace period does not guarantee another job. It provides a limited opportunity to seek new employment and evaluate available immigration options. Removing that opportunity would make a layoff substantially more disruptive.
My family would face significant consequences
After more than a decade in the United States, my life here extends beyond a single employer. It includes my wife’s career, our young child, our home, and long-term financial commitments.
Our mortgage and household expenses would continue if I lost my job. At the same time, I would need to search for another sponsoring employer and address my immigration situation. The possibility of relocation would create additional financial and practical difficulties.
My wife holds her own H-1B status, rather than dependent status tied to mine. Nevertheless, disruption to my ability to remain and work here would affect our entire household. We would have to consider how to keep our family together while maintaining her employment, caring for our toddler, and meeting our financial obligations.
Our son was born in the United States. Providing him with a stable home and keeping his parents together are central priorities for us. A reasonable transition period would help us make informed decisions rather than respond to an immediate crisis.
An approved I-140 does not eliminate my concerns
Although I have an approved I-140 immigrant petition, I remain in H-1B status. That approval is an important milestone, but it does not remove my concern about the consequences of losing my employment.
I want to continue contributing through my work and raising my family here. An unexpected employment interruption should not unnecessarily derail the life we have built over more than 10 years.
I ask DHS to consider workers who have approved immigrant petitions but still rely on temporary employment-based status. We need a realistic opportunity to manage job loss and evaluate our options.
Preserve a reasonable transition period
I understand that H-1B status is connected to qualifying employment. I am not asking for an unlimited right to remain without meeting immigration requirements. I am asking DHS to preserve a limited, practical transition period following an unexpected loss of employment.
If DHS has concerns about administering the grace period, it should consider less disruptive alternatives. For example, applicants could clearly identify their reliance on the grace period and provide the date employment ended. Clear instructions and documentation requirements could address administrative concerns without eliminating this protection.
DHS should also consider the practical costs to families: lost income, continuing mortgage payments, difficulty finding sponsorship, potential relocation expenses, and disruption to a spouse’s career and a young child’s home life. These consequences matter even when a family cannot assign an exact dollar amount to them.
I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the 60-day grace period. For my family, it provides essential time to respond to an unexpected job loss while pursuing new sponsorship and protecting our household’s stability.

Maryland

To U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:

I am writing to oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to retain this provision because its removal could negatively affect foreign workers, American employers, and the broader economy.

1. Loss of skilled talent

Since layoffs often result from economic downturns or corporate restructuring rather than individual performance, eliminating the grace period could force qualified professionals to leave the country unnecessarily, weakening America’s ability to retain global talent.

The existing grace period gives workers time to seek new employment and maintain lawful immigration status. Without it, employees would become more dependent on their sponsoring employers and less able to report workplace misconduct, negotiate fair compensation, or pursue better opportunities. This could undermine fair employment practices and create an unhealthy imbalance in the workplace.

3. Disproportionate impact on families

Unexpected job loss is already financially and emotionally challenging. Many affected individuals have spouses, children attending American schools, housing commitments, and other established responsibilities. Requiring them to leave the country immediately would create unnecessary hardship and disruption. The existing grace period provides a reasonable opportunity to evaluate alternatives and make responsible decisions.

4. Additional burdens on American businesses

It may also increase administrative burdens, complicate hiring processes, and delay recruitment. Retaining the provision helps employers access an existing pool of qualified talent.

The current grace period is discretionary and time-limited; it does not provide indefinite authorization to remain in the United States. Eliminating it could create substantial uncertainty without clearly established benefits that outweigh the economic and personal consequences. DHS should carefully evaluate these potential impacts before implementing the proposed change.

Conclusion

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing protections under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Maintaining a reasonable transition period supports American businesses, protects workers and their families from unnecessary hardship, and helps the United States remain competitive in attracting and retaining skilled professionals.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write to oppose the proposed removal of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I am an international graduate student in accounting at a U.S. university, and I previously worked in audit at a U.S. accounting firm. I expect to work in the United States after graduation through OPT and, if selected, H-1B status. The grace period is one of the few protections a skilled worker has against a sudden layoff that is not their fault. Removing it would harm workers, their families and U.S. employers. Its stated justifications don’t hold up.

1. The rule ignores real costs. The regulatory analysis lists no quantified or qualitative cost to beneficiaries or petitioners. That isn’t credible. Under the proposal, a worker laid off without warning, and their spouse and children, would be out of status the next day. They would face an immediate international move, broken leases, children pulled out of school mid-year, and lost wages and retirement savings. Employers who would have hired them through a change-of-employer petition would lose a qualified candidate. An agency that does not consider such an important aspect of the problem acts arbitrarily (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983)).

2. Reliance interests are real, and DHS dismisses them. DHS adopted the grace period in its 2016 final rule (81 FR 82398) after finding that the lack of any transition period harmed workers and employers. Since then, workers, families, employers and counsel have planned around it. DHS says that reliance is “misplaced” because the period is discretionary, but it is generally available in practice. An agency changing a long-standing policy must weigh serious reliance interests, not assume them away (DHS v. Regents of the Univ. of Cal., 591 U.S. 1 (2020)).

3. The burden rationale supports a different fix. DHS says checking whether a worker stayed within the 60 days is burdensome. The obvious answer is to make the period a clear, non-discretionary rule, not to abolish it. A fixed period would cut adjudication burden and improve consistency without harming the people the rule affects. DHS should explain why it rejected this and other less harmful options, such as a shorter fixed period.

4. It weakens workers in abusive situations. If losing a job means losing status the next day, a worker cannot safely leave an employer that underpays them, violates wage rules or retaliates. This gives employers excessive leverage and works against DHS’s own interest in program integrity and protecting U.S. wage standards.

5. It undercuts other DHS programs. The compelling-circumstances EAD and change-of-employer portability depend on a worker remaining in status long enough to file. Without the grace period, the worker would usually have to file on the day the job ends. These pathways would become largely unusable in the involuntary job-loss situations they were designed for.

6. It will drive skilled workers away. As someone investing in a U.S. graduate degree after training at a U.S. firm, I weigh the stability of my status when deciding where to build a career. Competitor countries give laid-off skilled workers a reasonable period to find new work. Without one, the U.S. becomes far less attractive to the graduates its universities train, and U.S. employers lose talent they have already spent years recruiting and training.

Requests. DHS should withdraw the proposal. If it proceeds anyway, it should:

Keep a grace period of at least 60 days and make it non-discretionary.
Exempt dependents, or give them an independent transition period.
Include transition provisions so that no one already in a grace period on the effective date loses status.
Publish a revised economic analysis that quantifies costs to workers, families and employers before finalizing any rule.

Thank you for considering these comments.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed removal of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and urge DHS to retain the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days for employment-based nonimmigrant workers and their dependents.

A temporary loss of employment, particularly through an unexpected layoff, should not erase years of lawful compliance or force otherwise law-abiding professionals and their families to leave the United States immediately. The existing grace period provides a reasonable and necessary safeguard that balances immigration enforcement with economic stability, workforce mobility, and administrative efficiency.

1. The grace period supports lawful transitions; it does not authorize unauthorized work.

The existing regulation provides a limited window to find a qualifying employer, have a new petition filed, pursue a permissible change of status, or arrange departure. It does not generally authorize employment during the grace period. Treating a brief, regulated transition as inconsistent with employment-based status overlooks its purpose: helping qualified workers remain in compliance when circumstances change.

2. Immediate departure is incompatible with ordinary hiring and immigration processes.

Recruitment, interviews, background checks, employer approvals, attorney preparation, and petition filing routinely take time. Even a qualified worker with an interested employer cannot necessarily complete these steps the day their job ends. Eliminating the grace period could force workers to leave before a new employer can file a petition, adding travel, consular-processing, relocation, and delay costs. U.S. employers may lose access to candidates already living here and previously vetted through the immigration system.

3. The proposal understates reliance interests and family disruption.

Section IV.D acknowledges that employees, employers, and family members have structured careers, housing, finances, and community ties around the current rule. Many employment-based nonimmigrant workers also spend years pursuing permanent residence while maintaining temporary status. An unexpected job loss should not automatically create an immediate departure crisis for workers and their dependent family members. DHS should meaningfully weigh these foreseeable consequences rather than dismissing reliance because the existing grace period is discretionary.

4. The agency's own data warrant a more complete cost-benefit analysis.

Table 3 reports 18,975 new Form I-129 filings by new employers within 60 days of withdrawal of the prior petition during FY 2021–2025. This is evidence that the transition period has a practical function. The NPRM also states that DHS cannot distinguish voluntary from involuntary separations in the underlying withdrawal data and cannot reliably estimate how many dependents would have used the grace period. Its discussion recognizes possible lost wages, travel and lease-termination expenses, employer productivity losses, and additional removal-related proceedings, yet many of these costs remain unquantified. Before removing a longstanding safeguard, DHS should estimate these impacts more fully and compare them with demonstrable administrative savings.

5. Administrative simplification can be achieved without abolishing the protection.

Section IV.E rejects alternatives such as clearer evidentiary requirements because officers would still need to review some documentation. But the existence of some review does not establish that full elimination is the least burdensome or most proportionate approach. DHS could instead standardize proof of the last day of employment, clarify required supporting evidence, and streamline adjudication while retaining the existing maximum 60-day period and agency discretion in individual cases.

Finally, removing the grace period would place workers in a more dependent position relative to their employers, making it harder to leave exploitative conditions or report workplace problems without risking an immediate status crisis. A policy intended to protect program integrity should not inadvertently discourage compliance or legitimate labor mobility.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal, retain 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), and conduct a more complete analysis of affected workers, families, employers, and government costs before considering any change. A limited, discretionary transition period is a practical safeguard that supports compliance, economic continuity, and orderly administration.

Thank you for considering this comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing as an H-1B visa holder to strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period. This change would create severe financial, professional, and emotional hardships for law-abiding immigrants and their families who have spent years contributing to the American economy.

1. Families Cannot Uproot Their Lives Overnight

Many H-1B professionals have lived in the United States for years, purchased homes and vehicles, accumulated household belongings, and established financial commitments. Losing a job does not mean someone can immediately sell their property, settle mortgages and loans, dispose of household possessions, and relocate internationally.

Selling a house alone can take several months due to market conditions, inspections, negotiations, and closing procedures. Selling vehicles, terminating leases, arranging international shipping, and settling financial obligations also require time.

Even the existing 60-day grace period may be insufficient for these responsibilities. Eliminating it would expose families to substantial financial losses, potentially forcing them to sell assets below market value or continue paying mortgages and loans after leaving the country.

2. Unexpected Layoffs Are Beyond Employees’ Control

Employees can lose their jobs because of restructuring, budget cuts, or economic downturns despite excellent performance. Individuals who have maintained lawful immigration status and paid taxes for years should not face immediate immigration uncertainty because of decisions made by their employers.

3. Finding Another Employer Requires Time

H-1B transfers involve interviews, background checks, legal reviews, Labor Condition Applications, and immigration petition preparation. These processes cannot always be completed immediately, even when another American employer is willing to hire the individual.

Eliminating the grace period could result in the unnecessary departure of skilled professionals who would otherwise continue contributing to U.S. businesses.

4. Families and Children Will Suffer

Many H-1B holders have spouses and children whose immigration status depends on their employment. Children attend American schools, spouses have careers, and families have ongoing medical and financial responsibilities.

Sudden relocation can disrupt children’s education, healthcare, and family stability. Families cannot reasonably arrange international relocation, school transfers, housing, and financial settlements immediately following an unexpected layoff.

5. Increased Risk of Employer Exploitation

Removing the grace period would increase employees’ dependence on their employers. Workers may hesitate to report discrimination, harassment, wage violations, or unfair working conditions if losing employment could immediately jeopardize their immigration status.

A reasonable transition period helps protect employees and supports fair employment practices.

6. Green Card Backlogs Make the Situation Worse

Many H-1B professionals have spent years waiting for employment-based green cards, despite having approved immigrant petitions. They continue paying taxes, purchasing homes, and supporting American communities while remaining dependent on temporary work visas.

Removing the grace period would further destabilize families who have complied with immigration laws for years.

7. Negative Economic Consequences

H-1B professionals contribute through income taxes, property taxes, home purchases, consumer spending, and specialized expertise. Forcing skilled workers to leave without reasonable transition time can disrupt businesses, reduce productivity, and create unnecessary economic losses for both employees and employers.

8. Reasonable Alternatives Exist

Immigration compliance can be maintained through improved reporting, efficient petition processing, and enforcement against actual violations without eliminating essential transition protections.

DHS should preserve the existing 60-day grace period and consider additional flexibility for individuals facing documented financial, family, or relocation hardships.

Conclusion

A person who has spent 10 or 15 years building a life in America cannot simply pack a suitcase and leave after losing a job. They have homes, vehicles, mortgages, children, financial obligations, and years of investments that cannot be liquidated overnight. Even two months may not be enough to responsibly settle these commitments.

Losing employment should not automatically turn into a financial catastrophe for an entire family.

The 60-day grace period is not a special privilege or exemption from immigration laws. It is a reasonable transition mechanism that recognizes the practical realities of employment, family responsibilities, and financial commitments.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and their families.

comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for immigrant workers and their families.
Losing a job is already a difficult and stressful experience. But losing a job should not mean that an entire family must leave the country immediately, without having enough time to organize their lives.
Many immigrants have lived in the United States for several years. They have purchased homes, raised children, built careers, established relationships, and become part of their local communities. Their lives cannot simply be packed into suitcases and moved to another country overnight.
Consider the practical challenges families would face without a reasonable transition period:
•Homeowners: Selling a house is not an overnight process. Finding a buyer, completing inspections, negotiating offers, and closing a mortgage can take months. Families could face significant financial losses if forced to leave immediately.
•Rental housing: Lease agreements require advance notice. Families need time to notify landlords, terminate leases, settle payments, and arrange alternative housing.
•Children's education: Children are enrolled in schools, attending classes, preparing for examinations, and participating in activities. Abrupt relocation can interrupt their education and cause emotional distress. Parents need time to obtain school records and arrange transfers.
•Medical care and pregnancy: Families may be undergoing ongoing medical treatments, scheduled surgeries, or regular healthcare appointments. Pregnant women need continuity of prenatal care and proper delivery planning. These situations cannot be handled safely through sudden relocation.
•Financial commitments: Families have mortgages, car loans, credit card balances, insurance policies, utility bills, and other pending payments. Selling a car, transferring ownership, closing accounts, and settling outstanding loans all require time.
•Family responsibilities: Spouses and children need time to prepare emotionally and practically for a major change. Finding flights, arranging international relocation, shipping belongings, and coordinating with family members in another country are not immediate tasks.
These are not luxuries or special privileges. They are normal responsibilities of families who have built their lives in this country.
Immigrants contribute to the US economy, pay taxes, purchase homes, support local businesses, and invest in their children's future. Many have made long-term commitments based on their employment and lives in the United States.
An unexpected job loss should not turn into an immediate family crisis that forces people to abandon their homes, financial investments, medical care, and children's education.
The existing 60-day grace period provides a small but extremely important window to find another employment opportunity, explore lawful alternatives, or make an orderly departure. It does not give anyone permission to remain in the country indefinitely.
My request is simple: Please do not eliminate the 60-day grace period.
Preserve this reasonable transition time so that individuals and families can handle unexpected employment changes with dignity, responsibility, and basic financial and family security.
Immigration policies should maintain compliance while also recognizing the realities of human life. A family deserves reasonable time to close one chapter of life before being forced to begin another.
Please consider the human impact and reject this proposal.
Respectfully,
Anonymous Public Commenter
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing hardships for families and logistics.

I urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and maintain the existing 60-day grace period. Every worker deserves a reasonable opportunity to recover from unexpected circumstances and find another lawful employment opportunity.

I am writing to respectfully request that the Department of Homeland Security reconsider the proposal to eliminate the 60 day discretionary grace period. I strongly advocate for maintaining this essential window, which supports both the integrity of our immigration system and the stability of our workforce.
The existing 60 day transition period is a compassionate and practical measure for highly skilled professionals facing unexpected employment changes. The vast majority of these legal workers, over 99% have consistently paid their taxes, contributed to their local communities, and strictly adhered to all U.S. laws throughout their stay. Providing them with a predictable, reasonable window allows these law-abiding families the necessary time to responsibly organize their affairs, manage immigration transitions, plan for property, medical children school, and plan their next steps without facing immediate hardship.

By keeping highly specialized, pre-vetted talent within the country during a job transition, the policy allows other U.S. employers to readily identify and hire exceptionally skilled individuals who are already located within the United States. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**Comment on DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 – RIN 1615-AD22**
**Re: Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period**

I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I urge DHS to retain the existing grace period for affected employment-based nonimmigrant workers and their dependent family members.

Employment termination affects more than the individual worker. Many H-1B and other employment-based workers have established their lives in the United States with spouses and children. They have purchased homes, enrolled children in schools and daycare, taken on mortgages and other financial commitments, and built connections in their communities. Eliminating the grace period would force families to make significant decisions without reasonable time to evaluate their options.

**1. Impact on Children and Education**
Children should not have their education and daily routines abruptly disrupted because of a parent's unexpected job loss. Families need time to explore new employment, other lawful immigration options, or relocation. An immediate departure requirement could interrupt children's schooling, daycare, friendships, and emotional stability. The grace period allows families to plan these transitions responsibly.

**2. Homeownership and Financial Commitments**
Many workers have purchased homes and taken on substantial commitments, including mortgages, vehicle payments, and household expenses. Selling a home requires time to prepare the property, find buyers, negotiate offers, and complete the transaction. Eliminating the grace period could force families to manage these responsibilities under extreme time pressure, potentially resulting in financial losses and rushed decisions.

**3. Opportunity to Find New Employment**
Finding a new employer willing to sponsor an immigration petition involves applications, interviews, technical assessments, background checks, negotiations, and petition preparation. These processes cannot always be completed immediately after an unexpected termination. The existing grace period gives skilled professionals a reasonable opportunity to find new employment and continue contributing their skills to U.S. employers.

**4. Opportunity to Explore Alternative Immigration and Education Pathways**
Not every affected worker will immediately find another sponsoring employer. Depending on individual eligibility, some may need to explore higher education through an appropriate student status, extraordinary ability classifications such as O-1 or EB-1A, or eligible entrepreneur and investor pathways. Evaluating these options requires time to understand eligibility, consult qualified professionals, and prepare documentation. Removing the grace period could prevent individuals from meaningfully considering these lawful alternatives.

**5. Consideration of Family Well-Being**
In Section V.F, Family Assessment, DHS concludes that eliminating the grace period would not negatively affect family well-being, reasoning that financial consequences result from employment termination rather than the proposed rule.

However, employment termination is the triggering event; eliminating the grace period directly reduces the time families have to respond. Having up to 60 days to organize children's education, housing, finances, travel, and immigration alternatives is materially different from having to make those decisions immediately. I urge DHS to reconsider its assessment and give greater consideration to the practical consequences for dependent spouses, children, and households.

**6. Retirement Savings, Healthcare Accounts, and Financial Planning**
Many workers contribute substantial amounts to retirement and healthcare accounts, including 401(k), Roth 401(k), and Health Savings Accounts (HSA). These savings can represent thousands of dollars accumulated over years of employment and are important to families' long-term financial security.

Sudden job loss combined with an immediate departure requirement creates additional pressure to understand account options, investment allocations, potential rollovers, healthcare balances, and related tax considerations. Workers may need time to consult financial and tax professionals and make informed decisions. Employment termination can also interrupt future contributions, employer matching, and other benefits.

These workers also participate in the U.S. financial system through their savings and investments. DHS should consider the broader financial and household consequences of removing the time needed to manage these transitions.

**Conclusion**
The 60-day grace period is an important safeguard for entire families facing unexpected employment and immigration changes. Without it, children may face immediate educational disruption, families may be forced into rushed housing and financial decisions. I respectfully urge DHS to preserve the existing discretionary 60-day grace period
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the grace period and urges DHS to retain it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). My concern is not with the government's objective of enforcing immigration laws or protecting American workers. It is whether this particular change would accomplish those goals, and whether its benefits would outweigh its economic and administrative costs.

The existing grace period serves a practical purpose. It allows a worker whose employment ends to arrange a transfer to another employer, apply for a different immigration status, or prepare to leave the country. It is limited to 60 days or the remaining period of authorized stay, whichever is shorter, and does not independently authorize employment. In other words, it provides time to comply with immigration requirements without removing those requirements.

I see several problems with eliminating it.

First, the proposal could reduce efficiency in the American labor market. Suppose a company lays off an H-1B employee because it no longer needs that position. Another American company may have an immediate need for the same employee's skills. Under the current system, the second company has a reasonable opportunity to complete its hiring process and file the necessary petition. Without the grace period, even a short gap between jobs could complicate that transition. The result may be that an American business loses access to a qualified candidate who is already in the country and legally eligible to pursue employment through the H-1B process.

It is difficult to see how making this transition more complicated benefits American employers or workers. The government should distinguish between preventing misuse of a visa program and creating unnecessary obstacles to legitimate hiring.

Second, the change could weaken competition between employers. When workers have fewer practical options to change jobs, their current employers gain additional bargaining power. This can reduce pressure on employers to offer competitive wages and working conditions. It could also make workers more reluctant to report labor violations. If protecting wages and preventing employer abuse are important policy objectives, DHS should examine whether removing the grace period would work against those objectives.

Third, I question whether the administrative benefits justify the disruption. DHS identifies administrative burden as a reason for the proposed change, but removing one step from the immigration adjudication process does not necessarily reduce the total burden on the government. A more difficult job-transition process could lead to additional filings, requests for discretionary relief, departures followed by new visa applications, or enforcement proceedings. These costs should be evaluated together, rather than considering only the work saved during individual petition adjudications.

Fourth, the proposal should be supported by evidence of a problem that cannot be addressed through narrower measures. If DHS has identified misuse of the current grace period, it should explain the nature and scale of that misuse. The existing rule is already discretionary, time-limited, and does not permit unauthorized employment. Those are meaningful safeguards. Eliminating the provision entirely seems broader than necessary unless DHS can demonstrate that these safeguards are insufficient.

There is also a question of regulatory consistency. The government introduced the grace period in 2017 to improve employment mobility and provide flexibility during job transitions. If those benefits were considered important enough to establish the rule, DHS should explain what evidence has changed and why the original reasoning is no longer valid. A change in policy direction alone does not answer that question.

I would encourage DHS to consider alternatives that preserve the grace period while addressing any legitimate administrative concerns. Clearer documentation requirements, standardized methods for verifying employment termination dates, or more efficient adjudication procedures could help without creating additional barriers to lawful employment transitions.

Ultimately, I believe this proposal should be evaluated on a straightforward question: What measurable benefit does eliminating the 60-day grace period provide that could not be achieved through a less disruptive approach?

The current provision does not grant permanent status, waive sponsorship requirements, or authorize unauthorized employment. It simply allows a short, controlled period for individuals and employers to complete lawful transitions. Removing it could reduce labor-market flexibility, increase employer leverage, and create additional costs for businesses and government agencies, without a clearly demonstrated improvement in program integrity.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that DHS retain the existing 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and consider more targeted measures to address any documented problems.

Thank you.
comments.reason: The commenter argues against eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing negative impacts on labor market efficiency.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that seeks to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period provided in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to reconsider this proposal and maintain the current regulatory framework.

The Disruption of Immediate Transitions and Family Stability
The proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period fails to account for the logistical realities of the modern labor market and the severe hardships it imposes on families. Transitioning to a new specialized role requires time for interviewing, offer negotiation, and the filing of a new Labor Condition Application (LCA) and visa petition. Treating a highly skilled worker as out of status immediately upon the unexpected cessation of employment creates deeply destabilizing conditions.

This burden falls disproportionately on families with dependent children. An immediate loss of status abruptly severs a child's access to their school—often mid-academic year—and destabilizes their established community ties. Without a transition window, parents are unable to arrange for the continuity of pediatric healthcare or manage a coordinated educational transfer. Instead of a systematic transition to a new employer or an orderly departure, families are forced into sudden, chaotic upheavals while scrambling to unwind long-term financial commitments such as leases and mortgages. The 60-day buffer is an essential, practical necessity that prevents children from bearing the brunt of sudden administrative displacement.

Impact on U.S. Economic Competitiveness
The discretionary grace period was implemented to enhance job portability and stability for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers. By removing this buffer, the proposed rule inadvertently undermines U.S. competitiveness. When workforce reductions occur, the 60-day window allows other American companies to retain specialized, in-demand talent within the U.S. economy. Forcing these skilled workers to immediately depart the country disrupts technology hiring pipelines and ultimately harms the domestic employers who actively rely on this talent pool.

Addressing DHS's Rationale
While DHS cites a reduction in administrative burdens as a rationale for this change, this must be weighed against the significant economic and social disruptions it will cause. Industry estimates indicate that removing the grace period could generate substantial annual net economic costs, which far outweigh the anticipated administrative savings. Furthermore, placing workers in immediate legal jeopardy upon termination creates an imbalanced workforce dynamic that discourages long-term investment in the U.S. economy by highly skilled professionals.

For nearly a decade, workers and employers have relied on this 60-day grace period to make long-term housing, education, and employment decisions. Punishing legal, highly skilled immigrants and their families with immediate loss of status upon cessation of employment is unjust and economically counterproductive.

I strongly urge DHS to abandon this proposal and preserve the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes eliminating the grace period, citing severe hardships for workers and families.

Subject: Please Do Not Eliminate the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I strongly urge policymakers not to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers.

I moved to the United States eight years ago with the hope of building a better future through hard work and professional opportunities. During these eight years, I have built my life here, purchased a home, and started a family. My son was born in the United States, and this country is the only home he has ever known.

As an Indian national, I am already facing an extremely long and uncertain green card process, with no clear timeline for when I will receive permanent residency. Many Indian professionals have spent years, sometimes decades, waiting in the green card backlog while continuing to contribute to the U.S. economy, pay taxes, purchase homes, and raise their families.

Eliminating the 60-day grace period would create enormous uncertainty and unnecessary hardship for thousands of families like mine. If someone loses their job, finding another employer and completing the necessary immigration process within a very limited timeframe is not always possible. Without this grace period, losing a job could mean being forced to leave the country, regardless of how many years we have invested in building our lives here.

The consequences would extend beyond individual families. Many H-1B professionals have purchased homes, taken out long-term mortgages, invested in local communities, and made significant financial commitments. Forcing families to leave the country on short notice could result in distressed home sales, mortgage defaults, financial losses, and increased instability in the U.S. housing market. It could also negatively affect local economies, businesses, schools, and communities.

We are not asking for special treatment or an exemption from immigration laws. We are simply asking for a reasonable transition period that allows hardworking professionals to find new employment and maintain their legal status during an already stressful situation.

Please consider the human, economic, and long-term consequences before eliminating this important protection.

The 60-day grace period provides essential flexibility, stability, and dignity to families who have spent years contributing to this country. Please preserve the discretionary 60-day grace period and do not put thousands of American-born children and their families at risk of losing the lives they have built here.

My suggestion: Keep the personal story about your U.S.-born son and your home. Those details make the comment more powerful because they demonstrate that this is not just an employment policy issue; it is also about family stability, housing, and the future of children growing up in America.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly urges policymakers not to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the existing up-to-60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers following the termination of their employment. For families like mine, this grace period is far more than an opportunity to seek new employment. It provides a reasonable and essential transition period to make informed, lawful decisions and navigate an unexpected disruption with dignity and stability.

My family has lived legally in the United States since 2009. Over the years, we have worked, paid taxes, purchased a home, contributed to our community, and built our lives here. We are raising a nine-year-old U.S. citizen child who was born in this country and attends school here. After nearly 17 years in the United States, this is the only home our child has ever known.

An unexpected job loss is already a significant financial and emotional challenge. Eliminating the grace period would add an enormous layer of uncertainty and distress by potentially forcing families to make life-altering decisions within an extremely short timeframe. Selling or managing a home, addressing financial obligations, closing accounts, arranging international travel, and preparing a child to leave their school, friends, and familiar environment cannot realistically be accomplished in a matter of days. Even when departure becomes necessary, families deserve a reasonable opportunity to make those arrangements responsibly.

The existing grace period provides this essential flexibility. It allows eligible workers to explore alternative lawful immigration or employment options, understand their circumstances, and, if necessary, prepare for an orderly departure. It does not exempt anyone from immigration laws or regulatory requirements. Rather, it acknowledges the practical realities of people's lives and provides a reasonable transition period for individuals and families who have otherwise complied with U.S. immigration laws.

If the DHS believes that changes to the existing grace period are necessary, I encourage consideration of reasonable alternatives rather than completely eliminating this provision. For example, the duration of the grace period could be determined, in part, by the number of years an individual has legally lived and worked in the United States. Alternatively, the existing 60-day period could be reduced to 45 days as a compromise. These approaches would provide DHS with flexibility to revise the policy while still allowing affected workers and their families a reasonable amount of time to make necessary arrangements. Completely eliminating the grace period, however, could create immediate immigration uncertainty and place law-abiding families at risk of losing their lawful status without adequate time to explore available options or prepare for departure. A balanced approach would be far more reasonable and humane.

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to consider the broader consequences of this proposed change, particularly for U.S. citizen children who may have spent their entire lives in the United States and have little or no experience living in another country. Such a change could abruptly disrupt their education, social development, emotional well-being, and sense of stability.

The impact would also be particularly severe for employment-based immigrants who have spent many years waiting for permanent residency due to significant green card backlogs. Many of these individuals and their families have established deep roots in the United States while continuing to maintain lawful immigration status and fulfill their responsibilities. They should not be placed in an unnecessarily vulnerable position because of circumstances beyond their control, such as an unexpected employment termination.

I am genuinely grateful for the opportunities my family has received in this country, and I fully recognize the importance of maintaining clear and effective immigration policies. However, eliminating this reasonable transition period would create disproportionate hardship for law-abiding workers and their families without adequately accounting for the real-life consequences.

I strongly urge the DHS to withdraw the proposed elimination and retain the existing up-to-60-day grace period. If revisions are considered necessary, I encourage DHS to explore alternatives such as a service-based grace period or a reasonable reduction to 45 days rather than eliminating this important protection altogether. This provision offers a practical, humane, and balanced approach that protects families from unnecessary disruption while continuing to uphold U.S. immigration laws.

Thank you for considering the experiences and concerns of affected workers and their families.

Respectfully submitted,
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes eliminating the grace period, arguing it harms families facing unexpected job loss.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose removing the up to 60-day discretionary grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and urge USCIS to keep it.

1. Layoffs are not the worker’s fault. Restructurings, budget cuts and project cancellations happen often, especially in technology. Workers who have followed every rule should not fall out of status the moment an employer makes a business decision they had no part in.

2. Sixty days is already very short. In that time a worker has to find a new job, interview, receive an offer, and wait for the new employer to get a certified LCA and file a petition. Removing the grace period would make a lawful transition nearly impossible and push workers into rushed or unsuitable filings, or into leaving the country abruptly.

3. It harms U.S. employers. Companies depend on hiring experienced professionals who are already in the U.S. and already vetted. With no grace period, employers lose that talent pool and face more delays, more consular processing and higher costs.

4. It harms families and communities. Workers have leases, mortgages, children in school and spouses with their own commitments. Forcing them to leave on short notice causes serious financial loss and disruption, both for the families and for the communities they live in.

5. The grace period is already discretionary. USCIS already reviews each case and can deny the grace period where there is misuse. The current rule gives the agency the tools it needs to address abuse, so removing it entirely punishes the large majority of compliant workers.

6. It reverses a balanced policy that has worked. DHS created the grace period in 2017 to improve job portability and retention for high-skilled workers. The reasons behind it are just as valid today.

If DHS goes forward anyway, I urge it at least to (a) keep a grace period for involuntary job loss such as layoffs and restructurings, and (b) apply any change only to employment that ends after a final rule takes effect, with a meaningful transition period.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes removing the grace period and provides several reasons why keeping it is necessary.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To: U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS)

I strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the existing 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and other affected employment-based nonimmigrant visa holders.

The 60-day grace period is an essential safeguard that provides highly skilled foreign professionals with a reasonable opportunity to find new employment, secure a qualifying H-1B transfer, explore other lawful immigration options, or make arrangements to depart the United States responsibly.

Losing employment is already an extremely stressful and financially challenging experience. Eliminating the grace period would turn an employment-related setback into an immediate immigration crisis, placing thousands of hardworking professionals and their families at unnecessary risk.

I urge DHS to consider the following concerns:

1. Unfair hardship during unexpected job loss

2. Sixty days is already a limited period to secure new employment

3. Negative impact on U.S. employers and businesses

4. Severe consequences for families and H-4 dependents

5. Financial and emotional hardship

6. The proposal undermines the purpose of attracting highly skilled global talent

7. The proposed change is disproportionate to the administrative burden it seeks to address

8. The rule creates unnecessary uncertainty and discourages long-term stability

My Recommendations to DHS

I respectfully request that DHS:

Withdraw the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

Preserve the existing provision allowing eligible H-1B workers and affected dependents up to 60 days, or until the end of their authorized validity period, whichever is shorter.

Recognize that unexpected job loss does not necessarily reflect an individual's ability, professional qualifications, or willingness to comply with U.S. immigration laws.

Continue allowing eligible workers a reasonable opportunity to secure new employment, file qualifying immigration petitions, pursue other lawful immigration options, or arrange an orderly departure.

Consider the significant economic, social, financial, and family consequences before implementing any policy that removes this protection.

Conclusion

The 60-day grace period is not an unnecessary benefit. It is a reasonable and essential transition safeguard for professionals who have followed U.S. immigration laws and contributed to the country's economy.

People should not be forced to abandon their careers, homes, children's education, and established lives in the United States simply because they unexpectedly lose their jobs.

A fair immigration system should protect national interests while also recognizing the contributions, dignity, and legitimate circumstances of the people who work and build their lives in this country.

I strongly urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and retain the existing 60-day grace period for eligible H-1B workers and other affected nonimmigrant visa holders.

Thank you for considering my comments.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states they strongly oppose the rule to eliminate the grace period, citing hardships for workers and families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the discretionary grace period in 8 CFR § 214.1(l)(2). I support immigration enforcement and program integrity, but eliminating this limited protection would impose substantial costs on compliant workers, U.S. employers, and families without a sufficiently demonstrated public benefit.

Workers can lose jobs for reasons beyond their control: AI-driven restructuring, automation, mergers, budget cuts, and market conditions. A skilled worker who has maintained status and followed the rules should have a reasonable opportunity to seek another qualifying employer or arrange departure. The current period is capped at 60 days (or the end of authorized validity, if earlier), is discretionary, and does not itself grant work authorization. It is a narrow transition mechanism, not open-ended permission to remain.

Recruiting, interviewing, conducting background checks, securing approvals, and preparing an H-1B petition can take weeks, even when an employer urgently needs a specialist. Eliminating the protection could force qualified workers abroad while employers attempt to hire them, adding consular, travel, and onboarding delays. In cybersecurity, healthcare technology, engineering, and AI, such disruption can affect projects, customers, and critical services. DHS should quantify these costs rather than assume replacements will be readily available.

DHS's impact analysis does not demonstrate that benefits outweigh costs. The proposal recognizes lost wages, travel, lease termination, employer productivity losses, and potential additional proceedings, yet lists annualized monetized costs and benefits as "Not Estimated." DHS reports an annual average of approximately 3,795 new-employer I-129 filings within its estimated 60-day window for FY 2021–2025, while acknowledging that petition withdrawals are an imperfect proxy and its data cannot identify everyone who used the grace period. These limitations make the full impact uncertain. Before repeal, DHS should estimate effects on employer hiring, tax contributions, family stability, public resources, and the costs of departure and reentry.

DHS cites officers' time spent verifying when employment ended and whether the grace period applies. But eliminating the protection would transfer costs and uncertainty to workers and employers. DHS should evaluate standardized termination notices, clearer evidence rules, improved employer reporting, and targeted scrutiny of fraud or unauthorized work. The current regulation already allows DHS to shorten or eliminate the period in individual cases. DHS should explain why those tools and less disruptive options cannot meet its objectives.

The grace period also helps workers leave unsuitable employment without being forced to choose between remaining with a particular sponsor and an abrupt immigration disruption. Removing it could weaken workers' bargaining power and discourage reporting of workplace violations, potentially undermining labor protections for U.S. and foreign workers alike. DHS should examine these risks and whether repeal could inadvertently increase employers' leverage over sponsored workers.

Workers and their dependents may have leases, mortgages, school enrollment, healthcare needs, and other obligations. Job loss is difficult enough; removing time to plan a lawful transition compounds the harm. People and businesses have made decisions in reliance on this regulation since 2017. DHS should separately assess the disruption caused by repeal rather than attributing it entirely to the underlying layoff.

AI makes flexibility more important, not less. Technology is changing job requirements quickly. The grace period gives skilled workers a limited opportunity to move to U.S. employers needing their expertise instead of turning a temporary layoff into a loss of domestic talent. Finally, DHS should evaluate how repeal would affect hiring in different industries and regions, including states with major technology, healthcare, engineering, and research employers. National averages can conceal concentrated harm to specialized employers and local communities. An absence of state-level estimates should not be treated as evidence that no meaningful local impact exists.

I ask DHS to (a) retain 8 CFR § 214.1(l)(2); (b) provide a fuller quantitative cost-benefit, regional, and family-impact analysis; (c) meaningfully assess less restrictive administrative alternatives; and (d) address the reliance interests and labor-market consequences for lawful workers and U.S. employers. Immigration integrity and a short, enforceable transition period are compatible. A job loss should not automatically become an immediate immigration crisis.

Re: USCIS-2026-0364 — Opposition to Eliminating the 60-Day Grace Period

I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other employment-based nonimmigrant workers. As an H-1B professional in the United States, I believe this change would harm not only lawful immigrants, but also American employers, universities, and the economy.

America’s prosperity is inseparable from its ability to attract talented people from around the world. Immigrants have helped build businesses, advance scientific research, strengthen financial markets, create jobs, and support communities. The ability to welcome ambitious people and give them a fair opportunity to contribute is one of America’s greatest strengths.

Many H-1B professionals first came as international students. We paid substantial tuition, often far more than in-state students, as well as rent, living expenses, and taxes. Our families invested years of savings in our education. We then navigated competitive recruiting, visa uncertainty, and demanding careers to earn the opportunity to work legally in this country. According to NAFSA, international students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported over 355,000 jobs in the 2024–25 academic year. These contributions extend far beyond tuition payments.

Students considering an American education must weigh its cost against their future opportunities. If even graduates who secure lawful employment can suddenly lose a reasonable chance to find another job after an unexpected layoff, the return on that investment becomes less predictable. Some will choose other countries. American universities, local businesses, and employers could ultimately lose talent and revenue as a result.

A layoff is not a moral failure or evidence that someone’s skills no longer matter. Companies reduce staff because of mergers, restructuring, budget cuts, or economic conditions beyond employees’ control. Yet ending the grace period could turn one such event into an immediate immigration crisis for a person who has spent years studying, working, paying taxes, and building a life here.

In finance, technology, healthcare, and other specialized fields, hiring often requires multiple interviews, background checks, internal approvals, and immigration filings. These processes cannot reasonably be completed overnight. A limited 60-day period helps American companies retain access to qualified candidates who are already here. Removing it could also increase workers’ dependence on a single employer, making them less willing to report mistreatment or change jobs.

DHS has legitimate interests in enforcing immigration rules and limiting administrative burdens. But the existing grace period is already capped at 60 days, is discretionary, and does not create unlimited work authorization. Rather than removing this safeguard entirely, DHS should explain why less disruptive approaches would not meet its objectives and fully assess the consequences for employers, universities, and affected workers.

Behind every visa is a person, and often a family, that has made enormous sacrifices. Many of us chose America because we believed in its opportunities, its openness, and the promise that hard work and lawful participation could build a future. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Statement Opposing the Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period for Nonimmigrant Workers

To: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS)

I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider any proposal to eliminate the existing 60-day grace period for certain nonimmigrant workers following the termination of their employment.

The 60-day grace period serves a critical purpose: it provides highly skilled foreign professionals with a reasonable opportunity to secure new employment, maintain lawful immigration status, and avoid unnecessary disruption to their lives and families.

1. Preventing the Loss of Highly Skilled Talent

Job loss can happen to anyone, regardless of their performance or qualifications. Corporate restructuring, layoffs, budget cuts, and business decisions are often beyond an employee’s control.

Eliminating the 60-day grace period would force highly skilled professionals to find another employer within an extremely short timeframe. Even exceptionally talented individuals need time to interview, receive offers, negotiate terms, and complete immigration formalities.

The United States risks losing valuable professionals, not because they lack the skills or willingness to contribute, but because they are not given a reasonable opportunity to transition between jobs.

2. Maintaining the United States as a Destination for Global Talent

The United States has long attracted some of the world’s brightest professionals. However, attracting global talent requires not only career opportunities but also a predictable and stable immigration framework.

Professionals considering moving to the United States evaluate the long-term security of their careers and families. If an unexpected job loss could immediately jeopardize their ability to remain in the country, many talented individuals may think twice before choosing the United States.

This uncertainty could make the country less competitive in attracting and retaining international talent, particularly when other nations are actively competing for the same skilled professionals.

3. Protecting Families and Children’s Futures

Behind every skilled professional is often a family that has built a life in the United States. Many have spent years establishing careers, purchasing homes, paying taxes, contributing to communities, and raising children.

Their children attend local schools, build friendships, and develop their futures around the stability of their lives here.

An unexpected employment change should not put an entire family’s future at risk. Eliminating the grace period could force families to uproot their lives, disrupt their children’s education, leave established communities, and abandon years of personal and professional investment.

The 60-day period provides a reasonable opportunity to navigate an unexpected employment situation without immediately placing an entire family in uncertainty.

4. A Reasonable Transition Period Benefits Everyone

Sixty days is a limited and practical window, not an indefinite immigration benefit. It allows qualified professionals to pursue opportunities and prospective employers to complete interviews, internal approvals, background checks, and necessary immigration paperwork.

A talented individual can often secure another position and continue contributing to the American economy, provided they are given sufficient time to do so.

Without this opportunity, the country risks turning a temporary employment transition into a permanent loss of skilled talent.

Conclusion and Request

I respectfully urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period and consider the broader consequences of eliminating it for the American workforce, global competitiveness, and families.

Losing a job should not immediately erase the years of professional contribution, economic investment, and personal commitment that an individual and their family have made to the United States.

The 60-day grace period strikes a reasonable balance between immigration compliance and the practical realities of employment. It gives individuals an opportunity to find new employment while allowing the United States to retain professionals who are willing and qualified to continue contributing to its economy.

Sixty days is not an unreasonable extension of opportunity. It is a reasonable safeguard that allows talented individuals to overcome an unexpected employment setback, continue contributing to the country, and preserve the stability of their families.

I strongly encourage DHS to preserve this important provision and avoid a policy change that could result in the unnecessary departure of highly skilled professionals and the disruption of countless families.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly urges DHS to reconsider and keep the existing 60-day grace period.

Dear Department of Homeland Security and USCIS,

Thank you for providing the opportunity to share public comments on the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

Many employment-based visa holders have spent years building their lives in the United States. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Dennis Ma
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (91 FR 57807)

I write as an individual to oppose the proposed rule. My objection is different in kind from most: the proposal identifies no problem it actually solves, and its predictable effect is to undermine the orderly compliance and enforcement visibility that the current regulation provides.

1. The grace period cannot be "abused" in any way the proposal documents. The 60 days under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) carry no employment authorization and confer no benefit. A worker in the grace period may only look for a new employer, prepare to depart, or pursue a lawful change of status. The proposed rule identifies no documented pattern — no data, no enforcement statistics — showing that workers use these 60 days for anything else. A provision that grants nothing but time cannot be gamed, and an undocumented premise is not a basis for repeal.

2. Elimination converts orderly departures into overstays and absconders. Today, a laid-off worker who cannot find a new sponsor uses the grace period to close out a lease, withdraw children from school, and leave the country in compliance — at a known address, visible in DHS systems throughout. Repeal does not make that worker leave faster; it makes him out of status on the day his job ends. Faced with the choice between an abrupt, chaotic departure and remaining while a pending transition resolves, some workers will remain — now at no current address on file and far harder for ICE to locate. The population DHS says it wants to police becomes less visible, not more. A policy that manufactures absconders out of compliant departures works against interior enforcement, not for it.

3. The immediate harm falls on Americans who never appear in the impact analysis. H-1B physicians — including Conrad waiver doctors serving in health professional shortage areas — nurses, and other essential workers who lose a position through a hospital closure, a funding cut, or a practice collapse would be out of status the same day, in the middle of treating U.S. patients. A rural hospital cannot replace a physician in zero days. The proposal counts costs to the workers; it does not count the cancelled clinics and interrupted care in the communities they serve.

4. Visibility is an enforcement asset the current rule supplies for free. During the grace period the worker remains documented: address on file, employer of record known, departure or new petition tracked. That is exactly the posture an enforcement agency should want from a population in transition. Repeal trades that posture for instant noncompliance at scale, with no corresponding gain identified anywhere in the proposal.

For these reasons, the proposed rule should be withdrawn. If DHS believes the grace period is being misused, it should first publish the evidence and propose a remedy proportioned to the documented problem.

Dennis Ma

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jeremy Carson
comments.commentText:
DHS's administrative burden analysis must distinguish between immigration filings that could potentially involve consideration of the grace period and cases in which the grace period was actually invoked or required additional adjudicative work.

The total number of Forms I-129, I-539, I-485, and I-765 filed cannot automatically be treated as the number of cases generating additional administrative burden attributable to the grace-period regulation.

These are different statistical categories.

DHS should disclose:

1. The number of potentially affected filings.
2. The number of cases in which the grace period was actually applicable.
3. The number of cases requiring additional adjudicator review.
4. The average additional adjudicator time per affected case.
5. The number of cases in which the grace period was shortened or eliminated.
6. The actual incremental administrative cost attributable to the existing regulation.

Without these distinctions, the Department risks overstating the administrative burden and understating the consequences of rescission.

A rulemaking based on an inaccurate or insufficiently explained factual premise raises concerns under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).

DHS should publish its underlying methodology and supporting data before proceeding.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Instead of eliminating 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and ending the up-to-60-day grace period, DHS should adopt the less harmful regulatory alternative it already identified in Section IV.E of the proposed rule. There, DHS acknowledges that standardized evidence requirements "may ostensibly reduce administrative burden." Requiring a simple employer statement of the last day of employment would resolve DHS's administrative concerns while preserving stability for workers, families, and U.S. employers. Relying on the data and statements in the proposed rule itself, I respectfully oppose this proposal and urge DHS to withdraw it and retain 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

THE CLAIMED REDUCTION IN ADMINISTRATIVE BURDEN IS UNQUANTIFIED AND MAY NOT HAPPEN (Section IV.C, footnote 29, Table 2)
The primary rationale for removing the grace period is unsubstantiated by the rule's own findings:

DHS states it "cannot estimate the time this analysis adds to each adjudication," and the accounting statement lists monetized benefits as "Not Estimated."

Extension and change-of-status requests generally require that the beneficiary maintained status (8 CFR 214.1(c)(4); 8 CFR 248.1). Adjudicators would still need to determine when prior employment ended, requiring the exact same evidence review DHS describes as burdensome.

DHS acknowledges the rule would increase NTAs, EOIR referrals, and workload for DOJ and ICE (Section V.A.3.c), shifting the burden to other agencies rather than removing it.

THE GRACE PERIOD IS USED FOR ITS INTENDED, LAWFUL PURPOSE (Section V.A.2, Table 3; Section IV.B, footnote 26)
The grace period was adopted in the 2016 rule (81 FR 82398) implementing AC21—the same law in which Congress created H-1B portability (INA 214(n)), showing congressional support for workers moving between employers. DHS's data show that from FY 2021 to FY 2025, 328,758 primary beneficiaries lost or changed jobs. During the grace period, they made lawful filings to remain in status, exactly as the 2016 rule intended:

18,975 had a new Form I-129 filed by a new employer;

5,596 filed Form I-539;

1,924 filed Form I-485; and

49 requested a compelling-circumstances EAD.

By contrast, DHS reports only 37 NTAs in FY 2025 for H-1B workers who failed to maintain status beyond the grace period, and presents no data showing that the grace period has been abused. Limited grace periods are also consistent with the statute and other DHS rules (Section IV.B, footnote 26), which keep comparable periods elsewhere: 60 days for F-1 students after completing their studies (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(iv)), 30 days for J-1 exchange visitors (8 CFR 214.2(j)(1)(ii)), and the 10-day period in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(1) that this proposal leaves in place.

SIGNIFICANT UNMEASURED COSTS, IMPRACTICAL DEPARTURE RULES, AND RELIANCE INTERESTS (Sections IV.D, V.A.3, V.B, V.F)
Removing the grace period imposes severe harms while listing total costs as "Not Estimated":

Impractical Departure Requirement (Section IV.D, footnote 32): A worker and family would need to depart "on the day of the cessation of the employment" to avoid falling out of status. Because workers often learn of a layoff the day it takes effect, a family cannot reasonably end a lease, withdraw children from school, and arrange international travel within hours. Footnote 13 acknowledges that falling out of status can lead to unlawful presence, negative discretionary factors, and bars to adjustment of status under INA 245(c)(2).

Worker and Family Costs (Sections V.A.3, V.B, V.F): DHS estimates a median wage of $131,000 for affected H-1B workers and potential lost income of up to $21,877 per worker (footnote 54) for about 3,795 workers per year. Table 4 shows an average of 208,187 dependents approved each year in these classifications. Spouses with work authorization (H-4, L-2, E) would also lose their jobs when the principal's job ends, yet the Family Assessment concludes there is no negative effect on family well-being.

Employer and Small Entity Costs: In FY 2025, 2,886 employers filed for workers during the grace period, of which 1,852 (64%) were small entities (Table 5). Additionally, H-1B and O-1 employers would newly bear return-transportation costs (INA 214(c)(5)).

Reliance Interests (Section IV.D): In effect since January 17, 2017, the grace period has been relied upon by workers who bought homes, paid taxes, and planned careers and family life around it, and by employers who made business arrangements based on it. DHS calls this reliance "misplaced" because the grace period is discretionary, even though DHS itself states in Section IV.C that "many cases might result in grants."

For these reasons, I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and retain 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

Critical Impact on Healthcare and Technology Infrastructure

The integration of technology and healthcare is one of the fastest-growing and most sensitive sectors in the United States. Eliminating the 60-day grace period directly threatens the stability of these systems.

I respectfully oppose any proposal to eliminate or substantially shorten the grace period available to H-1B workers following the loss of employment.
