Dear Desk Officer, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period," published on September 11, 2026. Stripping this cushion callously ignores public reliance interests, destabilizes long-term legal immigrant families, breaks statutory portability frameworks, and exposes vulnerable workers to severe employer abuse.
DHS must consider the profound reliance interests of families rooted permanently under the current framework. I am a homeowner, taxpayer, and active community member. Both my spouse and I have resided legally in the United States for over a decade, arriving individually to pursue our Master’s degrees at American universities. I previously worked directly on an H-1B visa and transitioned to an H-4 EAD, while my spouse has maintained continuous H-1B status, working at the same company for nearly a decade in Software Engineering. We purchased our home several years ago. Throughout our entire careers, we have worked exclusively as direct, internal corporate employees—never through third-party IT consultancies, staffing agencies, or at external client sites. My spouse holds an established, long-standing, nearly a decade-old green card priority date. Together, we are a dual-income, high-skilled household that has done everything right.
Despite our strict compliance, my career stability has been repeatedly challenged by inefficiencies outside my control, including corporate PERM delays. Due to market fluctuations entirely beyond my individual control, I have been personally subjected to two separate corporate layoffs—the first citing macroeconomic conditions, and the second due to an abrupt, company-wide structural reorganization. Because these were direct corporate roles, these layoffs prove that no position is immune to market fluctuations, demonstrating why a regulatory cushion is vital to protect compliant households from sudden economic shifts. Eliminating the 60-day window creates compounding risk; because the immigration system penalizes applicants by prioritizing green card allocation based on country of birth first, and only chronologically by priority date within capped individual country pools, a single sudden restructuring at my spouse’s employer would instantly uproot our lives on zero days' notice despite our nearly a decade-old priority date, placing our home and savings at immediate risk.
Overnight departure is a physical impossibility. Wrapping up a life requires time to sell property, break lease agreements, settle financial obligations, liquidate assets, and close bank accounts. More critically, a zero-day departure window completely ignores acute medical and family dependencies. If enacted, a sudden layoff would strip away a family's legal status instantly, forcing individuals mid-treatment for chronic illnesses or families navigating high-risk pregnancies to immediately board long-haul international flights on zero days' notice. This shatters all continuity of care and severely endangers health by prioritizing immediate removal over basic human safety. Furthermore, for households with school-aged children, many of whom are U.S. citizens born here, an abrupt educational disruption on zero days' notice would inflict severe emotional and academic trauma.
The rule also creates a structural contradiction with statutory portability provisions under the AC21 Act. Layoffs are unexpected events. It is logistically impossible for a new hiring employer to instantly file and secure an agency receipt notice for a visa transfer on the exact day of termination. Zero-day status effectively destroys statutory portability. Furthermore, tying status entirely to an employment's final millisecond hands coercive leverage to unscrupulous employers. Highly skilled professionals will become too terrified to report wage theft or safety violations out of fear of immediate retaliatory firing and subsequent overnight deportation.
Removing the grace period will vastly increase federal burdens by triggering a surge in emergency, defensive filings to USCIS, while flooding enforcement agencies with unnecessary removal proceedings for individuals who could otherwise find lawful openings within weeks. Ultimately, stripping this window permanently drives elite, U.S.-educated technical innovation to competitive foreign markets, creating massive hiring gaps for domestic U.S. employers. DHS has failed to demonstrate a compelling justification for reversing this stabilizing policy. I urge the Department to honor the public's reliance interests, protect vulnerable families, and preserve American innovation by withdrawing this proposed rule in its entirety.
Sincerely,
A Concerned Homeowner and High-Skilled Professional

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Opposition to Proposed Rule Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364)
To the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS):
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers, including H-1B visa holders.
Many H-1B workers have lived and worked lawfully in the United States for many years, often waiting in lengthy green card backlogs while building their lives here. Throughout this time, these workers contribute essential skills to American companies, support local businesses, and pay federal, state, and local taxes consistently without fail.
Eliminating the 60-day grace period places an unreasonable and destabilizing burden on law-abiding workers and their families. In today’s economy, corporate restructuring and layoffs often happen without advance notice. Without a grace period, an employee who loses their job through no fault of their own falls out of lawful status immediately. Finding a new employer, completing a Labor Condition Application (LCA), and filing an H-1B transfer petition takes several weeks—a process that is virtually impossible to complete in a single day.
Most importantly, this rule severely disrupts families with children enrolled in U.S. schools. Forcing a family to uproot their lives, pull children out of school mid-year, sell property, and leave the country immediately without a reasonable transition window causes profound emotional and financial hardship.
Rather than eliminating the 60-day grace period entirely, I urge DHS to retain this critical safeguard. Keeping the 60-day window protects American businesses by allowing skilled talent to transition smoothly to new roles, upholds basic fairness for taxpayers and their children, and ensures orderly compliance with U.S. immigration laws.
Thank you for your time and consideration of these concerns

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashley Chen
comments.commentText:
I am an international graduate of an American university, currently working in the United States under Optional Practical Training (OPT). I hope to continue my career here and eventually obtain H-1B status.

I came to this country legally. I pursued higher education here, invested years of my life and substantial financial resources into my future, and worked hard to become part of the American workforce.

And yet, despite doing everything through the legal immigration system, I am constantly reminded of how fragile my future in this country could be.

The proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period makes that uncertainty even more alarming.

For someone like me who hopes to transition from OPT to H-1B status, this is not an abstract policy debate. It concerns the conditions under which I may be able to live and work in the future.

If I eventually obtain H-1B status, losing my job could also mean facing an immediate immigration crisis. Without a reasonable grace period, I could have little time to find another employer, pursue another lawful immigration option, or make arrangements to leave the country.

Why should losing a job threaten to uproot an entire life?

Why should workers who have followed the law, contributed to the economy, and built their futures here be placed in such a vulnerable position?

A system that makes a worker's ability to remain in the country so dependent on a single employer also raises serious concerns about workplace exploitation. Workers should not have to choose between tolerating mistreatment and risking their immigration status.

International students are repeatedly encouraged to pursue American education, develop their skills, and contribute to the American economy. But what message does it send when the country that welcomed us as students makes it increasingly difficult for us to build stable careers afterward?

I want to contribute to this country. I want to work, grow professionally, pay taxes, and build a future here. I should not have to live in constant fear that one unexpected change in employment could undo years of effort.

The 60-day grace period provides an important measure of stability for eligible nonimmigrant workers. Eliminating it would make an already uncertain immigration process even more precarious.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jason Komutrattananon
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposed rule and recommend withdrawal. I am a U.S. citizen
commenting as a member of the public; these comments address Sections IV.A
through IV.E of the preamble.

1. THE BURDEN RATIONALE IS CONTRADICTED BY DHS'S OWN DATA.
DHS asserts 1.9 million filings since FY2018 required an initial grace
period assessment (p. 57815). But its own analysis shows only 3,795
beneficiaries annually - 5.77% of 65,752 whose employment ceased -- actually
filed a new I-129 within 60 days (Table 3, p. 57821). The rule never
estimates officer hours saved, and the RIA reports annualized monetized
costs and benefits as "Not Estimated" (Table 2, p. 57817). A rule OMB
designated a "significant regulatory action" (p. 57816) cannot rest its
central justification on an unquantified burden. State Farm requires a
rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.

2. THE BURDEN IS RELOCATED, NOT ELIMINATED.
DHS rejected the "stringent evidentiary requirements" alternative because
officers "would still have the added burden of scrutinizing the
documentation and verifying the end date of the alien's prior employment"
(p. 57816). But under this rule officers must still fix the cessation date
exactly, because that date now determines whether status was maintained.
The same verification task remains, now carrying removal consequences.

3. THE "MISALIGNMENT" RATIONALE PROVES TOO MUCH.
DHS reasons that a grace period "disconnects" status from the eligibility
basis (p. 57813). That logic applies identically to the F-1 60-day
post-completion period and the J-1 30-day period, which DHS expressly
leaves intact (fn. 26, p. 57814). DHS offers no explanation for treating
employment-based nonimmigrants differently from students and exchange
visitors on the same statutory reasoning.

4. "IMMEDIATE DEPARTURE" IS UNDEFINED AND UNADMINISTRABLE.
DHS would treat status as ending "the day after" cessation (p. 57815) and
require departure "immediately" (p. 57814). No regulatory text defines the
interval. A worker terminated on a Friday must obtain travel documents,
break a lease, withdraw children from school, and secure international
passage within hours. The rule converts conduct that is practically
impossible into a status violation as a matter of law.

5. THE RULE DESTROYS H-1B PORTABILITY WITHOUT ANALYSIS.
AC21 sec. 214(n) lets an H-1B begin new employment on filing a nonfrivolous
petition (p. 57822). Portability presupposes maintained status. If status
ends the day after termination, the worker is out of status before any
petition can be filed. DHS's answer -- that the alien may "apply for
readmission" (p. 57814) -- does not preserve portability and does not
address sec. 214(n) at all.

6. IMMIGRATION CONSEQUENCES ARE SEVERE AND UNANALYZED.
Footnote 13 concedes exposure to unlawful presence and the 3- and 10-year
bars under INA sec. 212(a)(9)(B) (p. 57811). A one-day delay in departure
can produce a multi-year bar. Neither the preamble nor the RIA analyzes
this cost.

7. THE FAMILY ASSESSMENT IS CIRCULAR.
DHS finds family impact "negligible" because any financial effect "would
not stem from this rulemaking but rather, is incidental to the alien's ...
obligation ... to depart" (p. 57827). The immediate-departure obligation is
created by this rule. Attributing the rule's own effect to pre-existing law
does not satisfy 5 U.S.C. 654.

8. RELIANCE INTERESTS ARE UNDERSTATED AND GROWING.
Grace period use rose from 2,138 (FY2021) to 5,178 (FY2025), and I-539
change-of-status filings within the grace period rose from 258 to 2,733 --
a tenfold increase (Table 3). This is a codified entitlement in force since
January 17, 2017, not discretionary forbearance. Wages & White Lion
(fn. 34) concerns enforcement discretion and does not govern a published
regulation.

9. THE RFA CONCLUSION CONTRADICTS THE RULE'S OWN TABLE.
DHS finds "no significant economic impact on substantial number of small
entities" (p. 57826) while identifying 1,852 of 2,886 affected petitioners
-- 64% -- as small entities (Table 5).

10. TRANSITION IS UNADDRESSED.
The rule states no effective date and no treatment for individuals in an
active grace period on that date. DHS should specify both.

CONCLUSION
For these reasons the rule should be withdrawn. At minimum, DHS must
quantify the claimed burden, define "immediate," address INA sec. 214(n),
and reconcile its treatment of F-1 and J-1 grace periods.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the proposed rule and recommends its withdrawal.

I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers.

Many of us came to the United States as F-1 students, completed our education here, transitioned to H-1B status, and spent nearly a decade or more building our careers and families. We have followed immigration laws, paid taxes, and contributed to the American economy.

An unexpected layoff due to company restructuring, financial difficulties, or project cancellations can happen to anyone. Eliminating the grace period would severely impact workers and their families for circumstances completely outside their control.

What about children who have spent most of their lives in the United States? They attend American schools, have friends here, and have adapted to American culture. Expecting families to suddenly relocate to another country would disrupt their education, friendships, financial stability, and entire way of life.

Finding another job is not an overnight process. Interviews, background checks, employer approvals, and H-1B petition preparation can take several weeks. Even 60 days can be challenging, especially for professionals in specialized industries.

The 60-day grace period was introduced to provide reasonable flexibility during unexpected employment transitions. Many families have made long-term commitments based on existing immigration regulations.

Rather than eliminating the grace period, DHS could consider an alternative approach. For example, workers could pay a reasonable, one-time, nonrefundable administrative fee within 48 hours of termination to request the existing 60-day period. Subject to legal authority, the funds collected could support additional administrative processing, employment verification, and compliance monitoring. This could help address administrative burdens while protecting workers and their families.

We are not asking for special treatment or permanent immigration status. We are simply requesting a reasonable opportunity to find another employer after an unexpected job loss.

I respectfully urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period and consider practical alternatives instead of eliminating a protection that thousands of workers and families rely upon.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I oppose the proposed elimination of the up to 60-day discretionary grace period and urge DHS to retain 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

An unexpected loss of employment should not deprive otherwise compliant workers and their dependents of a reasonable opportunity to arrange their next lawful steps. Finding a qualifying employer, completing interviews, obtaining legal advice, and preparing an immigration filing all take time. Workers also need time to arrange an orderly departure when continued lawful stay is not feasible.

The existing grace period is limited and does not itself authorize employment. Retaining it therefore provides a practical transition without creating an unrestricted right to remain or work in the United States. Eliminating it could increase rushed or incomplete filings and make orderly compliance more difficult.

The proposal could also disrupt employers seeking to recruit qualified workers already in the United States and families dealing with housing, schooling, and relocation after an unexpected job loss. These effects deserve careful consideration alongside any claimed reduction in administrative burden.

Before making any change, DHS should provide a fuller assessment of the costs to workers, dependents, and employers, explain why existing discretion is insufficient, and evaluate less disruptive alternatives such as clearer guidance and more consistent administration of the current provision.

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw this proposal and preserve the up to 60-day discretionary grace period. Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes the elimination of the 60-day grace period and urges DHS to retain it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other employment-based nonimmigrant workers, and to ask DHS to consider what it would mean for their families.

I am the spouse of an H-1B worker and hold H-4 status. [We have lived in the United States for more than a decade.] My immigration status, and my family’s stability, depend entirely on my spouse’s employment. When a worker loses a job through a layoff, dependents have no ability to protect themselves or to influence what happens next.

1. Dependents lose their footing the moment the worker does. Under the current rule, the grace period gives a family time to make an orderly plan. Without it, a layoff could put an entire household out of status immediately, even though no one in the family did anything wrong.

2. Families make long-term commitments in reliance on this rule. Leases, mortgages, [children’s schooling, my own work or studies,] and community ties are built on the expectation that a job loss will not mean immediate loss of status. Ending the grace period changes the risk of those commitments after the fact.

3. The cost falls on people who did nothing wrong. Layoffs are an ordinary part of the economy. People who are laid off, and the family members who depend on them, should have a reasonable window to find a new sponsoring employer before facing status consequences.

4. Dependents deserve their own analysis. The proposal covers spouses and children, but the public discussion has focused mostly on workers. I ask DHS to study and publish the specific effects on dependents before moving forward.

I respectfully request that DHS:

Retain the 60-day grace period.
If DHS changes it, make it a fixed, non-discretionary period instead of eliminating it, so families can plan with certainty.
Include transition protections for anyone whose employment ended, or whose pending filings were made, before any effective date.
Assess and publish the impact on dependents.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that eliminating the grace period harms families and leaves dependents with no time to plan.
